title: CE/ME 507 — Class Notes
text:
Welcome
These are the class notes for CE/ME 507: Finite Element Methods, one chapter per class period.
The notes move from a pair of concrete engineering problems — a loaded beam and a heated circuit board — to the boundary value problem they share, then build the full machinery to solve such problems approximately: the strong and weak forms (and their equivalence in both directions), the Galerkin method, basis functions and Lagrange polynomials, the resulting discrete matrix system, element-wise assembly and sparsity, the isoparametric map and its Jacobian, and finally quadrature and assembly on a real mesh via the IEN array.
Figures are generated programmatically rather than scanned, and the worked results are computed on the page so that the text and the drawings always agree.

title: 2  Class 2: Linear FEM
text:
3.1 In Summary

\[
\frac{d^2u}{dx^2} + \frac{q(x)}{EA} = 0
\qquad
u(L) = 0
\qquad
\left.\frac{du}{dx}\right|_{x=0} = \frac{F}{EA}
\]

Define

\[
f(x) = \frac{q(x)}{EA}
\qquad\qquad
h = \frac{-F}{EA}
\]

Then our problem matches the Hughes FEM book:

\[
\frac{d^2u}{dx^2} + f(x) = 0
\qquad
u(L) = 0
\qquad
-\frac{du}{dx} = h
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\left(\;
\begin{aligned}
u_{,xx} + f &= 0 \\
u(L) &= 0 \\
-u_{,x} &= h
\end{aligned}
\;\right)
\]

title: 2  Class 2: Linear FEM
text:
4.1 In higher dimensions
In higher dimensions, the Poisson Equation is as follows, with the Laplace equation being the case when \(f = 0\).
Given \(f : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\), \(h : \Gamma_h \to \mathbb{R}\), \(g : \Gamma_g \to \mathbb{R}\), find \(u \in H^1(\Omega)\) such that

\[
\begin{aligned}
-\Delta u &= f && \text{in } \Omega && \leftarrow \text{Poisson equation} \\
u &= g && \text{on } \Gamma_g && \leftarrow \text{known values} \\
\nabla u \cdot \underline{n} &= h && \text{on } \Gamma_h && \leftarrow \text{known flux}
\end{aligned}
\]

Or, more generally, for anisotropic behavior, assuming \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\) is also known, find \(u\) such that

\[
\begin{aligned}
-\nabla \cdot \left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right) &= f && \text{in } \Omega \\
u &= g && \text{on } \Gamma_g \\
\nabla\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}u\right)\cdot \underline{n} &= h && \text{on } \Gamma_h
\end{aligned}
\]







Figure 4.1





\(\Omega\) is the geometry of interest (called the “domain”)
\(\partial\Omega \equiv \Gamma\) is the boundary of the domain
\(\Gamma_g\) is the part of the boundary where we know \(u = g\)
\(\Gamma_h\) is the part of the boundary where we know the flux


The entire boundary is such that

\[
\Gamma = \Gamma_g \cup \Gamma_h
\qquad\qquad
\Gamma_g \cap \Gamma_h = \emptyset
\]



\(\cup\)   union
\(\cap\)   intersect
\(\emptyset\)   empty set (nothing)

title: 3  Class 3: Index Notation, Function Spaces, and the Weak Form
text:
It is often easier to write multivariable calculus ideas in “index” notation, or “Einstein Summation” notation.

\[
f := f \qquad \leftarrow \text{a function or value}
\]


\[
\text{(gradient)}\qquad \nabla f := f_{,i}
\qquad \leftarrow
\text{commas indicate derivatives, } i\text{'s indicate indices}
\]


e.g. in 2D


\[
\nabla f = \begin{bmatrix} \partial f_1/\partial x \\[2pt] \partial f_2/\partial x \end{bmatrix}
\qquad ; \qquad
f_{,1} = \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x}
\qquad
f_{,2} = \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x}
\]


\[
\text{(double gradient)}\qquad \nabla(\nabla f) := f_{,ij}
\qquad\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}
f_{,11} & f_{,12} & f_{,13} \\
f_{,21} & f_{,22} & f_{,23} \\
f_{,31} & f_{,32} & f_{,33}
\end{bmatrix}
\]


\[
\text{(Laplacian)}\qquad \Delta f := \nabla \cdot \nabla f := f_{,ii}
\qquad \leftarrow
\text{repeated indices are "dummy" indices \& indicate sums}
\]


\[
f_{,ii} = f_{,11} + f_{,22} + f_{,33}
= \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2}
+ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2}
\]


\[
\text{a vector (-valued function)}\qquad \underline{V} := V_i
\qquad\qquad
\underline{V} = \begin{bmatrix} V_1 \\ V_2 \\ V_3 \end{bmatrix}
\]


\[
\text{(divergence)}\qquad \nabla \cdot \underline{V} := V_{i,i}
\qquad\qquad
V_{i,i} = \frac{\partial v_1}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_2}{\partial y}
+ \frac{\partial v_3}{\partial z} \quad \text{in 3D}
\]


\[
\text{(dot product)}\qquad \underline{V}\cdot\underline{n} := V_i n_i
\qquad\qquad
V_i n_i = V_1 n_1 + V_2 n_2 + V_3 n_3
\]


\[
\underline{\underline{A}} = A_{ij}
\qquad \text{(matrix w/ row entries in } i \text{, column entries in } j)
\]


\[
\underline{\underline{A}}\,\underline{x} = \underline{b}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
A_{ij} x_j = b_i
\qquad \text{(matrix-vector multiplication)}
\]

If time… let

\[
\underline{\underline{A}} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\underline{f} = \begin{bmatrix} x^2 + y \\ y + z \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\underline{V} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}
\]


what is   \(A_{ij} f_j\) ?    \(A_{ij,j}\) ?    \(f_{j,k}\) ?    \(f_i V_i\) ?    \(f_i V_j\) ?


4 Notation

\[
u_{,xx} := \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}
\qquad
u_{,x} := \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}
\qquad
\dot{u} = \frac{Du}{Dt}
\qquad
\ddot{u} = \frac{D^2 u}{Dt^2}
\]


(\(D/Dt\) is the total derivative — don’t worry about it for now.)

Function

\[
f : \Omega \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}
\]



\(\Omega\) is the domain, \(\mathbb{R}\) is the range




\(\mathbb{R}\)   real #s
\(\mathbb{R}^2\)   Euclidean plane
\(\mathbb{R}^3\)   Euclidean 3-space (real world)
\(\mathbb{I}\)   unit interval
\(\mathbb{I}\times\mathbb{I} = \mathbb{I}^2\)   unit square




\([a,b]\)   closed interval from \(a\) to \(b\)
\((a,b)\)   open interval from \(a\) to \(b\)
\(\bar{\Omega}\)   closed domain (include the boundary)
\(a \in \mathbb{R}\)   \(a\) is in \(\mathbb{R}\) (so it is \(1\), \(\sqrt{3}\), \(-\pi\), etc.)




5 The 1D Poisson equation
The following is important for diffusion-related problems (heat, contaminant), well drawdown, electromagnetics, axial rod deformation, etc.
Called the 1D Poisson equation (but potentially w/ different boundary conditions).
Given \(f : \bar{\Omega} \to \mathbb{R}\) & constants \(g, h \in \mathbb{R}\), find \(u : \bar{\Omega} \to \mathbb{R}\) such that

\[
(\mathrm{S})\quad
\begin{cases}
u_{,xx} + f = 0 & \text{on } \Omega \\[6pt]
u(1) = g \\[6pt]
-u_{,x}(0) = h
\end{cases}
\]

If \(f = 0\), it is called the Laplace equation, & the \(\partial_{xx}\) operator is the 1D Laplace operator.
Exact Solution:

\[
u(x) = g + (1-x)h + \int_x^1\left(\int_0^y f(z)\,dz\right) dy
\]


…but we want to approximate & understand so we can do similar for 2D / 3D.








Figure 5.1: The exact solution for \(f(x) = 1 + 2x\), \(g = 0.7\), \(h = 1.3\) — the Dirichlet condition fixes the value at \(x=1\), the Neumann condition fixes the slope at \(x=0\).






6 Function spaces
For FEM, we need to write down \((\mathrm{S})\) in an alternative, but equivalent, manner: the variational form or weak form.
Need to talk about kinds of functions we can have, or “function spaces”.






Figure 6.1





\(C^0 \to\) continuous function
\(C^{-1} \to\) discontinuous function
\(C^1 \to\) continuous function w/ continuous derivatives
\(C^\infty \to\) continuous function w/ every derivative continuous


\(H^1(\mathbb{R}) \to\) First Sobolev Space of \(\mathbb{R}\)… quite a complicated group of functions, we will discuss more later in class.

See Support: Norms and Function Spaces for where these integrals come from.


The Sobolev Embedding Theorem says these are essentially continuous functions (actually Hölder continuous).

Alternatively, \(H^1\) functions are functions such that

\[
\left.
\begin{aligned}
\int_\Omega (f)^2 \, d\Omega &< \infty \qquad \leftarrow L^2 \text{ functions} \\[6pt]
\int_\Omega (f_{,x})^2 \, d\Omega &< \infty
\end{aligned}
\;\right\}
\quad \text{when } \Omega \subset \mathbb{R}
\]



7 The weak form
Then define two sets:

\[
\text{trial solutions}\qquad
\mathcal{S} = \left\{\, u \;\middle|\; u \in H^1(\mathbb{I}),\; u(1) = g \,\right\}
\]


\[
\text{test solutions / variations}\qquad
\mathcal{V} = \left\{\, w \;\middle|\; w \in H^1,\; w(1) = 0 \,\right\}
\]

Weak (variational) formulation:
Given \(f\), \(g\), & \(h\) as before, find \(u \in \mathcal{S}\) such that \(\forall\, w \in \mathcal{V}\)

\[
(\mathrm{W})\qquad
\int_0^1 w_{,x}\, u_{,x}\, dx = \int_0^1 w f\, dx + w(0)\, h
\]


Inner product — or just multiply by \(w\) & integrate.


\[
(\mathrm{W}) \iff (\mathrm{S})
\]



8 A brief note on bilinearity
Assume \(\underline{v}\), \(\underline{w}\) are vectors. The inner product of \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\), written \(\langle \underline{v}, \underline{w}\rangle\), is defined as

\[
\langle \underline{v}, \underline{w}\rangle = v_i w_i = \sum_{i=1}^{n} v_i w_i
= v_1 w_1 + \cdots + v_n w_n
\]

We show that \(\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle\) is bilinear if for an arbitrary set of coefficients \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), & arbitrary vectors \(\underline{v}\), \(\underline{w}\), \(\underline{z}\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle \alpha\underline{v} + \beta\underline{z},\; \underline{w}\rangle
  &= \alpha\langle \underline{v}, \underline{w}\rangle
   + \beta\langle \underline{z}, \underline{w}\rangle \\[6pt]
\text{\&}\qquad
\langle \underline{v},\; \alpha\underline{w} + \beta\underline{z}\rangle
  &= \alpha\langle \underline{v}, \underline{w}\rangle
   + \beta\langle \underline{v}, \underline{z}\rangle
\end{aligned}
\]

How do we show this? Go back to the definition.

e.g.


\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle \alpha\underline{v} + \beta\underline{z},\; \underline{w}\rangle
  &= \left(\alpha\underline{v} + \beta\underline{z}\right)_i w_i \\
  &= \left(\alpha v_i + \beta z_i\right) w_i \\
  &= \alpha v_i w_i + \beta z_i w_i \\
  &= \alpha\langle \underline{v}, \underline{w}\rangle
   + \beta\langle \underline{z}, \underline{w}\rangle
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 4  Class 4: Strong and Weak Forms of the Boundary Value Problem
text:
5 Strong form of the boundary value problem (Poisson)

Given \(f : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\), \(g : \Gamma_g \to \mathbb{R}\), and \(h : \Gamma_h \to \mathbb{R}\), find \(u : \bar\Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
-\nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)
= -\left(\kappa_{ij}u_{,j}\right)_{,i} = f
\qquad \text{in } \Omega
\]
\[
u = g \qquad \text{on } \Gamma_g
\]
\[
\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n}
= \kappa_{ij}u_{,j}\,n_i = h
\qquad \text{on } \Gamma_h
\]







Figure 5.1





6 In one dimension

\[
-\left(K u_{,x}\right)_{,x} = f \qquad \text{in } \Omega
\qquad\qquad
u = g \qquad \text{on } \Gamma_g
\qquad\qquad
(Ku_{,x})\,n = h \qquad \text{on } \Gamma_h
\]

The one-dimensional boundary \(\Gamma\) is just the two endpoints, so \(n\) can only be \(-1\) or \(+1\) — the outward normal at the left end always points in \(-x\), and at the right end always in \(+x\).






Figure 6.1




The Neumann boundary is wherever a flux \(h\) is prescribed instead of a value \(g\). At the left end, the outward normal is \(-1\); at the right end, it is \(+1\) — that sign is why the Neumann condition in one dimension is written \(-u_{,x}(0) = h\) but \(+u_{,x}(L) = h\): both are \((Ku_{,x})\cdot n = h\) once \(K=1\) is included and \(n\) is substituted in.



7 Coming from the exact solution
Last time, we found the exact solution to the 1D Poisson problem to be

\[
u(x) = g + (1-x)h + \int_x^1\left(\int_0^y f(z)\,dz\right)dy
\]


So we’re done… why do anything more?



What if we don’t have a simple function \(f\)?
What if the domain is not one-dimensional?


Want to convert this into a representation we can compute on. Idea: use an inner product and function space to “describe” our function.

\[
\mathcal{S} = \left\{\, u \in H^1(\Omega) \;\middle|\; u(x) = g(x) \text{ for } x \in \Gamma_g \,\right\}
\qquad \leftarrow \textbf{trial function space}
\]
\[
\mathcal{V} = \left\{\, w \in H^1(\Omega) \;\middle|\; w(x) = 0 \text{ for } x \in \Gamma_g \,\right\}
\qquad \leftarrow \textbf{test function space}
\]


Recall \(H^1(\Omega) = \left\{ f : \Omega \to \mathbb{R} \;\middle|\;
\int_\Omega f^2 + \nabla f \cdot \nabla f \; d\Omega < \infty \right\}\) — in 1D, these are continuous functions. (See the function-space appendix for more.)



8 Weak form of the boundary value problem

Given \(f : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\), \(g : \Gamma_g \to \mathbb{R}\), \(h : \Gamma_h \to \mathbb{R}\), and \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^{n_{sd} \times n_{sd}}\) symmetric positive definite, find \(u \in \mathcal{S}\) such that for every \(w \in \mathcal{V}\),
\[
(\mathrm{W}) \qquad
\int_\Omega \nabla w \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}} \nabla u \; d\Omega
= \int_\Omega wf\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} wh\;d\Gamma
\]

In one dimension, this is

\[
(\mathrm{W}) \qquad
\int_0^L w_{,x}\,K\,u_{,x}\;dx
= \int_0^L wf\;dx + w u_{,x}\Big\rvert_{x=0}^{x=L}
\qquad \text{or, in our case,} \qquad
\int_0^L w_{,x}\,K\,u_{,x}\;dx = \int_0^1 wf\;dx + w(0)\,h
\]



9 What does this mean?

Example: put an object in a bag, try to guess the object.



→ bag size is the “space” of objects you’re guessing in
→ people can come look in the bag & describe with 1 word



(In class, a mousetrap toy.)

The words are what we use to “test” or “measure” our object against.
If we have all possible descriptors, we should know precisely what the object is. Otherwise, we pick a set of “best” words with which to describe.

Think about this — it is sort of the way we come to know God.



→ descriptors, experiences, etc., but we have limited knowledge; at some point we will know — John 17:3




10 Formal proof of equivalence (strong \(\Rightarrow\) weak)
Start from the strong form and multiply by an arbitrary \(w\), then integrate over \(\Omega\):

\[
-\nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right) = f
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
-\int_\Omega w\,\nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\,d\Omega
= \int_\Omega wf\,d\Omega
\qquad (w \text{ arbitrary})
\]

The left side needs the product rule, applied to \(\nabla\cdot(w\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u)\):

\[
\nabla\cdot\left(w\,\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)
= \nabla w\cdot\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u
+ w\,\nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)
\]

so that, integrating the left side and applying the Divergence Theorem,

\[
\int_\Omega \nabla\cdot\left(w\,\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right) d\Omega
= \int_\Gamma \left(w\,\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot \underline{n}\;d\Gamma
\]

Combining these two facts, the term we wanted rearranges into

\[
-\left(\int_\Gamma \left(w\,\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n}\;d\Gamma
- \int_\Omega \nabla w \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u \;d\Omega\right)
= \int_\Omega wf\,d\Omega
\]


\[
\Longrightarrow \qquad
\int_\Omega \nabla w \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u \; d\Omega
= \int_\Omega wf\,d\Omega + \int_\Gamma \left(w\,\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n}\;d\Gamma
\]


\[
\Longrightarrow \qquad
\int_\Omega w_{,i}\kappa_{ij}u_{,j}\;d\Omega
= \int_\Omega wf\,d\Omega + \int_\Gamma w \kappa_{ij}u_{,j}\,n_i\;d\Gamma
\]


But \(w(x) = 0\) on \(\Gamma_g\), and \(\Gamma = \Gamma_g \cup \Gamma_h\), so the boundary integral only survives over \(\Gamma_h\) — where the strong form tells us \(\kappa_{ij}u_{,j}n_i = h\):


\[
\boxed{\int_\Omega w_{,i}\kappa_{ij}u_{,j}\;d\Omega
= \int_\Omega wf\,d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} wh\;d\Gamma}
\]

which is exactly \((\mathrm{W})\). The next class continues the other direction — \((\mathrm{W}) \Rightarrow (\mathrm{S})\) — which is a genuinely different (and more delicate) argument.

6 Weak form \(\Rightarrow\) strong form
Last time, given \(f\), \(g\), \(h\), and \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\), we let
and showed that if \(u\) solves the strong form, then it also satisfies: find \(u \in \mathcal{S}\) such that for every \(w \in \mathcal{V}\),
Goals:
Run the previous class’s steps in reverse, starting from \((\mathrm{W})\) written in multivariate-calculus form:
Now run the Divergence Theorem in reverse — the same identity used last time, applied to pull \(\nabla w \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\) back into a divergence:
crumbs: 5  Class 5: Weak Form ⇒ Strong Form, and the Galerkin Method

title: 5  Class 5: Weak Form ⇒ Strong Form, and the Galerkin Method
text:
6.1 Recovering the PDE on \(\Omega\)
Pick \(w = \left[f + \nabla\cdot(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u)\right]\phi\) for some smooth \(\phi\) with \(\phi > 0\) on \(\Omega\) and \(\phi = 0\) on \(\Gamma\) (so that \(w \in \mathcal{V} \cap H^1(\Omega)\)). This choice makes the boundary integral vanish identically, leaving

\[
0 = \int_\Omega \left(f + \nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\right)^2 \phi\;d\Omega
\]


But \(\phi > 0\) on \(\Omega\) and \(\left(f + \nabla\cdot(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u)\right)^2 \ge 0\) everywhere. An integral of a non-negative quantity that comes out to zero forces the integrand itself to be zero:


\[
\Longrightarrow \qquad
\left(f + \nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\right)^2 = 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\boxed{-\nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right) = f} \qquad \text{on } \Omega
\]
crumbs: 5  Class 5: Weak Form ⇒ Strong Form, and the Galerkin Method

title: 5  Class 5: Weak Form ⇒ Strong Form, and the Galerkin Method
text:
6.2 Recovering the flux condition on \(\Gamma_h\)
Next, pick \(w = \left[h - \left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n}\right]\psi\) for some smooth \(\psi\) with \(\psi > 0\) on \(\Gamma_h\) and \(\psi = 0\) on \(\Gamma_g\). Because the PDE result above already makes the domain integral vanish for any \(w\), this choice leaves only

\[
0 = \int_{\Gamma_h} \left[h - \left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n}\right]^2 \psi\;d\Gamma
\]


By the same argument — \(\psi > 0\) on \(\Gamma_h\), and the bracketed quantity is squared —


\[
\Longrightarrow \qquad
\boxed{\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} = h} \qquad \text{on } \Gamma_h
\]
crumbs: 5  Class 5: Weak Form ⇒ Strong Form, and the Galerkin Method

title: 5  Class 5: Weak Form ⇒ Strong Form, and the Galerkin Method
text:
6.3 Summarizing

\[
-\nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right) = f \quad \text{on } \Omega
\qquad\text{(from the domain argument)}
\]
\[
\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} = h \quad \text{on } \Gamma_h
\qquad\text{(from the boundary argument)}
\]
\[
u(x) = g(x) \quad \text{on } \Gamma_g
\qquad\text{(because } u \in \mathcal{S} \text{ by assumption)}
\]


In sum: if we pick two really, really good choices for \(w \in \mathcal{V}\), we exactly recover the strong form for \(u \in \mathcal{S}\). Together with last class’s argument, this shows \((\mathrm{S}) \Leftrightarrow (\mathrm{W})\) — the two formulations are truly equivalent, not merely “the weak form is an approximation.”

8.1 Basis: a linear-algebra idea


linearly independent
span the space



Together, these mean you can represent any item in the space uniquely as a sum of coefficients times members of the basis.







Figure 8.1: Which of these are bases for \(\mathbb{R}^2\), and why?




The first two are bases (their vectors are linearly independent — the determinant of the matrix formed from them is nonzero). The third pair, \(\{[-1,1],[1,-1]\}\), is not a basis: the two vectors are scalar multiples of each other (anti-parallel), so they span only a line, not the plane. The fourth set has three vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) — too many to be a basis, since a basis for \(\mathbb{R}^2\) has exactly two elements, though any two of the three (chosen to be independent) would work.

section: 8.2 Choosing a basis for piecewise polynomials
text:
8.2 Choosing a basis for piecewise polynomials
For us, we want bases of piecewise polynomials — use the Lagrange polynomials.

Example: \(y = mx + b\) on domain \([0, 1]\). Then


\[
y \approx b\,\ell_1(x) + (m+b)\,\ell_2(x)
\qquad \text{(polynomial degree 1)}
\]
\[
\ell_1(x) = \frac{x - 1}{0 - 1}
\qquad\qquad
\ell_2(x) = \frac{x - 0}{1 - 0}
\]








Figure 8.2




For a quadratic, \(y = \alpha x^2 + \beta x + \gamma\) on domain \([-1, 1]\):

\[
y(x) \approx (\alpha - \beta + \gamma)\,\ell_1(x) + \gamma\,\ell_2(x)
             + (\alpha + \beta + \gamma)\,\ell_3(x)
\qquad \text{(polynomial degree 2)}
\]
\[
\ell_1(x) = \frac{(x-0)(x-1)}{(-1-0)(-1-1)}
\qquad
\ell_2(x) = \frac{(x-(-1))(x-1)}{(0-(-1))(0-1)}
\qquad
\ell_3(x) = \frac{(x-(-1))(x-0)}{(1-(-1))(1-0)}
\]

title: 7  Class 7: From Galerkin to a Matrix Equation
text:
8 Last time
Pick \(\mathcal{S}^h \subset \mathcal{S}\), \(\mathcal{V}^h \subset \mathcal{V}\). Given \(f\), \(g\), \(h\), \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\) as before, find \(u^h \in \mathcal{S}^h \subset \mathcal{S}\) such that \(\forall\, w^h \in \mathcal{V}^h \subset \mathcal{V}\),

\[
\int_\Omega \nabla w^h \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u^h\;d\Omega
= \int_\Omega w f\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} w h\;d\Gamma
\qquad \text{or} \qquad
a(w, u) = (w, f) + (w, h)_{\Gamma_h}
\]

Assume \(u^h = v^h + g^h\), where \(u^h \in \mathcal{S}^h\), \(v^h \in \mathcal{V}^h\), \(g^h \in \mathcal{S}^h\):

\[
v^h = \sum_{B=0,\,B \notin \Gamma_g}^{n_{bf}-1} d_B\,N_B
\qquad\qquad
g^h = \sum_{B=0,\,B \in \Gamma_g}^{n_{bf}-1} g_B\,N_B
\qquad\qquad
w^h = \sum_{A=0,\,A \notin \Gamma_g}^{n_{bf}-1} c_A\,N_A
\]


where \(n_{bf}\) is the number of basis functions.







Figure 8.1: One- and two-dimensional meshes: open circles are basis functions unconstrained by \(\Gamma_g\) (these carry the \(c_A\)/\(d_B\) unknowns), filled circles are basis functions on \(\Gamma_g\) (these carry the known \(g_B\)).





9 Deriving the matrix system

\[
\int_\Omega \nabla w^h \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}} \nabla u^h\;d\Omega
= \int_\Omega w^h f\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} w^h h\;d\Gamma
\]

Substitute the expansions for \(w^h\) and \(u^h = v^h + g^h\) — note \(c_A\), \(d_B\), \(g_B\) are all constants, so they come out of the integrals:

\[
\int_\Omega \nabla\left(\sum_A c_A N_A\right) \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}}
\nabla\left(\sum_B d_B N_B + \sum_B g_B N_B\right) d\Omega
= \int_\Omega \left(\sum_A c_A N_A\right) f\;d\Omega
+ \int_{\Gamma_h} \left(\sum_A c_A N_A\right) h\;d\Gamma
\]


\[
\sum_A \sum_B c_A\left[\int_\Omega \nabla N_A \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}} \nabla N_B\;d\Omega\right] d_B
= \sum_A c_A\left[\int_\Omega N_A f\;d\Omega\right]
+ \sum_A c_A\left[\int_{\Gamma_h} N_A h\;d\Gamma\right]
- \sum_A \sum_B c_A\left[\int_\Omega \nabla N_A \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}} \nabla N_B\;d\Omega\right] g_B
\]


This is dense, but every term is one of three integral “shapes” that we will name shortly. Collecting terms so that all of them are multiplied by \(c_A\):


\[
0 = \sum_A c_A \left[-\sum_B d_B \int_\Omega \nabla N_A \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla N_B\;d\Omega
    + \int_\Omega N_A f\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} N_A h\;d\Gamma
    - \sum_B g_B \int_\Omega \nabla N_A \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla N_B\;d\Omega\right]
\]


\[
0 = \sum_A c_A\,G_A
\]


Now, remember that \(w^h\) was arbitrary, meaning this is true for all choices \(\{c_A\}_{A=0}^{n}\), \(w^h = \sum c_A N_A\). Choose \(w^h\) such that \(c_0 = 1\), all other \(c_A = 0\): this forces \(0 = 1 \cdot G_0 \Rightarrow G_0 = 0\). Choose \(w^h\) such that \(c_1 = 1\), all other \(c_A = 0\): \(G_1 = 0\). Repeating for every index, \(G_A = 0\) for every \(A\) — exactly the same “pick a really good test function” trick from Class 5, now applied coefficient by coefficient.

Consequently, for any \(A\) (an index of a basis function in \(\mathcal{V}^h\)), we have

\[
\sum_B d_B\left[\int_\Omega \nabla N_A \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla N_B\;d\Omega\right]
= \int_\Omega N_A f\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} N_A h\;d\Gamma
- \sum_B g_B\int_\Omega \nabla N_A \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla N_B\;d\Omega
\]

or, naming the two integral shapes,

\[
\sum_B d_B\,a(N_A, N_B) = \underbrace{(N_A, f) + (N_A, h)_{\Gamma_h}
                                       - \sum_B g_B\,a(N_A, N_B)}_{F_A}
\qquad\qquad
a(N_A, N_B) =: K_{AB}
\]

Putting all of these together, we get a large matrix equation — in index notation it is

\[
K_{AB}\,d_B = F_A
\qquad\qquad (\text{dummy indices; } B \text{ denotes a sum})
\]


\[
\boxed{\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\,\underline{d} = \underline{F}}
\]


To solve this equation, we will need numerical integration methods. The most general and effective methods for piecewise-polynomial functions are called Gaussian quadrature methods, and are the subject of a later class — after we’ve built up the machinery for assembling \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\) and \(\underline{F}\) concretely.

title: 8  Class 8: Assembly, Sparsity, and the Road to Quadrature
section: 9.1 The basis functions on this mesh
text:
9.1 The basis functions on this mesh
The four nodes sit at \(x_0 = 0\), \(x_1\), \(x_2\), and \(x_3 = L\), and the three elements between them have lengths \(\ell_e = x_{e+1} - x_e\). Each node carries one basis function: \(N_A\) is the piecewise-linear function that is \(1\) at its own node and \(0\) at every other node,

\[
N_A(x_B) = \delta_{AB} =
\begin{cases} 1, & A = B \\ 0, & A \neq B \end{cases}
\]


“Linear on each element”, plus that one requirement, fixes all four functions completely.







Figure 9.2: One basis function per plot, on the mesh of Figure 9.1. Each \(N_A\) rises to \(1\) at its own node, falls back to \(0\) at its neighbours, and is zero everywhere else. The two end functions, \(N_0\) and \(N_3\), are half of a hat.



Written out, each one is a straight line on every element it touches:

\[
N_A(x) =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{x - x_{A-1}}{\ell_{A-1}}, & x_{A-1} \le x \le x_A \quad (\text{if } A > 0) \\[10pt]
\dfrac{x_{A+1} - x}{\ell_A}, & x_A \le x \le x_{A+1} \quad (\text{if } A < 3) \\[10pt]
0, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]

The end functions, \(N_0\) and \(N_3\), simply lose one of the two branches, because there is no element on the far side of their node.

Two properties to keep hold of: each \(N_A\) is zero outside the one or two elements that touch node \(A\) (this is what will make \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\) sparse), and at every \(x\) the four functions sum to one, \(\sum_A N_A(x) = 1\).
crumbs: 8  Class 8: Assembly, Sparsity, and the Road to Quadrature

title: 8  Class 8: Assembly, Sparsity, and the Road to Quadrature
section: 9.2 The derivatives of the basis functions
text:
9.2 The derivatives of the basis functions
Each branch above is linear in \(x\), so each derivative is a constant on each element: differentiating \((x - x_{A-1})/\ell_{A-1}\) gives \(+1/\ell_{A-1}\), and differentiating \((x_{A+1} - x)/\ell_A\) gives \(-1/\ell_A\). The shorter the element, the steeper the ramp and the larger that constant.

\[
N_{A,x}(x) =
\begin{cases}
+\dfrac{1}{\ell_{A-1}}, & x_{A-1} < x < x_A \quad (\text{if } A > 0) \\[10pt]
-\dfrac{1}{\ell_A}, & x_A < x < x_{A+1} \quad (\text{if } A < 3) \\[10pt]
0, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]







Figure 9.3: The derivative of each basis function: one constant per element, jumping at the nodes. The sign flips where the hat turns from rising to falling, and the size is set by the length of the element.





At the nodes themselves the derivative jumps and is undefined. Those are finitely many points, so no integral ever notices them — which is precisely why the weak form, needing only one derivative, is the right setting for these functions.
On any one element the four values add to zero. That follows from \(\sum_A N_A = 1\): differentiate both sides, and \(\sum_A N_{A,x} = 0\) on every element. It is also why the all-node matrix below is singular until a Dirichlet value is imposed.

title: 8  Class 8: Assembly, Sparsity, and the Road to Quadrature
text:
9.5 Evaluating the entries
Every integrand left in \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\) is a product of two of the piecewise-constant derivatives in Figure 9.3. On any one element that product is itself a constant, so the integral over that element is just the constant times the element’s length:

\[
\int_{x_e}^{x_{e+1}} N_{A,x}\,N_{B,x}\;dx
= \underbrace{N_{A,x}\,N_{B,x}}_{\text{constant on element } e}\;\ell_e .
\]


\[
\begin{aligned}
K_{11} &= \int_0^L N_{1,x}N_{1,x}\,dx
= \left(\frac{1}{\ell_0}\right)^{2}\ell_0 + \left(-\frac{1}{\ell_1}\right)^{2}\ell_1
= \frac{1}{\ell_0} + \frac{1}{\ell_1}, \\[6pt]
K_{12} &= \int_0^L N_{1,x}N_{2,x}\,dx
= \left(-\frac{1}{\ell_1}\right)\left(+\frac{1}{\ell_1}\right)\ell_1
= -\frac{1}{\ell_1}, \\[6pt]
K_{02} &= \int_0^L N_{0,x}N_{2,x}\,dx = 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]


In general \(K_{AA} = \dfrac{1}{\ell_{A-1}} + \dfrac{1}{\ell_A}\) (drop whichever term does not exist, at the two ends), \(K_{A,A+1} = K_{A+1,A} = -\dfrac{1}{\ell_A}\), and every other entry is zero. Nothing here depends on \(f\), \(g\), or \(h\): the stiffness matrix is a property of the mesh alone.

With the lengths of Figure 9.1, \(\ell_0 = 1.5\), \(\ell_1 = 2\), and \(\ell_2 = 2.5\), so \(1/\ell_0 = 2/3\), \(1/\ell_1 = 1/2\), and \(1/\ell_2 = 2/5\). Striking out the row and column of the Dirichlet node leaves the system that is actually solved:

\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{2}{3} & -\frac{2}{3} & 0 \\[4pt]
-\frac{2}{3} & \frac{7}{6} & -\frac{1}{2} \\[4pt]
0 & -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{9}{10}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} d_0 \\ d_1 \\ d_2 \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\int_0^L N_0 f\,dx + h \\[4pt]
\int_0^L N_1 f\,dx \\[4pt]
\int_0^L N_2 f\,dx + \frac{2}{5}\,g
\end{bmatrix}
\]


The \(g\) term changed sign on its way across the equals sign, because the entry it came from is negative: \(-g\int_0^L N_{2,x}N_{3,x}\,dx = -g\left(-\frac{1}{\ell_2}\right)
= +\frac{g}{\ell_2}\). Every entry of the matrix is now a number. The only integrals still standing are the ones containing \(f\), and those are what quadrature is for.


Notice that all the integrals in \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\) look the same, in some way:



Dirichlet (known) boundary-condition data looks the same as the integrals in \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\) — it is just \(\int \nabla N_A \cdot
\underline{\underline{\kappa}} \nabla N_B\) against a known coefficient \(g_B\).
Neumann (known-flux) boundary-condition data is a number in 1D — but a curve in 2D and a surface in 3D.
Integrals with forcing functions on the right-hand side all look the same as each other.



That observation is what makes a general-purpose code possible: there are only a handful of distinct integral shapes to implement, no matter the problem or the dimension.

We want to solve

title: 9  Class 9: The Isoparametric Map and the Jacobian
text:
10.1 The deformation gradient

What is \(\dfrac{\partial x_i}{\partial \xi_j}\)? This is called the deformation gradient (also the Jacobian matrix), \(DF = \nabla_\xi \underline{x}\). How do we compute it?


\[
\nabla_\xi \underline{x} = \nabla_\xi\left(\sum_a \underline{x}_a^e N_a(\xi)\right)
= \sum_a \underline{x}_a^e \nabla_\xi N_a(\xi)
\qquad\qquad \text{or} \qquad
\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial \xi_j} = \sum_a x_{a,i}^e \frac{\partial N_a(\xi,\eta)}{\partial\xi_j}
\]


For the quadrilateral element in Figure 9.1, this check verifies something worth noticing: integrating \(J(\xi,\eta)\) over the reference square with a \(2\times2\) Gauss rule reproduces the exact physical area of the quad (via the shoelace formula) to machine precision — because \(J\) for a bilinear map is itself only bilinear in each direction, and \(2\)-point Gauss integrates such polynomials exactly. (Gauss quadrature itself is next class’s topic — for now, take it as “a good rule for polynomials.”)

Only one step in that chain loses anything: \((\mathrm{W}) \Rightarrow (\mathrm{G})\), where we restrict to a finite-dimensional subspace. \((\mathrm{S}) \Leftrightarrow

\]








Figure 10.2



What is \(\Gamma_{g_1}, \Gamma_{g_2}\)? \(\Gamma_{h_1}, \Gamma_{h_2}\)? — Each component of displacement (or flux) can have its own Dirichlet or Neumann boundary, which need not coincide with the others. A pin support fixes both displacement components; a roller fixes only one.

\sum_B \left(\int_\Omega \nabla N_A \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla N_B\;d\Omega\right) d_B
= \int_\Omega N_A f\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} N_A h\;d\Gamma - \sum_B g_B \int_\Omega \nabla N_A \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla N_B\;d\Omega

we must first be able to solve, on one element \(\Omega^e\),

The IEN (element \(\to\) node) array maps a local basis-function index \(a\) on element \(e\) to the global basis-function index \(A\): \(a, e \xrightarrow{\text{IEN}} A\).






Figure 12.1: A central element \(e_0\) shares each edge with a neighboring element \(e_1\)–\(e_4\). Local corner indices \(a=0,1,2,3\) on \(e_0\) map to global indices \(A = 0, 5, 6, 7\).

13 Global stiffness from local (element) stiffness

\[
K_{AB} = \int_{\Omega} \nabla N_A \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla N_B\;d\Omega
= \sum_e \int_{\Omega^e} \nabla_x N_A \cdot \underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla_x N_B\;d\Omega
\qquad \leftarrow \textbf{global stiffness}
\]


Use the IEN array to only work on relevant basis functions: \(a, e \xrightarrow{\text{IEN}} A\), \(b, e \xrightarrow{\text{IEN}} B\).


\[
K_{ab}^e = \int_{\Omega^e} \nabla_x N_A^{(x)}\,\underline{\underline{\kappa}}(x)\,\nabla_x N_B^{(x)}\;d\Omega
\qquad \leftarrow \textbf{local stiffness, spatial domain}
\]

Pulling this back to the reference domain, as in the last class:

\[
K_{ab}^e = \int_{\hat\Omega} \nabla_x N_a(\xi)\,\underline{\underline{\kappa}}(x(\xi))\,
           \nabla_x N_b(\xi)\;J(\xi)\;d\hat\Omega
\]


where \(\dfrac{\partial N_a}{\partial x_i} = \dfrac{\partial N_a}{\partial \xi_j}\dfrac{\partial \xi_j}{\partial x_i}
= (DF^{-1})^T \nabla_\xi N_a\) — the inverse of the deformation gradient, from last class:


\[
K_{ab}^e = \int_{\hat\Omega} \left[(DF)^{-T}\nabla_\xi N_a\right]
           \underline{\underline{\kappa}}\left[(DF)^{-T}\nabla_\xi N_b\right] J\;d\hat\Omega
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
K_{ab}^e = \sum_{g=0}^{n_{quad}} w_g \left[(DF)^{-T}(\xi_g)\nabla_\xi N_a(\xi_g)\right]
           \underline{\underline{\kappa}}(x^e(\xi_g))
           \left[(DF)^{-T}(\xi_g)\nabla_\xi N_b(\xi_g)\right] J(\xi_g)
\]


This sum over quadrature points \(g\) is what a finite element code evaluates for every element, every time it assembles \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\).

title: 11  Class 11: Tensor-Product Basis Functions in 2D

11.1 The 1D factors
A 2D Lagrange basis function on the parent square \([-1,1]^2\) is the product of one 1D basis function in \(\xi\) and one in \(\eta\):
\[
N_A(\xi,\eta) = N_a(\xi)\,N_b(\eta), \qquad A = a + (p_\xi+1)\,b .
\]
The index \(\xi\) varies fastest.  The interpolation points are equally spaced.

Drag the 3D plot to rotate it; the view is kept when you change a slider. Hover over the surface or curves to read values.
Each panel shows every 1D basis function of that degree (grey), the active one (solid), and the 2D slice along that direction (dashed), which is the active one scaled by the printed constant.

11.2 Strides: from \((a,b)\) to \(A\)
Looking straight down on the element, the basis functions sit on a \((p_\xi+1)\times(p_\eta+1)\) grid of nodes. Each direction gets a stride, \(s_0 = 1\) and \(s_i = \prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(p_j+1)\), so
\[
A = \sum_i a_i\,s_i = a\cdot 1 + b\,(p_\xi+1)\;\big[\,+\;c\,(p_\xi+1)(p_\eta+1)\text{ in 3D}\big],
\qquad a_i = (A \,/\!/\, s_i) \bmod (p_i+1).
\]
A step in \(\xi\) changes \(A\) by 1; a step in \(\eta\) jumps a whole row, \(p_\xi+1\). The plot is the current \(N_A\) seen from above, with each node labelled by its \(A\). Click any node to select that basis function; the sliders and plots above follow.

text:
11.3 Things to try

Set \(p_\xi = p_\eta = 1\). Every basis function is a bilinear “tent corner”, and each slice is a straight line.
Set \(p_\xi = p_\eta = 2\) and pick the center node \((a,b) = (1,1)\). This is the interior “bubble” function; it is zero on the whole boundary of the element.
Pick an edge node such as \((a,b) = (1,0)\) and move \(\eta_0\) onto \(\eta = 0\) or \(\eta = 1\). The dashed \(\xi\)-slice collapses to zero, because \(N_0(\eta)\) vanishes at the other \(\eta\) nodes.
Raise the degree to 5 or 6 and look at a basis function next to the boundary. The large oscillations in the 1D factors (the Runge effect) carry straight over into the 2D surface.

title: 12  Class 12: The Spatial Mapping
text:
12.1 The general form
Class 11 showed how to build 2D basis functions on the parent domain (also called the reference domain), the square \(\hat\Omega = [-1,1]^2\) with coordinates \((\xi,\eta)\). Elements in a mesh may not be squares, and if they are, they aren’t always centered around the origin, so we need a method that takes a point of the parent domain to a point of the element. That rule is the spatial mapping, and it uses the same basis functions. In two dimensions, this looks like
\[
\underline{x}^e(\xi,\eta) = \sum_{A=0}^{n_{en}-1} \underline{x}_A^e \, N_A(\xi,\eta),
\]
where \(\underline{x}_A^e\) is the position of node \(A\) of element \(e\), and \(n_{en} = (p_\xi+1)(p_\eta+1)\) is the number of nodes on the element. The above equation can be represented by two coordinate mappings for both the \(x\) and the \(y\) coordinates from the parent domain as
\[
x(\xi,\eta) = \sum_A x_A\,N_A(\xi,\eta), \qquad
y(\xi,\eta) = \sum_A y_A\,N_A(\xi,\eta).
\]
Compare this with the approximate solution,
\[
u^h(\xi,\eta) = \sum_A d_A\,N_A(\xi,\eta).
\]
Both of these maps use the same basis functions but different coefficients, which coefficients are defined by the nodal positions of the element geometry. Using the same \(N_A\) for both the solution, \(u^h,\) and for the geometry is what isoparametric means.
If we write \(\underline{\xi}\) for the parametric coordinates, \(\underline{\xi} = (\xi,\eta)\) in 2D and \(\underline{\xi} = (\xi,\eta,\zeta)\) in 3D. Then
\[
\underline{x}^e(\underline{\xi}) = \sum_{A=0}^{n_{en}-1} \underline{x}_A^e \, N_A(\underline{\xi}),
\]
with the basis functions and the single index built as in Class 11,
\[
N_A(\underline{\xi}) = \prod_{i=0}^{n_{sd}-1} \ell^{p_i}_{a_i}(\xi_i),
\qquad
A = \sum_{i=0}^{n_{sd}-1} a_i\,s_i,
\qquad
s_0 = 1, \quad s_i = \prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(p_j+1),
\]
and \(n_{en} = \prod_{i=0}^{n_{sd}-1}(p_i+1)\). In 2D this is \(N_A(\xi,\eta) = \ell^{p_\xi}_a(\xi)\,\ell^{p_\eta}_b(\eta)\) with \(A = a + (p_\xi+1)b\), which is what the viewer below uses. The interpolation points are typicallly equally spaced in each direction.

title: 12  Class 12: The Spatial Mapping
text:
12.3 Reading the four lines
The block to the right of the table is the same computation written four times.

The sum, symbolically. One term per node, so the number of terms changes with the degree: \(n_{en} = (p_\xi+1)(p_\eta+1)\).
Nodal coordinates substituted. The \(\underline{x}_A\) are now numbers, the ones in the table. The parametric point has not been used yet.
Basis functions evaluated. Now \((\xi,\eta)\) is used and each \(N_A\) becomes a number. This is the only line that changes when you move the dot without changing the element.
The mapped point. Multiply and add.

The term in red has the largest weight. Move the dot to a node and that weight becomes \(1\) while the others become \(0\), which is the interpolation property from Class 11.
Below the table is the running value of \(\sum_A N_A(\xi,\eta)\), which is \(1\) everywhere. This is the partition of unity, and it says a constant is reproduced exactly: if every \(\underline{x}_A\) were the same point, the map would return that point for any \((\xi,\eta)\). It is the \([0,0]\) case of the reproduction question in Homework 6, Problem 3.

title: 12  Class 12: The Spatial Mapping
text:
12.5 Things to try

Drag the dot to the corner \((\xi,\eta) = (-1,-1)\). The mapped point is control point \(0\), and in line 3 every weight is zero except that one.
Set \(p_\xi = p_\eta = 1\). There are four nodes and the edges are straight: a bilinear map cannot curve an edge. The mapped grid lines are still not parallel, so the map is not affine.
Go back to degree 2 and drag the mid-edge control point \(A = 1\), at \((a,b) = (1,0)\), away from the edge. The edge bends. This is how a quadratic element follows a curved boundary.
Keep moving that node past its neighbours until the mapped grid lines cross. The map is no longer one-to-one and the element has folded. Nothing in the sum prevents this.
Set \(p_\xi = 3\), \(p_\eta = 1\): cubic in \(\xi\), linear in \(\eta\), eight nodes. The stride \(A = a + (p_\xi+1)b\) renumbers the table.
Put the dot at \((\xi,\eta) = (0,0)\) and read line 3. At degree 2 in both directions the centre node has weight \(1\) and the rest have weight \(0\); at degree 1 the four corners each have weight \(0.25\). The centre of the element is a node only when the degree is even.

title: 12  Class 12: The Spatial Mapping
text:
12.6 Next
The map says where a parametric point goes. It does not say how much a small piece of the parent domain is stretched or rotated on the way, and we need that to write \(\int_{\Omega^e} (\cdot)\,d\Omega\) as an integral over the parent domain that quadrature can evaluate. Differentiating the sum with respect to \(\underline{\xi}\) gives the deformation gradient and its determinant, the Jacobian, in Class 13. Item 4 above is the case where that determinant changes sign.
crumbs: 12  Class 12: The Spatial Mapping

title: 13  Class 13: The Jacobian Matrix
text:
13.1 The deformation gradient
In Class 12 the spatial mapping told us where a parametric point goes:
\[
\underline{x}^e(\underline{\xi}) = \sum_{A=0}^{n_{en}-1} \underline{x}_A^e\,N_A(\underline{\xi}).
\]
It does not say how much a small piece of the parent domain is stretched or turned on the way. We need that to change an integral over \(\Omega^e\) into an integral over the parent domain, and we need it to tell whether the element is usable at all. Both come from the derivative of the map.
Differentiating the sum gives the deformation gradient, also called the Jacobian matrix. Symbolically,
\[
DF = \frac{\partial \underline{x}}{\partial \underline{\xi}}
   = \sum_{A=0}^{n_{en}-1} \underline{x}_A^e \left(\nabla_\xi N_A\right)^T .
\]
In index notation, with \(i\) running over spatial directions and \(j\) over parametric directions,
\[
\left(DF\right)_{ij} = \frac{\partial x_i}{\partial \xi_j}
   = \sum_{A=0}^{n_{en}-1} x^e_{iA}\,\frac{\partial N_A}{\partial \xi_j}.
\]
In matrix form in 2D, with \(\underline{\xi} = (\xi,\eta)\),
\[
DF =
\begin{bmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial \xi} & \dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial \eta} \\[10pt]
\dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial \xi} & \dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial \eta}
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\displaystyle\sum_A x_A \dfrac{\partial N_A}{\partial \xi} &
\displaystyle\sum_A x_A \dfrac{\partial N_A}{\partial \eta} \\[14pt]
\displaystyle\sum_A y_A \dfrac{\partial N_A}{\partial \xi} &
\displaystyle\sum_A y_A \dfrac{\partial N_A}{\partial \eta}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Two things to notice. The nodal coordinates \(\underline{x}_A^e\) are constants, so the only thing being differentiated is the basis functions: \(DF\) is built from \(\partial N_A/\partial \xi_j\), which is Homework 6 work. And \(DF\) depends on \(\underline{\xi}\), so unless the element is a parallelogram it is a different matrix at every point.
The determinant is the Jacobian,
\[
J = \det DF = \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial \xi}\frac{\partial x_2}{\partial \eta}
            - \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial \eta}\frac{\partial x_2}{\partial \xi},
\qquad
d\Omega = J\,d\xi\,d\eta,
\]
which is what lets every element integral be computed on the parent domain:
\[
\int_{\Omega^e} (\cdot)\,d\Omega = \int_{-1}^{1}\!\!\int_{-1}^{1} (\cdot)\;J(\xi,\eta)\,d\xi\,d\eta .
\]
crumbs: 13  Class 13: The Jacobian Matrix

title: 13  Class 13: The Jacobian Matrix
text:
13.2 What the columns are
The first column of \(DF\) is \(\partial\underline{x}/\partial\xi\) and the second is \(\partial\underline{x}/\partial\eta\). These are tangent vectors: column 1 points along the image of a line of constant \(\eta\), column 2 along the image of a line of constant \(\xi\). Those are the curves already drawn on the Class 12 viewer.
Taken on their own, two arrows are not very informative. They become informative when you see what they are the edges of. Take a small square of side \(h\) in the parent domain. Its image under the map is a slightly curved patch. The parallelogram spanned by \(h\) times the two columns of \(DF\) is the flat approximation of that patch, and
\[
\text{area of the parallelogram} = |J|\,h^2 .
\]
As \(h\) shrinks the curved patch and the parallelogram become the same shape. That is the statement that \(DF\) is the derivative. The sign of \(J\) says whether the image keeps the orientation of the original square or reverses it.
crumbs: 13  Class 13: The Jacobian Matrix

title: 13  Class 13: The Jacobian Matrix
text:
13.4 Reading the output
The table holds the ingredients. Columns \(\partial N_A/\partial\xi\) and \(\partial N_A/\partial\eta\) are the two components of \(\nabla_\xi N_A\), and the footer row is each of them weighted by the nodal coordinates, which is to say the two columns of \(DF\). Nothing in the matrix comes from anywhere else.
Under \(J = \det DF\) the three areas are printed together:

\(h^2\), the area of the square in the parent domain;
\(J h^2\), the area of the parallelogram \(DF\) predicts;
the signed area of the image of that square. 

Shrink \(h\) and the ratio of the last two goes to \(1\). That limit is the definition of the derivative, and it is the reason \(d\Omega = J\,d\xi\,d\eta\) is allowed inside an integral.
crumbs: 13  Class 13: The Jacobian Matrix

title: 13  Class 13: The Jacobian Matrix
text:
13.5 Things to try

Move the point around the default element. \(J\) changes from place to place: the quarter annulus stretches more at the outer radius than the inner one. A single number does not describe the whole element.
Set \(h = 1.2\) and compare the filled patch with the dashed parallelogram. They differ. Now drag \(h\) down to \(0.05\) and they coincide. \(DF\) is a local statement.
Set \(p_\xi = p_\eta = 1\). The four-node element is a bilinear map, and \(J\) is not constant: the shading still varies. A bilinear element is only a pure stretch when it is a parallelogram.
Drag control point \(A = 1\) toward the interior of the element, past its neighbours, until part of the shading turns red. The \(J = 0\) curve appears, the image of the square flips over, and its arrowheads run opposite to the ones on the gold square. That is the 2D version of \(dx^e/d\xi < 0\) from Homework 7, case 4.
Put the point on the \(J = 0\) curve. The parallelogram collapses to a line: the two columns of \(DF\) have become parallel, so the map squashes a 2D neighbourhood onto a 1D one and \(DF\) has no inverse. Derivatives with respect to \(x\), which need \(DF^{-1}\), are undefined there.
Swap two control points that are not neighbours, for instance give \(A = 1\) the coordinates of \(A = 3\) and vice versa. The element outline may still look reasonable while the shading is entirely red. The outline does not tell you whether an element is valid; the sign of \(J\) does.
crumbs: 13  Class 13: The Jacobian Matrix

title: 13  Class 13: The Jacobian Matrix
text:
13.6 Derivatives with respect to \(x\)
The weak form needs \(\nabla_x N_A\), the gradient in physical coordinates. But \(N_A\) is defined on the parent domain, so the only derivatives we can take directly are \(\partial N_A/\partial \xi_j\). The chain rule connects them. Since \(N_A\) reaches \(\underline{\xi}\) only through \(\underline{x}\),
\[
\frac{\partial N_A}{\partial \xi_j}
= \frac{\partial N_A}{\partial x_i}\,\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial \xi_j}
= \frac{\partial x_i}{\partial \xi_j}\,\frac{\partial N_A}{\partial x_i},
\]
which in matrix form is \(\nabla_\xi N_A = \left(DF\right)^T \nabla_x N_A\). Solving for the part we want,
\[
\boxed{\;\nabla_x N_A = \left(DF\right)^{-T}\,\nabla_\xi N_A\;}
\]
In 2D the inverse is written out easily, since
\[
DF^{-1} = \frac{1}{J}
\begin{bmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial \eta} & -\dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial \eta} \\[10pt]
-\dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial \xi} & \dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial \xi}
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
DF^{-T} = \frac{1}{J}
\begin{bmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial \eta} & -\dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial \xi} \\[10pt]
-\dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial \eta} & \dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial \xi}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Note the \(1/J\). Everything said above about \(J\) changing sign now has a second consequence: at \(J = 0\) the spatial gradient does not exist, and near \(J = 0\) it is large. An element that is merely folded gives wrong areas; an element that is folded also gives unusable derivatives, which is what actually enters the stiffness matrix.
The viewer below shows one basis function at a time. In each panel the thin curve is the level set of \(N_A\) through the current point, and the arrow is the gradient, which is perpendicular to its own level set in its own domain. The two arrows generally point in different directions: \(DF^{-T}\) rotates and rescales, so a gradient that points one way in the parent domain need not point that way in the element.

title: 13  Class 13: The Jacobian Matrix
text:
13.7 Next
\(J\) is a polynomial in \(\xi\) and \(\eta\) whose degree depends on the element, and that degree is what decides how many quadrature points are enough. With \(J\) for the area change and \(DF^{-T}\) for the derivatives, every piece of the element stiffness matrix can now be written as an integral over the parent domain and evaluated by quadrature.

title: 14  Class 14: The ID and IEN Arrays
text:
14.1 The mesh
Assembly needs two pieces of bookkeeping, and they do different jobs.
IEN describes given an element and a local basis function, which global basis function is this? Given a local index \(a\) on element \(e\), it returns the global index \(A\):
\[
A = \mathrm{IEN}(a,e).
\]
For a tensor-product element the local index itself comes from the stride rule of Class 11, \(a = a_\xi + (p+1)\,a_\eta\), so each element carries \(n_{en} = (p+1)^2\) of them.
ID clarifies whether this basis function has an unknown attached to it? Given a global index \(A\), it returns the equation number, or \(-1\) when the value there is prescribed:
\[
\mathrm{ID}[A] =
\begin{cases}
\text{equation number}, & u(A) \text{ unknown} \\
-1, & u(A) \text{ prescribed}
\end{cases}
\]
Equation numbers run consecutively from \(0\), skipping the prescribed nodes, so the global system is \(n_{eq} \times n_{eq}\) rather than \(n_{bf} \times n_{bf}\).
Composed, they are what the assembly loop actually uses:
\[
A = \mathrm{ID}\big[\mathrm{IEN}(a,e)\big],
\]
sometimes written as its own array, \(\mathrm{LM}(a,e)\).
Five elements: four around the boundary and one in the middle. At degree 1 the boundary edges are straight and the domain is a square with four trapezoids around a central square. At degree 2 and above the extra nodes on each boundary edge are placed on a circle, and the same five elements describe a disk.
The local origin of each element has been rotated so that they do not all start in the same corner. That is deliberate: nothing requires element 3’s local node 0 to sit where element 0’s does, and the domain boundary ends up on a different local edge in each of the four outer elements.

title: 14  Class 14: The ID and IEN Arrays
text:
14.2 What the widget is showing
One global basis function, several local names. Click any node on a shared edge. It lights up in two elements, sometimes three or four at the inner corners, and the readout lists every \(\mathrm{IEN}(a,e)\) that returns it. That is the whole content of the IEN array: the same unknown is local node 6 in one element and local node 2 in its neighbour, and assembly has to add both contributions into the same global row.
The local numbering is arbitrary, the global numbering is not. Because the origins are rotated, element 1’s local node 0 is in a different physical corner from element 0’s. The mesh does not care. What matters is only that IEN is consistent with however each element chose to number itself.
Prescribed nodes drop out of the equations, not out of the mesh. Hatch an edge and watch the ID array: those nodes go to \(-1\), and every ID value after them shifts down by one, because equation numbers are consecutive over the unknowns. The node is still there, still has a basis function, still appears in IEN. It just has no equation of its own, and its known value moves to the right-hand side of its neighbours’ equations.
Two different lengths. IEN is indexed by local node and element, so it has \(n_{en} \times n_{el}\) entries no matter what the boundary conditions are. ID is indexed by global node, so it has \(n_{bf}\) entries, of which \(n_{eq}\) are equation numbers. Changing a boundary condition changes ID and leaves IEN untouched.
crumbs: 14  Class 14: The ID and IEN Arrays

title: 14  Class 14: The ID and IEN Arrays
text:
14.3 Things to try

Click the node at the centre of a shared edge between two outer elements. It has two local names. Now click an inner corner of the middle element: three elements meet there, so it has three.
Hatch one edge, then a second. Watch \(n_{eq}\) drop and the equation numbers renumber. The corner shared by the two hatched edges is prescribed once, not twice.
Set all four edges to Dirichlet. Every boundary node goes to \(-1\) and only the interior nodes carry equations — at degree 1 that leaves just the four inner corners.
Set every edge to Neumann. Nothing is prescribed, \(n_{eq} = n_{bf}\), and the global matrix would be singular: this is the two-prescribed-fluxes case from Project 1, Task 5, in two dimensions.
Change the degree from 2 to 1. The disk becomes a square and the mid-edge nodes disappear, but the five elements and their connectivity are unchanged — degree changes the number of basis functions, not the mesh.
Go to degree 3 and turn on all local indices. This is what the bookkeeping actually looks like at modest degree, and why nobody writes it out by hand.

title: 16  Class 16: Derivatives of the Solution
text:
16.1 One basis function, and its derivative
The solution \(u^h\) is built from basis functions. However, many quantities of interest, such as strain, stress, and flux, are built from the derivatives of \(u^h\). The derivative of the solution is built from the derivative of the basis functions used to approximate \(u^h\). This page aims to clarify that difference in one dimension and visually shows why approximation error is larger for these quantities of interest and describes how fast that error can shrink.
Pick a basis function and watch both curves. The function itself is continuous across element boundaries. Its derivative is not.

title: 16  Class 16: Derivatives of the Solution
text:
16.3 Why this matters for error
Pushing the sliders should clarify two things. First, the approximation of \(u\) looks good long before the approximation of \(du/dx\) does, and second the derivative for Lagrange basis functions are never required to be continuous.
To talk how error deteriorates, we need to be able to measure the energy of the error. To do so, we will use Sobolev norms. In one dimension, these look like
\[
\|e\|_{H^0(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 \, d\Omega,
\qquad
\|e\|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 + \left(e_{,x}\right)^2 d\Omega,
\]
and in general \(\|e\|_{H^s}\) includes every derivative up to the \(s\)-th. \(H^0\) is the same thing as \(L^2\): it only asks whether the values are close. \(H^1\) also asks whether the slopes are close — which, as the lower plot shows, is a harder thing to get right.
Approximation of a derivative, as opposed to a solution, reduces the convergence rate by one, meaning that the exponent on \(h\) (the size of the mesh, which forces error down as \(h\) decreases) decreases by one.
\[
\|e\|_{H^s(\Omega)} \;\leq\; C \, h^{\beta} \, \|u\|_{H^{k+1}(\Omega)}
\]
where typically in this class \(\beta = k+1-s\). Each derivative we want to measure in our error decreases accuracy by a power of \(h\). At degree \(k\), the solution converges at rate \(k+1,\) while the slope of the solution converges at rate \(k\). This will be made more precise and more concrete in the next class, where error estimates will be discussed more completely. We will also discuss how to measure the convergence rate, \(\beta\) in a software code to make sure that the finite element solver is working correctly.
crumbs: 16  Class 16: Derivatives of the Solution

title: 17  Class 17: Convergence Rates
text:
17.1 What we measure the error in
We have built a finite element solver and we have looked at its solution and its derivative. The obvious next question is whether the answer is any good, and that question has a surprisingly precise answer: not what the error is, but how fast it goes away as we refine the mesh.
The error is a function, not a number:
\[ e(x) := u(x) - u^h(x) . \]
To get a number out of it we need a norm, and we need one that can ask about derivatives, because we already know the derivative is approximated particularly poorly. The Sobolev norms do exactly that. In one dimension:
\[
\|e\|_{H^0(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 \, dx, \qquad
\|e\|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 + \left(e_{,x}\right)^2 dx, \qquad
\|e\|_{H^2(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 + \left(e_{,x}\right)^2 + \left(e_{,xx}\right)^2 dx .
\]
Each one includes everything the previous one had, plus one more derivative. \(H^0\) is the same thing as \(L^2\) — it only asks whether the values are close. \(H^1\) also asks whether the slopes are close. \(H^2\) also asks about curvature.
In several dimensions the same thing, written with the gradient:
\[
\|e\|_{H^0(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 \, d\Omega, \qquad
\|e\|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 + \nabla e \cdot \nabla e \; d\Omega, \qquad
\|e\|_{H^2(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 + \nabla e \cdot \nabla e + \nabla^2 e : \nabla^2 e \; d\Omega ,
\]
or in index notation, which is often easier to implement from:
\[
\|e\|_{H^0}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 \, d\Omega, \qquad
\|e\|_{H^1}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 + e_{,i}\,e_{,i} \; d\Omega, \qquad
\|e\|_{H^2}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 + e_{,i}\,e_{,i} + e_{,ij}\,e_{,ij} \; d\Omega .
\]
Repeated indices are summed, so \(e_{,i}e_{,i}\) in two dimensions is \(\left(e_{,x}\right)^2 + \left(e_{,y}\right)^2\), which is exactly \(\nabla e \cdot \nabla e\).
In practice we almost always report \(H^0\) and \(H^1\). \(H^0\) tells you whether the solution is right, while \(H^1\) tells you whether the fluxes and strains you extract from it are right, and those are usually the quantities of interest. \(H^2\) is not particularly usefule for the Poisson equation, but plays a bigger role in beam and shell problems and in mixing theory.

title: 17  Class 17: Convergence Rates
text:
17.2 What \(h\) means
Every element has a size. The one the estimate uses is the diameter of the element — the longest distance between any two of its points — and then \(h\) is the largest of those over the whole mesh:
\[ h_K = \mathrm{diam}\left(\Omega^K\right) = \max_{\underline{a},\underline{b}\,\in\,\Omega^K} \left|\underline{a}-\underline{b}\right| ,
\qquad h = \max_K h_K . \]
In one dimension that is just the length of the interval. In two and three dimensions it is a diagonal, not an edge — which matters, because a long thin element has a much larger diameter than its short edge suggests.

h is the diameter, not an edge length. In 2D and 3D it is the longest
diagonal across the element.The mesh's h is the largest of them.
Note the stretched element: its short edge is small, but its diameter — and
therefore its h — is not.



17.2.1 Quasi-uniformity is a property of a family of meshes
The estimates come with a hidden assumption, and it is easy to state imprecisely. A family of meshes \(\{\mathcal{T}_h\}\), indexed by \(h \to 0\), is quasi-uniform if there is a constant \(\rho > 0\) that does not depend on \(h\) such that
\[ \min_K h_K \;\geq\; \rho \, h \qquad \text{for every mesh in the family.} \]
The whole content is in does not depend on \(h\). Any single mesh has finitely many elements, so \(h/h_{\min}\) is automatically some finite number — you can always find a constant that works. You cannot look at one mesh and say whether it is quasi-uniform. The question is whether that ratio stays bounded as you refine, or grows without limit.

You have to watch a sequence, not a mesh. Top: uniform refinement, where
the ratio of largest to smallest element stays at 1 forever. Bottom: graded refinement toward
the left end, where the ratio grows at every level and is unbounded over the family. The
bottom family is not quasi-uniform.
The particular error estimators given here assume a quasi-uniform refinement, but we will see that in some cases not having such a quasi-uniform refinement may be good.
This goes to show that these a-priori error estimators are just one resource that we have to improve accuracy.



So why does the assumption appear at all? Because it is what lets us write the estimate in terms of a single number \(h\). The underlying approximation results are local — they hold element by element in terms of \(h_K\), and need only shape regularity, a bound on how stretched any individual element may be. Quasi-uniformity is the extra condition that lets us replace every \(h_K\) by one global \(h\) and still have a sharp statement. The error constant \(C\) that we will see later degrades as \(h/h_{\min}\) grows.


17.2.2 Refining in the right place beats refining everywhere
A non-quasi-uniform family for mesh refinement is not always bad. If the solution is hard to resolve in one small region, putting your elements there is far more effective than spreading them evenly — and the a-priori estimate below, written for a single \(h\), simply does not describe what you get.
Here is the demonstration. Take
\[ u(x) = \tanh\!\big(25(x-\tfrac{1}{2})\big), \qquad f = -u_{,xx} , \]
which is perfectly smooth — it has derivatives of every order — but swings from \(-1\) to \(1\) across a narrow layer in the middle and is nearly flat everywhere else. Use quadratic elements, \(k=2\). Refine three ways, always to the same number of elements.

Three things to take from this.
This has nothing to do with smoothness. \(\tanh\) is infinitely differentiable, so the solution is as regular as anyone could ask. The only thing that differs between the three rows is where the elements sit. Resolution and regularity are separate issues, and this is the resolution one.
Refining where it matters gives the least amount of error. Clustering at the layer reaches 2.91 — essentially the rate quadratic elements are capable of — and at 128 elements it is six times more accurate than uniform for exactly the same cost. That family is deliberately not quasi-uniform.
Refining in the wrong place doesn’t help. Clustering at the ends means that you don’t refine in the one region that needed elements. Its measured rate is 0.87, and at 128 elements it is still a thousand times less accurate than clustering at the layer. Putting elements somewhere is not the same as putting them somewhere useful.
Note also that the uniform row reads 2.60 rather than 3. The estimate is asymptotic, and on these meshes the layer is still only a few elements wide, so we are not yet in the range where it applies. That is a different effect again, and we return to it later.
So when we write \(\|e\| \leq C h^\beta \|u\|\) in the next section and talk about measuring a slope, understand what it describes: uniform refinement of a quasi-uniform family. That is the setting where a single \(h\) means something. Adaptive and graded meshes are common and are frequently better. Deciding where to put the elements needs different tools, a-posteriori estimators, which we are not covering here.

title: 17  Class 17: Convergence Rates
text:
17.3 A-priori error estimates
A priori means before the fact: before you solve anything, you can say how the error will behave, purely from the polynomial degree, the mesh size, and how smooth the exact solution is. You do not need the computed answer to write it down. (The contrast is an a-posteriori estimate, which is computed after you solve, out of the solution you got, and which can give you an actual number and tell you which elements to refine. We are not doing those here.)
The standard a-priori estimate, for a sufficiently smooth exact solution, is
\[
\boxed{\;\|e\|_{H^s(\Omega)} \;\leq\; C \, h^{\beta} \, \|u\|_{H^{k+1}(\Omega)},
\qquad \beta = \min\big(k+1-s,\; 2(k+1-m)\big)\;}
\]
with \(k\) the polynomial degree, \(s\) the norm we measure in, and \(m\) the number of derivatives on a single term of the weak form. For the problems we solve in this class, \(m=1\), and the second argument is never lower, so in practice
\[ \beta = k + 1 - s . \]

17.3.1 When the solution is not smooth enough
If you look at the right hand side of the above boxed equation carefully, you will see that it contains \(\|u\|_{H^{k+1}}\). The estimate is only meaningful if that quantity is finite — that is, if the exact solution actually lives in \(H^{k+1}(\Omega)\). If it does not, the bound is vacuous as written, and the correct statement replaces \(k+1\) by however much regularity the solution really has.
If \(u \in H^{r}(\Omega)\) and \(r < k+1\), then
\[
\boxed{\;\|e\|_{H^s(\Omega)} \;\leq\; C \, h^{\min(k+1,\,r)-s} \, \|u\|_{H^{r}(\Omega)}\;}
\]
so the rate is governed by the solution, not by the degree, and the norm bounding it is the one the solution actually belongs to. Once \(r\) drops below \(k+1\), using higher more polynomial degree does not improve the a priori error estimate because \(\min(k+1,r)\) stops moving.
This is not the \(\min\) in the earlier formula doing something. That one compares the approximation space against the variational form, and both of its arguments grow with \(k\). This is a third, separate limiter sitting outside that estimate entirely.
A worked example: suppose the exact solution happens to lie in \(H^{2}\), and we discretize it with quadratic elements, \(k=2\). Then \(\min(k+1, r) = \min(3, 2) = 2\), so
\[ \|e\|_{L^2} \leq C\,h^{2}\|u\|_{H^2}, \qquad \|e\|_{H^1} \leq C\,h^{1}\|u\|_{H^2} , \]
rather than the \(h^3\) and \(h^2\) that quadratic elements deliver on a smooth solution. One order has been lost in each norm, and switching to cubic elements would not recover it — \(\min(4,2)\) is still 2.
It is worth being clear in advance that it is a different mechanism from anything in Section 2.2: there, the solution was perfectly smooth and only the mesh was badly placed. Here the mesh may be flawless and the solution itself is the limit.


17.3.2 What the constant is
The constant in this above error estimate, \(C,\) is typically nebulous. While we don’t know exactly what it is, we do know that it is independent of:

the mesh size \(h\), so we can talk about the rate of error decrease, and
the exact solution \(u\), because the complexity of the error in from the solution has been factored into \(\|u\|_{H^{k+1}}\).

It depends on: the domain \(\Omega\), the polynomial degree \(k\), the shape-regularity and quasi-uniformity constants of the mesh family, and the coefficients of the problem (for us, \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\), through how strongly elliptic the operator is).
So the estimate tells you the slope of the error curve and not its height. You cannot use it to predict that your error will be \(10^{-4}\). You can use it to predict that halving \(h\) will divide the error by \(2^\beta\), and doing this in code tells you if your software is correct.

title: 17  Class 17: Convergence Rates
section: 17.4 Turning the estimate into a straight line
text:
17.4 Turning the estimate into a straight line
The estimate is a power law, which is awkward to look at. Take a logarithm of both sides:
\[
\log \|e\|_{H^s} \;\leq\; \log\left(C\,\|u\|_{H^{k+1}}\right) + \beta \log h .
\]
Everything in the first term on the right is a constant — it does not change as we refine. So if we plot \(\log\|e\|\) against \(\log h\), we should see a straight line of slope \(\beta\), sitting at a height we do not get to predict:
\[ \underbrace{\log\|e\|}_{y} = \beta \underbrace{\log h}_{x} + \underbrace{\log(C\|u\|)}_{\text{intercept}} . \]
Consequently, convergence results typically always shown on log–log axes. The quantity we care about is a slope, and only these axes make it a slope.

17.4.1 Dyadic refinement
To measure that slope we typically refine the mesh dyadically, where each level halves the element size, so \(h_{i+1} = h_i/2\). In one dimension that means splitting every element in two; in two dimensions, splitting every element into four.

Each level halves h. In 1D the element count doubles; in 2D it
quadruples, because each element splits in both directions. The element size halves
either way, which is what the estimate is written in terms of. Note what this costs: in 2D,
three levels of refinement is 64 times as many elements.


Because each level halves \(h\), the slope between two consecutive levels has a very simple form. Starting from
\[ \boxed{\;\beta \approx \frac{\log\|e_{i+1}\| - \log\|e_{i}\|}{\log h_{i+1} - \log h_{i}}\;} \]
and substituting \(h_{i+1} = h_i/2\), the denominator is just \(-\log 2\), so
\[ \beta \approx \log_2\!\left(\frac{\|e_i\|}{\|e_{i+1}\|}\right)\]
In words: halve the mesh, and the rate is the base-2 logarithm of how many times smaller the error got. If the error drops by a factor of 4, the rate is 2. By 8, the rate is 3.

And the measured values are clean integers, which is exactly why this is such a good test of whether your code is right: a bug in assembly usually shows up as a rate of 1.4 or 0.9 rather than as an obviously wrong picture.

On this same problem at \(k=5\), the rate holds at 6.00 out to 16 elements and then reads 4.94 at 32, where the error is already \(8.6\times10^{-13}\). If a high-degree run looks like it has stopped converging, check the size of the error before concluding that something is broken.

title: 17  Class 17: Convergence Rates
text:
17.5 Actually computing the error norm
The norms above are integrals over \(\Omega\), and we evaluate them the same way we evaluate every other integral in this course: break the domain into elements, push each element back to the parent domain, and apply Gaussian quadrature.
Step 1 — split the global integral into element integrals.
\[ \|e\|_{H^0(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega \left(u - u^h\right)^2 d\Omega
= \sum_{e} \int_{\Omega^e} \left(u - u^h\right)^2 d\Omega . \]
Step 2 — change variables to the parent domain. Each element integral becomes an integral over the parent element, with the Jacobian determinant accounting for the change of area (or length):
\[ \int_{\Omega^e} \left(u - u^h\right)^2 d\Omega
= \int_{\square} \left(u\!\left(\underline{x}^e(\underline{\xi})\right) - u^h(\underline{\xi})\right)^2
J^e(\underline{\xi}) \; d\square ,
\qquad J^e = \det\left(DF^e\right) . \]
Step 3 — apply quadrature.
\[ \boxed{\;\|e\|_{H^0(\Omega)}^2 \approx \sum_e \sum_q w_q
\left(u\!\left(\underline{x}^e(\underline{\xi}_q)\right) - u^h(\underline{\xi}_q)\right)^2
J^e(\underline{\xi}_q)\;} \]
For the \(H^1\) norm, add the gradient term, which also uses \(DF^{-T}\).
\[ \|e\|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2 \approx \sum_e \sum_q w_q \left[
\left(u - u^h\right)^2 +
\left(\nabla_{\underline{x}} u - DF^{-T}\nabla_{\underline{\xi}} u^h\right)\cdot
\left(\nabla_{\underline{x}} u - DF^{-T}\nabla_{\underline{\xi}} u^h\right)
\right] J^e \; . \]

17.5.1 The two solutions are evaluated differently
Inside that sum there are two things being evaluated at the same quadrature point, and they are reached by different routes.
The approximate solution is evaluated directly in the reference domain. It is built from local basis functions, and the IEN array tells us which coefficients to use:
\[ u^h(\underline{\xi}_q) = \sum_{a=0}^{n_{en}-1} d_{\,\mathrm{IEN}(a,e)} \; N_a(\underline{\xi}_q) . \]
No mapping is needed. The basis functions are defined on the parent element, so \(\xi_q\) is already the right input.
The exact solution must be evaluated at the physical point. \(u\) is a function of \(\underline{x}\), so we first have to find where this quadrature point actually sits in space, using the spatial mapping:
\[ \underline{x}^e(\underline{\xi}_q) = \sum_{a=0}^{n_{en}-1} \underline{x}_a \, N_a(\underline{\xi}_q),
\qquad\text{then evaluate } u\!\left(\underline{x}^e(\underline{\xi}_q)\right) . \]
This is the same two-step move you already made when assembling the local force vector, where \(f\) had to be evaluated at \(\underline{x}(\underline{\xi}_q)\) rather than at \(\underline{\xi}_q\). If you mix the two up — feeding \(\xi_q\) straight into \(u\) — the code runs, the error comes out finite, and the convergence rate is wrong.


17.5.2 A practical warning about quadrature
The error \(e = u - u^h\) is not a polynomial, because \(u\) generally is not one. So the quadrature rule that was exact for your stiffness matrix is not exact here, and if you use too few points you end up measuring your quadrature error instead of your discretization error. Use more points than you think you need and confirm that adding points does not change the answer.

title: 17  Class 17: Convergence Rates
text:
17.6 Where this is going

Class 17 works through the estimate itself, these plots, and how to interpret a measured slope that is not what you expected.
Class 18 takes up why the estimate is true — Galerkin orthogonality, and the fact that the finite element solution is the best approximation available in its space.

Note that there has been no statement about where the exact solution \(u\) comes from, and on a real problem you don’t know this already. As a result, we typically test convergence rates by manufacturing a contrived solution, which will be discussed next time.

title: 18  Class 18: Manufactured Solutions and Galerkin Orthogonality
text:
18.1 Manufacturing a solution
The discussion in Class 17 did not cover two important parts of convergence analysis. First, we spent a whole class measuring how far \(u^h\) is from \(u\), without ever saying where \(u\) is supposed to come from. On a real problem we don’t actually have \(u\), and that is why we are running the solver in the first place. The second is more theoretical: the error estimate we wrote down is a statement about polynomials, and we never justified using it to describe the answer our solver actually produced. Today will cover both of these issues.
crumbs: 18  Class 18: Manufactured Solutions and Galerkin Orthogonality

title: 18  Class 18: Manufactured Solutions and Galerkin Orthogonality
text:
18.1.1 Running the problem backwards
Normally you are handed \(f\), \(\mathcal{g}\) and \(\mathcal{h}\), and you go looking for \(u\). That is the hard direction, and in general there is no formula at the end of it.
The trick is to run the arrow the other way. Pick the answer first, then work out which problem it solves. Choosing \(u\) is free — you can write down any function you like — and once you have it, finding the data that produces it is just differentiation, which is easy.
For the problem we have been solving all semester,
\[
u_{,xx} + f = 0 \ \text{ on } \Omega = (0,L), \qquad
u(L) = \mathcal{g}, \qquad -u_{,x}(0) = \mathcal{h},
\]
the recipe is three steps:

Choose any \(u\) you like, as long as it is smooth enough to differentiate twice.
Differentiate it twice and set \(f = -u_{,xx}\).
Evaluate at the two ends: \(\mathcal{g} = u(L)\) and \(\mathcal{h} = -u_{,x}(0)\).

Now feed \(f\), \(\mathcal{g}\) and \(\mathcal{h}\) to your solver. It has no idea anything unusual has happened — it is solving an ordinary boundary value problem. But you know the exact answer, so you can subtract it from \(u^h\) and measure the error for real.
This is called a manufactured solution, and it is how essentially all finite element software is verified.


18.1.2 A worked example
Take
\[ u(x) = \sin(\pi x) \qquad \text{on } \Omega = (0,1) . \]
Differentiate twice:
\[ u_{,x} = \pi \cos(\pi x), \qquad u_{,xx} = -\pi^2 \sin(\pi x), \]
so the forcing that produces this solution is
\[ f = -u_{,xx} = \pi^2 \sin(\pi x) . \]
The boundary data comes straight from evaluating:
\[ \mathcal{g} = u(1) = \sin(\pi) = 0, \qquad \mathcal{h} = -u_{,x}(0) = -\pi . \]
That is the whole derivation. Hand \(f = \pi^2\sin(\pi x)\), \(\mathcal{g} = 0\) and \(\mathcal{h} = -\pi\) to the solver, run the convergence study from Class 17, and the measured rates come out as

For \(p=5\), notice that the rate flattens or even slightly regresses for error around \(10^{-12}\). This does not indicate that the solver is incorrect here. Instead, it is an artifact of using double-precision arithmetic. We cannot typically represent solutions more accurately than machine precision, and so the benefits for refinement in the \(L^2\) norm cannot be adequately measured. However, this is not to say that the solution does not improve: by looking at the \(H^1\) norm you can see that error continues to decrease over the depicted number of elements with refinement even after error bottoms out in the \(L^2\) norm.


18.1.3 What this does and does not tell you
A manufactured solution is a verification tool: it answers did I implement the method correctly? If your rates come out at the predicted \(\beta\), your basis functions, your Jacobians, your assembly and your boundary conditions are almost certainly all right. Most coding mistakes break the rate, not just the constant, because they break the method rather than merely making it less accurate.
What it does not tell you is whether you solved the right problem (i.e. used the correct input). The physics, the geometry, the material data and the boundary conditions you chose are all still your responsibility. Verification asks whether you solved the equations right; it does not ask whether you had the right equations.
One more caution. You are free to pick any \(u\), which means you are also free to pick one that makes the test easier than it should be. If you choose a \(u\) that your basis can represent exactly (e.g. a straight line with \(p = 1\)), the error is zero at every refinement and you don’t see the convergence rates play out. Pick something your space genuinely has to approximate.
