title: 18  Class 18: Manufactured Solutions and Galerkin Orthogonality
section: 18.2 Why the estimate describes our solution
text:
18.2 Why the estimate describes our solution
Here is the gap Class 17 left open. The a-priori estimate
\[ \|e\|_{H^s(\Omega)} \leq C h^{\beta} \|u\|_{H^{p+1}(\Omega)} \]
comes from approximation theory. It says: given a mesh and a polynomial degree, here is how close we can guarantee the best possible function in that space gets to your arbitrary choice of \(u\). The rest of the material for this class aims to help us understand where this estimate came from.

18.2.1 Step one: the error is invisible to the approximation space
Write the left side of the weak form as
\[ a(w, v) := \int_\Omega w_{,x}\, v_{,x} \, dx .\]
or in multiple dimensions as
\[ a(w, v) := \int_\Omega w_{,i}\, \kappa_{ij} v_{,j} \, d\Omega .\]
This is short notation for exactly what your stiffness matrix computes, since \(K_{AB} = a(N_A, N_B)\).
Now put the two problems side by side. The exact solution satisfies the weak form against every test function \(w\in \mathcal{V}\):
\[ a(u, w) = L(w) \qquad \text{for all } w \in \mathcal{V} ,\]
where \(L(w)\) accounts for the forcing and boundary terms. The computed finite element solution satisfies the same equation, but only against the functions we actually built:
\[ a(u^h, w^h) = L(w^h) \qquad \text{for all } w^h \in \mathcal{V}^h .\]
Now, recall that \(\mathcal{V}^h \subset \mathcal{V}\), meaning that every function in \(\mathcal{V}^h\) is also in \(\mathcal{V}\). The basis functions we use are legitimate test functions, but happen to be just a small subset of them. So the first equation is true for \(w = w^h\) as well, and we may subtract the second equation from it:
\[ \boxed{\; a\!\left(u - u^h,\; w^h\right) = 0 \qquad \text{for all } w^h \in \mathcal{V}^h \;}\]
This is Galerkin orthogonality. If you look at \(a(w,v)\) as an inner product between two functions, it says that \(u-u^h\) is orthogonal to \(w^h\) under this physics-based inner product. In other words: measured in this energy inner product, the error, \(e= u-u^h\), is orthogonal to everything our approximation space can represent. The space cannot see its own error. If it could, the method would have used that information and done better.


18.2.2 Step two: so \(u^h\) is the best the space can do
Using the above energy inner product, define the energy norm by
\[ \|v\|_E := \sqrt{a(v,v)} .\]
For our problem this is just the size of a function’s derivative, so it is the \(H^1\) part of the error you have already been computing, which in general is weighted by the (positive definite) thermal conductivity matrix.
Now take any \(w^h\) in the space and split the difference between \(u\) and it into two pieces:
\[ u - w^h = \underbrace{\left(u - u^h\right)}_{\text{the error}} + \underbrace{\left(u^h - w^h\right)}_{\text{lives in } \mathcal{V}^h} .\]
Measure the size of both sides in the energy norm. Because \(a(\cdot,\cdot)\) is symmetric, this expands the way a squared length does, and the cross term is \(a(u - u^h,\, u^h - w^h)\) — which is zero, by Galerkin orthogonality, since the second slot lives in \(\mathcal{V}^h\). What is left is
\[ \left\|u - w^h\right\|_E^2 = \left\|u - u^h\right\|_E^2 + \left\|u^h - w^h\right\|_E^2 .\]
That is the Pythagorean theorem, with \(a(\cdot,\cdot)\) playing the role of the dot product. The last term cannot be negative, so dropping it and rearranging gives
\[ \boxed{\; \left\|u - u^h\right\|_E \;\leq\; \left\|u - w^h\right\|_E \qquad \text{for every } w^h \in \mathcal{V}^h \;}\]
The finite element solution is the best approximation in its space, measured in the energy norm. No other combination of your basis functions gets closer. This result is called Céa’s lemma.
It also clarifies what we have indicated repeatedly, that the finite element method is not an interpolation but is instead a best fit or projection. Under our physics-informed energy inner product, the finite element method finds the best approximation/solution to the real solution in a similar sense that projecting a 2D point onto the \(x\)-axis finds the closest point on the 1D line.


18.2.3 Seeing both of these at once
The widget below runs the same problem as before, at \(p=1\) on four elements, and lets you move the finite element answer off its correct value. Pick a basis function, slide its coefficient away from what the solver produced, and watch three things at once.

  
    PERTURB
    
      N₀
      N₁
      N₂
      N₃
    
    BY 0.20
    MEASURE IN
    
      energy norm
      L² norm
    
  
  
  
  





18.2.4 Why this is not interpolation
Look again at the widget in Section 18.1.2, at \(p=1\) with a few elements. The finite element curve passes exactly through the exact solution at every node. It is very tempting to conclude that the method works by interpolation — that it reads off \(u\) at the nodes and joins the dots.
It does not, and one dimension is misleading. Nodal exactness in 1D for the Poisson equation is a genuine theorem, but it is special to one dimension, and it stops being true in higher dimensions.
Below is the same manufactured problem in two dimensions, \(u = \sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y)\) on the unit square, solved with code that will be developed in Project 2. Both panels are a slice along \(y = \tfrac{1}{2}\), where the exact solution is just \(\sin(\pi x)\) again. The grey dashed line is \(u\), the thin blue line joins the dots through \(u\) at the nodes, and the heavy red line is what the solver actually returns.

  
  
  A slice at y = ½ through the finite element solution of
  u = sin(πx) sin(πy) on [0, 1]².
  On the coarse mesh the finite element answer overshoots the exact solution by
  23% at the center, and it is still 5.3% high after one refinement. An
  interpolant cannot do that: it is pinned to u at every node by construction.
  What you are looking at is the method choosing the closest point in its space measured in
  the energy norm, which is a statement about slopes over the whole domain, not about values
  at points. In one dimension that choice happens to land on the nodal values. In two it
  does not, and the projection shows itself.
  





18.2.5 The whole argument in three lines
The error estimate of Class 17 is the result of Galerkin orthogonality to get Céa’s lemma and then composing this with another lemma about polynomial interpolation. Here, Galerkin Orthogonality allows us to prove Céa’s lemma, and Céa’s lemma lets us swap \(u^h\) for any function we like out of the space. The polynomial function that interpolates the actual solution is one such function that could be used. The Bramble–Hilbert lemma says how well polynomials can interpolate a smooth function, with the interpolant written as \(\mathcal{I}_h u\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\|u - u^h\right\|_E
  &= \min_{w^h \in \mathcal{V}^h} \left\|u - w^h\right\|_E
  && \text{(Céa's lemma)} \\[2pt]
  &\leq \left\|u - \mathcal{I}_h u\right\|_E
  && \text{(pick the interpolant)} \\[2pt]
  &\leq C \, h^{\,p} \, \left\|u\right\|_{H^{p+1}(\Omega)}
  && \text{(Bramble–Hilbert)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The convergence rate \(h^p\) and the norm \(\|u\|_{H^{p+1}}\) both appear only on the last line, and could be altered slightly for less smooth solutions. The constant \(C\) also comes as a result of this interpolation theory lemma in the last line. Here, \(C\) measures how well degree-\(p\) polynomials fit a smooth function on an element.


18.2.6 A reading of this worth carrying forward
Saying \(u^h\) is the closest point is the same as saying \(u^h\) minimizes the error over everything in the space:
\[ \left\|u - u^h\right\|_E = \min_{w^h \in \mathcal{V}^h} \left\|u - w^h\right\|_E .\]
Keep that word minimizes in mind. There are two different minimization statements in this course and it is worth not confusing them. This one is about the approximation: of all the answers we could have built, we got the closest. The other one, in Class 23, is about the physics: the true solution \(u\) is the one that minimizes the total potential energy of the system over all admissible (test) functions, not just the ones our mesh can build.

title: 18  Class 18: Manufactured Solutions and Galerkin Orthogonality
section: 18.3 When a measured rate is not what you expected
text:
18.3 When a measured rate is not what you expected
Sometime you may run a convergence study and get a number that is not \(\beta\). This still may mean that nothing is wrong if it is the result of one of the following cases.
You are not refined enough yet. The estimate is asymptotic — it describes behavior as \(h \to 0\). On coarse meshes the measured rate typically creeps up on \(\beta\) from below rather than hitting it. Seeing 1.94 where you expected 2.00 is normal, and is often resolved after one more level of refinement.
You have hit machine precision. This one surprises people. At high polynomial degree the error drops so fast that after two or three refinements it reaches roundoff, around \(10^{-16}\), and it cannot get any smaller. The slope then flattens toward zero, and a plot that was beautifully straight suddenly bends. The method has not stopped working, but double precision arithmetic limits continuing.
Your quadrature is not good enough for the error integral. The error \(e = u - u^h\) is not a polynomial, since \(u\) generally is not, so the rule that integrates your stiffness matrix exactly will not integrate the error norm exactly. Use more points than you think you need, and confirm that adding more does not change the answer.

Class 19 moves to multiple dimensions and takes up the surface integrals that Neumann conditions require, which have no one-dimensional counterpart.
Class 23 returns to the energy idea from the other side: the minimization form of the problem, symmetric positive definiteness, and the question of whether a solution exists at all.

title: 19  Class 19: The Same Code in Any Dimension
text:
19.1 What the picture is telling you
The flowchart in Class 15 laid out the one-dimensional solver step by step. Going to two or three dimensions does not add steps to that chart, and it does not reorder them. The architecture is the same: build the arrays, loop the elements, loop the quadrature points, scatter, solve.
What changes is what lives inside some of the boxes. Most of them scale up without any new idea — a longer vector here, a bigger element matrix there. Three of them change in kind, and those three are what the next few classes are really about.
The column down the middle below is that shared infrastructure, drawn the same way as the trajectory in Class 15: the steps, the element loop, the quadrature loop. It is the same in any number of dimensions. Click any box and the one-dimensional version of that step appears on the left and the multidimensional version on the right, tagged as unchanged, merely larger, or genuinely different.
Eight of the eleven steps are either identical or simply larger. You already know how to write them. Three are not, and they are worth naming before you meet them in code.
The Jacobian, and spatial gradients. These two go together. In one dimension the Jacobian is a single number and the chain rule is a division: \(dN/dx\) is \((dN/d\xi)\) over the Jacobian. In two dimensions it becomes \(\nabla_x N = (DF)^{-T}\,\nabla_\xi N\) — you invert a matrix and transpose it, at every quadrature point of every element. Using \(DF^{-1}\) instead of \(DF^{-T}\) is the single most common bug in a first 2D code, and on a mesh of rectangles it will not show up, because \(DF\) is then diagonal and the two agree. It only breaks once an element is distorted.
Neumann boundary terms. In one dimension the boundary of the domain is two points, and \(h\) enters as one number added to one entry of \(\mathbf{F}\). There is no integral. In two dimensions the boundary is a curve, and \(\int_{\Gamma_h} N_A\,h\;d\Gamma\) is a real integral that needs its own quadrature loop along each boundary face, with its own arc-length Jacobian — which is not \(\det DF\). That machinery has no one-dimensional counterpart at all, which is why it gets a class of its own.
crumbs: 19  Class 19: The Same Code in Any Dimension

title: 20  Class 20: Quadrature in 2D, and Integrating Over a Face
text:
20.1 The 2D rule is the 1D rule, twice
Two things stand between the one-dimensional code and a working multidimensional one, and both are about integration. The first is easy and is mostly bookkeeping: a quadrature rule on the parent square is built from the rule on the parent interval, by multiplying. The second is not bookkeeping at all: integrating over the boundary of an element needs a different Jacobian from the one you use inside it.
A Gauss rule on \([-1,1]\) is a list of points \(\xi_g\) and weights \(w_g\) chosen so that
\[ \int_{-1}^{1} f(\xi)\,d\xi \;\approx\; \sum_{g} w_g\, f(\xi_g) \]
is exact whenever \(f\) is a polynomial of degree \(2n-1\) or less. On the parent square we want the same thing in two variables, and because the square is a product of two intervals, we get it for free:
\[
\int_{-1}^{1}\!\!\int_{-1}^{1} f(\xi,\eta)\;d\xi\,d\eta
\;\approx\; \sum_{i}\sum_{j} \underbrace{w_i\,w_j}_{\text{one weight}}\;
f\big(\underbrace{\xi_i,\;\eta_j}_{\text{one point}}\big) .
\]
Every 2D point is a pair of 1D points, and its weight is the product of the two 1D weights. Nothing is re-derived. Move the sliders and watch the grid come from the two rules on the edges.

title: 20  Class 20: Quadrature in 2D, and Integrating Over a Face
text:
20.2 Integrating over a face
Everything so far has been about integrating over the inside of an element, where the Jacobian is \(\det(DF)\) and it converts \(d\xi\,d\eta\) into \(d\Omega\). A Neumann term is not that integral. It runs over one face (or more faces) of the element,
\[ \int_{\Gamma_h^e} N_A\, h \; d\Gamma , \]
and a face is a curve, not an area. This requires two additional changes.
A face is a one-dimensional parent domain. Fix one parent coordinate at \(\pm 1\) and the other one still runs over \([-1,1]\). So a face integral is a 1D quadrature operation.
You only use part of the deformation gradient. Along a face where \(\eta\) is held fixed, the curve is traced only by \(\xi\), so its tangent is
\[ \underline{t} = \frac{\partial \underline{x}}{\partial \xi}
    \]
The thing that converts \(d\xi\) into arc length \(d\Gamma\) is the length of that tangent,
\[ \boxed{\;d\Gamma = \left\| \underline{t} \right\| d\xi \;} \]
which is not \(\det(DF)\).
Similarly, along a face where \(\xi\) is held fixed, the curve is traced only by \(\eta\), so its tangent is
\[ \underline{t} = \frac{\partial \underline{x}}{\partial \eta}
    \]
and the arclength is
\[ \boxed{\;d\Gamma = \left\| \underline{t} \right\| d\eta. \;} \]
Consequently, integration over a face which, for instance has \(\xi=1\) can be approximated using quadrature as
\[ \int_{\Gamma_h^e} N_A(1,\eta)\, h\big(x(1,\eta)) \; d\Gamma \approx \sum_q^{n_g} w_g N_A(1,\eta_g) h\big(x(1,\eta_g)) \big|\big|\underline{t}\big(x(1,\eta_g)\big)\big|\big|. \]
Similarly, integration over a face which, for instance, has \(\eta=-1\) can be approximated as
\[ \int_{\Gamma_h^e} N_A(\xi,-1)\, h\big(x(\xi,-1)) \; d\Gamma \approx \sum_q^{n_g} w_g N_A(\xi_g,-1) h\big(x(\xi_g,-1)) \big|\big|\underline{t}\big(x(\xi_g,-1)\big)\big|\big|. \]

20.2.1 Where that length comes from
The boxed formula is not a definition. It falls out of asking one question: if I take a small step along the face in the parent domain, how far have I actually moved in the physical element?
Hold \(\eta\) fixed and step from \(\xi\) to \(\xi + \Delta\xi\). A Taylor expansion of the mapping gives
\[
\underline{x}(\xi + \Delta\xi,\, \eta)
\;\approx\; \underline{x}(\xi,\eta) \;+\; \frac{\partial \underline{x}}{\partial \xi}\,\Delta\xi
\;=\; \underline{x} + \underline{t}\,\Delta\xi ,
\]
so the physical displacement is the vector \(\underline{t}\,\Delta\xi\). Its length is \(\|\underline{t}\|\,\Delta\xi\). That is the entire derivation: \(\|\underline{t}\|\) is how much physical boundary you get per unit of parent boundary, at that point on the face.
The figure below makes the point by taking the same parent step on two different faces.

  
  
  The same Δη on two faces. On the left both marked intervals are identical:
  the parent domain has no idea which face is which. On the right the inner one has become a
  short piece of arc and the outer one a piece twice as long, because
  ∥t∥ on the outer face is exactly twice its value on the inner one (the figure prints both). That single number is the
  whole difference, and it is why the outer arc is twice the length of the inner one.
  

Three consequences worth stating out loud:

\(\|\underline{t}\|\) is a local stretch factor.
It varies along the face whenever the mapping is not affine. You cannot pull it out of the integral the way you can a constant element length in 1D.
Only the length matters. \(\underline{t}\) also tells you which way the face runs, but the direction cancels out of \(d\Gamma\); it comes back later, when you need the outward normal for a flux.



20.2.2 Why it is not \(\det(DF)\)
\(\det(DF)\) is the answer to a different question. It asks: given a small rectangle \(\Delta\xi \times \Delta\eta\) in the parent domain, what is the area of its image? That image is a parallelogram spanned by both columns of \(DF\), and its area is \(|\det(DF)|\,\Delta\xi\,\Delta\eta\).
On a face you have no second direction to span anything with. You are not carrying a rectangle across the mapping, you are carrying a segment. One column, not two; a length, not an area.

  
  
  Two different objects. Inside the element, both columns of DF are in play and
  they span a parallelogram — that area is what det DF measures. On the face only
  one column survives, and what you need is the length of that single arrow. They are not the
  same quantity and they do not even have the same units: one is a length per unit parent
  length, the other an area per unit parent area.
  



One more reason to be careful: on an axis-aligned rectangle the two are proportional. For an \(h_1 \times h_2\) element, \(DF\) is diagonal, \(\det(DF) = h_1h_2/4\), and on the \(\eta\)-face \(\|\underline{t}\| = h_1/2\). Their ratio is \(h_2/2\) — a constant. Use the wrong one on a rectangular mesh and every face integral is off by the same factor, which looks far more like a units slip than a bug, and does not disturb the convergence rate at all. It only becomes obvious once an element is curved or distorted, which is exactly the case the figure above shows.
See the following widget to help in understanding this.

  
    FACES
    
      ξ = −1 (inner)
      ξ = +1 (outer)
      η = −1
      η = +1
    
    POINTS 3
  
  
    INTEGRAND
    
      1  (length)
      Nₑ
      x²+y²
    
    NODE A 0
     show tangents

title: 20  Class 20: Quadrature in 2D, and Integrating Over a Face
text:
20.3 Summary

2D Quadrature is the Product of 1D Rules. 1D rules are established in each of the directions, coordinates are the union of individual 1D coordinates, and quadrature weights are the product of 1D quadrature weights. This is a similar story to how 2D tensor product basis functions were defined in Class 11.
A face integral is a mapped 1D operation. Hold one parent coordinate at \(\pm 1\), let the other vary, and reuse the same Gauss points you already have in 1D with the additional 2D coordinate.
The Jacobian on a face is \(\|\underline{t}\|\), not \(\det(DF)\), and \(\underline{t}\) is one column of \(DF\) corresponding to the derivative with respect to whichever parent coordinate is free.
A basis function contributes to a face only if its node is on it. Everything else integrates to zero there, which is why the element’s face vector has only \(p+1\) non-zero entries.
The widget’s lengths miss the true \(\pi/2\) and \(\pi\) by about half a percent, and adding quadrature points does not help. It is tempting to blame the quadrature, but that is not it: the rule converges perfectly well, settling on \(1.5624171\) by about eight points and staying there. What it is converging to is the length of the element’s own edge, which is a biquadratic curve through three points on the circle, not the circle. The half percent is geometry error, not integration error, and the only cures are a finer mesh or a higher-degree geometry.

title: 21  Class 21: CAD, Meshing, and Discretization Choice
text:
21.1 What a mesh is made of
The a finite element method requires a basis to approximate the solution to a problem of interest. These bases are defined using the structure of a number of cells glued together to approximate the intended shape as a mesh.
Meshes are typically created by pushing a computer-aided design (CAD) model through a specialized software, though sometimes they come as the result of processing geographic data or point cloud information. To get to a finite element mesh, somebody likely designed the part in CAD and somebody chose how to chop it up. Both of decisions are then baked into your answer before you assemble a single element matrix. This class is a very brief introduction to those two steps, as well as a proposed pipeline to use a the CAD model for analysis directly without the use of an intermediary mesh.
For traditional FEM, mesh elements are convex triangles or quadrilaterals in two dimensions, or convex tetrahedra, pyramids, prisms, or hexahedra in three dimensions.
crumbs: 21  Class 21: CAD, Meshing, and Discretization Choice

title: 21  Class 21: CAD, Meshing, and Discretization Choice
text:
Figure 21.1: Surface mesh elements include triangles and quadrilaterals. Triangles are fixed by three points and is always flat planar, while quadrilaterals have a fourth point that is free to leave the plane, which is why it uses a bilinear map. Quadrilaterals can fold or become otherwise problematic if care is not taken.









Figure 21.2: Four typical volumetric finite elements are shown. Most meshes rely primarily on tetrahedra and hexahedra, while prisms and pyramids mostly exist so that a hexahedral region can transition to an unstructured tetrahedral region.




21.1.1 Triangles and tetrahedra: easy to get but not always what you want
Generating a good triangular or tetrahedral mesh of an arbitrary shape is in many senses a solved problem. The algorithms to generate these are robust, automatic, and in some cases decades old. You can frequently hand a tet mesher a complicated part and get a usable mesh without user intervention, even if the model itself has problems. Local refinement on these meshes is also easily done by splitting a single tetrahedron and patching up its neighbours.
Triangular and tetrahedral elements (together called simplicial elements) work well for a large class of problems. However, they may perform poorly in some cases, such as

Directional physics. In a boundary layer the solution changes dramatically across the layer and barely at all along it. What you want there is a stack of elements aligned with the wall. Tetrahedra lack capacity to effectively operate for these directional problems, and typically give poor results here.
Nonlinear and constrained problems. Linear tetrahedra are notoriously stiff when the material is nearly incompressible or has gone plastic because there are not enough degrees of freedom per element to satisfy the constraint and still deform. This phenomenon is called locking and solutions using simplicial meshes are far too stiff compared to the actual solution without extensive mesh refinement.



21.1.2 Quadrilaterals and hexahedra: better elements but worse to build
A hex mesh will generally get you a given accuracy with far fewer elements, handles directional features gracefully, and behaves much better on the nonlinear problems above. The challenge is that automatic all-hex meshing of a general solid is not a solved problem. Real hex meshes are often built with substantial manual guidance — decomposing the part into mappable blocks by hand — and unstructured local refinement is challenging because you cannot split one hexahedron without propagating the change through a whole layer of its neighbours.
Prisms and pyramids are the glue. They are rarely the point of a mesh. A pyramid has a quadrilateral on one face and triangles on the others, which is exactly what you need to close the gap where a hex block meets a tet region. Prisms do the same job for extruded boundary layers sitting on top of a tet interior.


21.1.3 Meshes are usually straight, recent trends are going towards curvilinear representations






Figure 21.3: For an identical curved geometry, meshes can be defined in a variety of ways. On the left, a coarse straight-sided mesh approximates geometry dramatically. In the center, this can be reduced by additional mesh refinement with (bi-)linear elements, but the approximation is never fully removed. However, curving the elements (on the right) fixes the geometry without adding elements, but through the use of higher polynomials.



Most meshes in used in industry are piecewise linear, with straight edges, and flat faces. This allows for a simple representation and is directly usable for all finite element methods. However, this comes at the price of accurate geometry. For the quarter annulus of Class 20, this introduced a half-percent length error through geometry error, not quadrature error, and no refinement mechanism could address it. Curved (higher-order) meshes have extra nodes per edge so the element can bend to the real boundary, and they are becoming common wherever the geometry matters, including for boundary layers, electromagnetics, and anything run at high polynomial degree, where a straight-sided boundary caps convergence rate no matter how good the basis is.


21.1.4 More about mesh data structures
The above discussion describes what mesh elements are used. To learn more about how a mesh is actually described and how to navigate around a mesh, one should understand the half-edge data structure. The following is a good interactive page describing how surface meshes are defined and operate: jerryyin.info/geometry-processing-algorithms/half-edge.
crumbs: 21  Class 21: CAD, Meshing, and Discretization Choice

title: 21  Class 21: CAD, Meshing, and Discretization Choice
text:
21.2 Where meshes come from
A significant number of meshes are generated from a CAD model. Others come from measurement instead, such as a laser scan to produce a point cloud or a CT/MRI scan to produce voxels, both of which can be meshed. The CAD route is the most common one in traditional engineering design and will be discussed hereafter. While you should be aware that you can mesh other data, we will not cover this content in this class.
A CAD model stores smooth surfaces. A mesh stores kinked facets. Converting from CAD model to a mesh throws away exact geometry, which may affect both geometric and analysis precision.

21.2.1 Boundary representation
CAD describes a solid by describing only describing the outside surfaces. This is called a boundary representation, or B-rep, and the model is a collection of surfaces, many of which are cut in some form and then stitched together along shared edges so that they enclose a volume. There is no description of the inside. The solid is whatever the skin contains. On the occasion that a CAD model does not represent the outside of a volume, it is typically representative of the solid’s midsurface, and in these cases is called an open B-rep, whereas volume-enclosing B-reps are called closed B-reps or just simply B-reps.
Each surface of a B-rep is almost always a B-spline or NURBS surface. These are defined using the same kind of content learned in Class 12, where a spline surface is a mapping from a parametric square or rectangle into a curved patch in space,
\[ \underline{x}(u,v), \qquad (u,v) \in [0,1]^2 , \]
built from basis functions in \(u\) times basis functions in \(v\). (Note that here we typically use \(u\) and \(v\) for the parametric coordinates compared to \(\xi\) and \(\eta\) for the reference or parent coordinates.) The same tensor-productconstruction as is used for bilinear and biquadratic elements, is used for B-splines and NURBS, but just using a different basis, which will be discussed further below.
An example of a B-rep is shown in the widget below. The grey curves are isocurves, which are curves of constant \(u\) or constant \(v\) on each surface. They are the image of a grid in the parametric square, and they are the clearest way to see that a CAD surface is a mapped square. Cutting operations that mask parts of the curvilinear surfaces are called trimming curves, and can be turned on or off as well.



  
    DRAG TO ROTATE · SCROLL TO ZOOM
     isocurves
     surface boundaries
     trim curves
     surfaces
     closed solid
     side walls
     isocurves into the trimmed parts
    ISO LINES 
    reset view
  
  
  





21.2.2 Gluing and trimming
Very few shapes of interest can be described by a single mapped square. The midsurface of the bracket above, for example, is built from five surfaces: a web, two fillets, and two flanges. CAD builds shapes like this from simpler surfaces using two operations, called gluing and trimming.
Gluing joins surfaces along shared edges. The violet curves in the widget mark the edges where one surface stops and the next one starts. Gluing records that the two edges are the same curve in space, so the model has no gap there. It can also record how smoothly the surfaces meet. In the bracket, for example, each fillet joins the web and its flange without a corner.
Trimming removes part of a surface. The designer draws a closed curve in the parametric domain of the surface, and only the part of the surface inside that curve is kept in the model. Every red curve in the widget is a trimming curve, including the bands removed from the top and bottom, the steps and chamfered corners on the flanges, and the holes. A hole is the simplest case. The surface is not rebuilt with a hole in it; instead, an ellipse is drawn in its parametric domain, and everything inside the ellipse is ignored.
Trimming does not delete any of the underlying surface. Checking isocurves into the trimmed parts in the widget shows the rest of each surface continuing underneath the trimmed regions. Figure 21.4 takes one face out of the bracket to show the full surface from which it was cut.






Figure 21.4: One flange of the bracket, shown three ways. (a) The face as it appears in the model, with the rest of the bracket ghosted. (b) The untrimmed surface from which the face was cut, which is the image of the full parametric square, with the trimmed face drawn on top. The dashed blue outline and the dashed isocurves belong to the surface but not to the model. (c) The same face in its parametric domain \((u,v)\), which is where the trimming curves are stored. The arrows mark the same corner and the same two directions in (b) and (c); note that in the 3D view, \(u\) runs from right to left. The violet edge is where this flange is glued to its fillet.



Nearly every CAD model is built in this way: a collection of tensor-product surfaces, each trimmed by curves in its own parametric domain, and glued to its neighbours along shared edges. This is an effective way to describe a shape, but it is difficult to use directly for analysis, as described next.


21.2.3 Why trimming complicates analysis
Suppose we tried to perform an analysis directly on the face in panel (c) of Figure 21.4, using the grid of its parametric domain as our elements. The cells of that grid are squares, but the trimming curves do not follow the cell edges, and instead cut directly through them.






Figure 21.5: (a) The parametric domain of the flange, divided into the 7 × 7 cells between its isocurves. Each cell is shaded by the material it actually contains. Of the 49 cells, 22 are cut by a trimming curve (orange outline) and only 25 are kept whole. The two cells at the outer corners each contain only 0.13% material, since the chamfer passes just inside their inner corners. (b) The cell outlined in (a), enlarged. A 3 × 3 Gauss rule built for the whole cell places 3 of its 9 points inside the hole.



Each of the resulting problems relates to content from earlier in the course:

Integration. The Gauss rules of Classes 10 and 20 integrate over a whole element. On a cut cell, part of the square is not material, and the part that is has a curved boundary. In panel (b), a third of the quadrature points fall inside the hole. A cut cell requires an integration rule built for its own shape, and constructing one for every cut cell is a significant amount of work.
Slivers. A basis function whose support lies almost entirely in the trimmed region still has an unknown attached to it, even though it touches very little material, as in the corner cells. Its diagonal entry in the stiffness matrix is nearly zero compared with those of its neighbours, and the system of equations becomes poorly conditioned.
Boundary conditions. In Classes 14 and 19, boundary conditions were assigned to the nodes and element edges lying on \(\Gamma_g\) or \(\Gamma_h\). Here the boundary of the part is the trimming curve, which runs through the middle of cells, so there are no nodes on it to which a boundary condition can be assigned.
Seams that do not quite meet. Two glued faces each have their own trimming curve along the shared edge. These curves approximate the same edge in space but are generally not identical, so real models have small gaps and overlaps along their seams that a solver must tolerate.



21.2.4 Meshing the bracket
The usual alternative is to mesh the CAD surfaces rather than compute on them directly. A mesher works on the trimmed face, that is, on the part itself rather than on the square from which it was cut. Every element therefore lies inside the material, and every boundary is made up of element edges.






Figure 21.6: (a) A quad-dominant mesh of the midsurface of the bracket, which is the surface used by a shell analysis (the closed solid checkbox in the widget switches between this surface and the solid). The web and the fillets are bands of their parametric domains and use a structured grid. Each flange was triangulated, neighbouring triangles were then paired into quadrilaterals wherever the pair formed a well-shaped element, and the result was smoothed; quadrilaterals cover about 76% of the area of each flange. (b) The front flange laid flat, with the true boundary of the CAD face shown in red over the mesh. The hole is now a 12-sided polygon with 4.8% less area than the actual hole. Similarly, each fillet in (a) is now 3 flat strips, whose midpoints lie 3.4% of the fillet radius inside the true arc.



The four problems above no longer apply to this mesh. There are no cut cells or slivers, the boundary is again made up of element edges, and neighbouring faces share their nodes along each seam. The cost is the one described at the earlier in the reading, that the mesh is piecewise linear, so every curve has been replaced by straight segments. This geometry error does not decrease with better quadrature, and is only reduced by using smaller elements or curved elements. For many analyses of this bracket, an error of a few percent at the hole is acceptable. For the stress at the edge of that hole, which is where the stress is largest, it may not be.


21.2.5 An all-quadrilateral mesh of the same bracket
Many analysts prefer meshes without any triangles. Some element formulations exist only for quadrilaterals, and rows of quadrilaterals that follow the edges of a part are well suited to resolving behavior along those edges. Automatic all-quadrilateral meshing methods, such as paving, aim to produce these meshes by placing a row of quadrilaterals along every boundary and continuing inward until the rows meet. A depiction of such a quadrilateral mesh is shown below. Mesh smoothing operations are sometimes improve the quality of an initial output mesh.







Figure 21.7: (a) The midsurface of the bracket meshed with quadrilaterals only, using 236 elements. Rows follow every edge, including the seams shared with the fillets. (b) The front flange laid flat. Only 6 vertices inside the flange are irregular: 4 of valence 5 at the corners of the ring, and 2 of valence 3 at the centers of the corner fills.





21.2.6 Comparing the two meshes
Mesh quality is usually measured element by element, using a few simple measures of shape and size. The scaled Jacobian is found by evaluating the determinant of the Jacobian (Class 13) at each corner of an element, dividing it by the lengths of the two edges that meet there, and keeping the smallest value. It is scaled to equal 1 for a square or an equilateral triangle, and it decreases toward 0 as the corners of the element become more distorted. The edge ratio is the length of the longest edge of an element divided by the length of its shortest edge, and the size ratio is the area of the largest element in the mesh divided by the area of the smallest. Both equal 1 in an ideal mesh.






Figure 21.8: The elements of each flange shaded by their scaled Jacobian: (a) the quad-dominant flange of Figure 21.6 and (b) the quad-only flange of Figure 21.7. Darker elements are further from ideal. Both flanges use the same scale and are drawn in the same orientation as in the figures above.

By these shape measures, the two flanges are very similar. Their average element quality is the same, and the automatic quad-dominant mesh has a slightly better worst element and more uniform element sizes. This is worth noting, since an all-quadrilateral mesh is not by itself a guarantee of higher quality. However, use of triangles for certain kinds of analyses may be strongly discouraged.
The weaker elements of the quad-only mesh are all located in the upper chamfered corner, where the ring around the hole passes close to the chamfer and the three-block fill must fit into a long, thin triangle. Elsewhere, its elements are as good as or better than those of the quad-dominant mesh. Its smallest elements are in the ring around the hole, which is why its element sizes vary more.
The advantage of the quad-only mesh is its structure. It has no triangles, so element formulations that exist only for quadrilaterals can be used throughout. Its rows run parallel to every edge, which is where stress concentrations along an edge, or thin boundary layers in a flow, need to be resolved. It also has 6 irregular vertices per flange, compared with 16; the importance of this for splines is discussed at the end of this class. Frequently, though getting something with this structure requires manual intervention. This reflects the tradeoff described at the beginning of this class, where quadrilaterals and hexahedra are typically better elements but are more difficult to build.

title: 21  Class 21: CAD, Meshing, and Discretization Choice
section: 21.3 Using the CAD basis for analysis
text:
21.3 Using the CAD basis for analysis
The typical design-to-analysis path translates the model twice:
\[
\text{trimmed CAD surfaces}
\longrightarrow
\text{analysis-suitable geometry}
\longrightarrow
\text{finite element mesh and basis}.
\]
The first step includes repairing gaps along seams, removing small features that do not matter to the analysis, and deciding what fills the interior of the model. The second step is meshing, as described above. Both steps take time, and both can produce a geometry for the solver that is no longer exactly the one the designer created.
Isogeometric analysis (IGA) asks whether the spline functions that CAD already uses to describe the geometry could also be used to approximate the solution. If the CAD geometry is
\[
\underline{x}(\boldsymbol{\xi})
  = \sum_A R_A(\boldsymbol{\xi})\,\underline{P}_A,
\]
then an isogeometric approximation uses the same functions for the unknown field,
\[
u^h(\boldsymbol{\xi})
  = \sum_A R_A(\boldsymbol{\xi})\,d_A .
\]
This is the isoparametric concept of Class 9 applied in the opposite direction. There, the basis functions of an element were reused to describe its geometry; here, the basis functions of the geometry are reused to describe the field. The coefficients \(\underline{P}_A\) are control points that place the geometry in space, and the coefficients \(d_A\) are the unknowns of the analysis. These coefficients play different roles even though they multiply the same functions.
There are two main obstacles to doing this for a part like the bracket.

A CAD model only describes surfaces. A B-rep describes the surfaces of the part and nothing inside them. Unchecking closed solid in the widget shows the midsurface, which is what a shell analysis needs, and shell analysis on CAD surfaces is one of the areas where IGA has been most successful. A three-dimensional solid analysis instead needs a map from a parametric cube onto the inside of the part, which CAD does not provide. Constructing this volumetric map is still a large part of preparing a solid model for IGA.
Trimming. Each of the problems described for Figure 21.5 applies directly to IGA on a trimmed surface, including integration over cut cells, slivers, and boundary conditions on curves that cross cells.

Research published between 2009 and 2023 has repeatedly found that, for problems with smooth solutions, B-spline and NURBS bases give more accuracy per basis function than Lagrange bases of the same degree. However, this does not mean faster solutions in every case, since singularities, sharp gradients, trimmed cells, and the cost of quadrature and of solving the system can all reduce or remove this advantage. Several of these studies are listed under Further reading at the end of this page.

21.3.1 Continuity between elements
Every Lagrange basis used so far in this course has been \(C^0\), meaning that neighbouring elements agree on the value of the field at their shared boundary, but its slope may jump there. Splines allow us to choose how smooth the field is at each element boundary, as summarized below.

\(C^{2}\)

A B-spline of degree \(p\) can be as smooth as \(C^{p-1}\) at each boundary, and this choice can be made separately at each boundary. The widget below shows the two bases on the same elements, with Lagrange functions above and B-splines below. Below each plot is the slope of the highlighted function, which is where continuity is most visible: at a \(C^0\) boundary the slope jumps (shown by open and filled dots), at \(C^1\) the slope is continuous but has a corner, and at \(C^2\) it is smooth.
Below the basis functions, the same functions are used as a map, in the same way as the geometry map above but in one dimension. The sum \(\underline{x}(\xi)=\sum_A N_A(\xi)\,\underline{x}_A\) defines a curve in the plane. The points \(\underline{x}_A\) are Lagrange nodes on the left and B-spline control points on the right, and each can be dragged. Each element boundary on the two curves is labelled with the angle through which the curve turns there.

Things to try:

Support. With the default settings, click a Lagrange function and then a B-spline function near the middle. The shaded band shows where each is nonzero. The quadratic B-spline extends across three elements, while a Lagrange function never extends past the elements that touch its node.
Number of functions. Five quadratic elements require 11 Lagrange functions but only 7 smooth B-splines. Each smoothness condition at a boundary removes one function, so the number of B-splines is \(p+1\) plus, for each interior boundary, \(p\) minus its continuity.
Slopes. Set the degree to 3 and observe the slope of a B-spline as one boundary is made less smooth. The slope is smooth at \(C^2\), has a corner at \(C^1\), and jumps at \(C^0\).
Every boundary \(C^0\). The number of B-splines becomes the number of Lagrange functions. The two bases then describe exactly the same set of functions, and on each element the B-splines are the Bernstein polynomials described in the next section.
One boundary at \(C^{-1}\). The B-spline basis separates there into two independent pieces, as if it were two separate patches.
Meaning of a coefficient. A Lagrange function equals 1 at its own node and 0 at every other node, so its coefficient is the value of the field there. Most B-splines never reach 1, and several are nonzero at every point, so a B-spline coefficient is generally not the value of the field at any particular point.
Drag a B-spline control point. The curve moves smoothly, and only along the shaded part, which is the support of the basis function associated with that point. Every boundary still reads 0.0°, since a curve built from \(C^1\) functions cannot form a corner, regardless of where its control points are placed.
Drag a Lagrange node. Its elements move, and corners appear at the neighbouring element boundaries. Even before any node is moved, the Lagrange curve has small corners. Its nodes lie exactly on a smooth arch, but an arch is not a piecewise quadratic, so the pieces meet at slightly different angles.
Put the Lagrange nodes on the B-spline curve. Every corner drops to 0.0°, and the two curves become identical. The Lagrange functions can represent any curve that the B-splines can represent, but nothing in the Lagrange basis keeps the curve smooth, so moving any node brings the corners back.
Lower one boundary to \(C^0\), then to \(C^{-1}\). The B-spline curve does not move. Instead, it gains a control point at that boundary. Dragging that point allows the B-spline curve to form a corner there or, at \(C^{-1}\), to separate.



21.3.2 Bernstein polynomials
On a single element, the degree-\(p\) Bernstein polynomials
\[
B_i^p(t)=\binom{p}{i}\,t^i(1-t)^{p-i}, \qquad i=0,\ldots,p, \qquad 0\le t\le 1,
\]
are another basis for the same polynomials as the degree-\(p\) Lagrange functions. Any cubic can be written as a combination of the four cubic Lagrange functions or as a combination of the four cubic Bernstein polynomials. Only the coefficients change, in the same way that the components of a vector change when the coordinate axes are rotated.






Figure 21.9: (a) and (b) The four cubic functions of each basis on one element. Each Lagrange function equals 1 at its own node and 0 at the others, while the Bernstein functions are never negative and sum to 1 everywhere. (c) and (d) One cubic polynomial written in each basis. The Lagrange coefficients \(d_i\) are the values of the polynomial at the four nodes. The Bernstein coefficients \(c_i\) are the heights of a control polygon; the curve starts and ends on this polygon, and is pulled toward the two interior points without passing through them.



Two properties make Bernstein polynomials useful. First, they are never negative and they sum to 1, so a curve built from them stays inside its control polygon, which is one reason they are used in CAD. Second, they are exactly the basis functions of a \(C^0\) B-spline: setting every boundary in the widget above to \(C^0\) makes the B-splines on each element exactly these polynomials. This connection, called Bézier extraction, allows a spline code to provide each element with a Bernstein basis and a small matrix, and then to assemble element by element in the same loop as a standard finite element code.


21.3.3 Cubic Hermite polynomials
Splines are one way to obtain \(C^1\) continuity. An older approach, used in beam theory, makes the slope itself an unknown at every node. The Euler–Bernoulli beam weak form contains second derivatives (\(m=2\)), so the slope of the deflection must not jump between elements. A cubic Hermite element uses the deflection \(w\) and the rotation \(\theta = dw/dx\) at each end,
\[
w^h(t)=h_{00}(t)\,w_1+L\,h_{10}(t)\,\theta_1
       +h_{01}(t)\,w_2+L\,h_{11}(t)\,\theta_2,
\qquad 0\le t\le 1,
\]
where \(L\) is the element length and
\[
\begin{aligned}
h_{00}&=2t^3-3t^2+1, & h_{10}&=t^3-2t^2+t,\\
h_{01}&=-2t^3+3t^2,  & h_{11}&=t^3-t^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Neighbouring elements share both \(w\) and \(\theta\) at their common node, so the deflection is \(C^1\).






Figure 21.10: (a) The four cubic Hermite functions. Two of them are associated with a value at one end, and two with a slope. (b) A beam clamped at both ends under a uniform load (dashed), approximated by two Hermite elements. The two pieces are different cubics, but they share the same deflection and the same slope at the middle node, so the approximation has no corner there. (c) The same beam approximated by two quadratic Lagrange elements through the same nodal deflections. Each element has its own slope at the middle node (+0.031 and −0.031), so the approximation has a peak where the beam is actually flat.



Hermite elements work well for beams and for rectangular plate elements, but they do not extend well to general shapes. In two and three dimensions, matching slopes across an element edge requires derivative unknowns in several directions at every node, including mixed derivatives, and these only fit together easily on rectangles. On curved or irregular elements, they become very difficult to match. Splines obtain their smoothness differently: rather than adding derivative unknowns, each function overlaps several elements.


21.3.4 From a Class 11 element to a spline patch
In Class 11, a basis function on a quadrilateral was defined as the product of two one-dimensional functions,
\[
N_A(\xi,\eta)=N_a(\xi)\,N_b(\eta).
\]
A B-spline patch is built in the same way, from one-dimensional B-splines,
\[
R_A(\xi,\eta)=B_a(\xi)\,B_b(\eta).
\]
The difference lies in the support of the one-dimensional factors. A Lagrange factor is nonzero on one element, or on two if its node lies on an element boundary. A B-spline factor extends across several elements of the patch. The widget below shows either basis over the same grid, with the two one-dimensional factors drawn on the back walls as in Class 11. The dark curves show the function along each element line, which is where a \(C^0\) function has a crease. Drag to rotate the view, and click a dot in the right-hand view to select a function.
Below that, the same functions are again used as a map, this time from the square onto a curved region of the plane, \(\underline{x}(\xi,\eta)=\sum_A R_A(\xi,\eta)\,\underline{x}_A\). The region initially is the quarter annulus of Classes 12, 13, and 20. The points \(\underline{x}_A\) belong to whichever basis is selected at the top of the widget (Lagrange nodes or B-spline control points), and each can be dragged. Red marks the locations where a grid line forms a corner as it crosses an element line.



  
    
      LagrangeB-spline

Things to try:

A Lagrange corner function (the default). It has creases along both element lines through its node, since each of its one-dimensional factors has a corner there.
Switch to B-spline. The widget stays at the same location on the patch. The B-spline function covers more cells and crosses the dark curves without a crease.
Number of functions. On \(3\times3\) quadratic elements, the Lagrange basis has \(7\times7=49\) functions and the \(C^1\) B-spline basis has \(5\times5=25\), which is the one-dimensional reduction from the previous widget, squared.
Lower the spline continuity to \(C^0\). The number of functions returns to 49, and the creases reappear.
Drag a Lagrange node at an element corner. The grid lines crossing the neighbouring element lines now form sharp corners there. Even before any node is moved, the Lagrange grid has small corners, since its nodes lie exactly on circles and a circle is not a piecewise quadratic.
Switch to B-spline and drag a control point. The region bends smoothly over a wider area, and no grid line forms a corner.
Put the Lagrange nodes on the B-spline region. Every corner disappears, since the Lagrange functions can represent exactly the same region. However, the Lagrange basis does not keep the region smooth, and moving any node brings the corners back.
Lower the spline continuity to \(C^0\). The region does not move, but control points appear on the element lines, and dragging one of these can now form a corner in the spline grid as well.

A tensor-product spline is defined on a single parametric square. This is well suited to a single CAD surface, such as one flange of the bracket, since mapping the square through \(\underline{x}(\xi,\eta)\) places the basis functions on the surface without changing which functions overlap which. A part made of several surfaces requires several patches glued together, and how well this can be done depends on the layout of the mesh.

title: 21  Class 21: CAD, Meshing, and Discretization Choice
text:
21.4 Quadrilateral mesh topology and splines
A tensor-product spline needs a grid that can be indexed by two coordinates, by stepping in either \(\xi\) or \(\eta\). A structured quadrilateral mesh has this property, but an arbitrary quadrilateral mesh generally does not.
At a regular interior vertex, four quadrilaterals meet. At an extraordinary vertex, a different number meets, such as three, five, or six. On the boundary, a regular vertex has two quadrilaterals, or one at a corner. A separatrix is obtained by starting at an irregular vertex, following one of its edges into the mesh, and continuing straight through every regular vertex (leaving by the edge opposite the one by which it entered) until reaching the boundary or another irregular vertex. Cutting the mesh along every separatrix leaves blocks that can each be indexed by two coordinates. These blocks are the patches that a tensor-product spline would need.






Figure 21.11: Three all-quadrilateral meshes of a square plate with a circular hole. Every separatrix was traced using the rule above (violet), and the resulting patches are shaded so that neighbouring patches differ. (a) Four structured blocks around the hole. The only irregular vertices are at the corners of the plate, where two quadrilaterals meet instead of one; their four separatrices divide 120 quadrilaterals into 4 patches. (b) A mesh built in the way many automatic quadrilateral meshers build one: triangulate, pair neighbouring triangles into quadrilaterals, and then split every element into quadrilaterals. It has 15 interior extraordinary vertices, of valence 3, 5 and 6, and its separatrices divide 131 quadrilaterals into 83 patches. (c) Twelve patches: a ring of four around the hole, four along the sides, and four in the corners. Its 4 extraordinary vertices, all of valence 5, are at the corners of the ring, and their separatrices connect to one another in a loop around the hole, dividing 112 quadrilaterals into 12 patches.



Mesh (b) is a (moderately) acceptable mesh for standard \(C^0\) Lagrange elements. A Lagrange code only requires neighbouring elements to agree on the values at their shared nodes, and never needs to know which direction is “straight through” a vertex. Raising the Lagrange polynomial degree does not change this.
Smooth splines are different. Their functions are intended to extend across element boundaries, and at a valence-3 or valence-5 vertex there is no unique way to continue a row of elements straight through. Mesh (a) can support four patches of smooth splines, glued along four seams. Mesh (b) separates into dozens of small patches. Each seam between patches is a location where continuity must be reduced or specially enforced, so on mesh (b) most of the smoothness that makes splines attractive is lost. A quadrilateral mesh can therefore be entirely suitable for \(C^0\) finite elements and still be a poor starting point for a standard B-spline analysis.
Extraordinary vertices are not problematic in themselves; what matters is how many there are and where they are located. Mesh (c) has four, placed deliberately at the corners of a ring of quadrilaterals around the hole, and their separatrices connect to one another rather than extending across the plate. The result is twelve well-structured patches. This is more seams than mesh (a) has, but they are long and regular, which multi-patch spline codes handle routinely. The cost is at the four valence-5 vertices, where smoothness must be reduced or specially constructed. Mesh (c) also has the best elements of the three meshes.

The weakest elements of mesh (a) are at the corners of the plate, where two quadrilaterals share a single right angle and each has a 45° corner. Smoothing cannot fix this, since it is determined by the layout. Mesh (c) gives each corner its own block. Its one weakness is element size: its smallest elements, around the hole, are a few times smaller than its largest, which is a slightly wider spread than in mesh (a).
This is an active area of research. Constructions such as T-splines, hierarchical and locally refined splines, subdivision surfaces, and spline spaces built specifically around extraordinary vertices all aim to preserve smooth basis functions on meshes with arbitrary layouts. 
Note that separatrices describe the topology of a mesh, not its quality. A well-structured separatrix layout can still produce a poor spline if its cells are folded, highly skewed, or crowded together, just as a Lagrange mesh can. The separatrices indicate whether a standard tensor-product patch layout is natural, while the quality of the analysis still depends on the Jacobians of Class 13 and on how well the basis can approximate the solution.

title: 21  Class 21: CAD, Meshing, and Discretization Choice
text:
21.5 Summary

CAD describes a part as trimmed surfaces glued together. This is an exact description of the shape, but cut cells, slivers, and seams make it difficult to use directly for analysis.
Meshing addresses these problems at the cost of geometric accuracy. A mesh of the trimmed surfaces has no cut cells, but it replaces every curve with straight edges.
Geometry and field have separate roles. IGA uses the same functions for both, but control points place the geometry, while the coefficients \(d_A\) are the unknowns of the analysis.
Continuity should be chosen, not maximized. Smoothness is beneficial for smooth solutions and for weak forms with higher derivatives, such as the beam. It should be reduced where the solution is not smooth, such as at material interfaces, cracks, and sharp corners.
An exact surface does not define a volume. CAD surfaces can be used directly for shell analysis, but solid analysis still requires a volumetric map or a mesh.
Fewer basis functions does not necessarily mean less computation. Smooth bases can give lower error per unknown, but each function overlaps more elements, so the matrix is less sparse and each element is more expensive to integrate.

Overall, Lagrange finite elements handle complicated geometry well by keeping continuity local, while isogeometric methods invest more effort in geometry and topology so that smooth, CAD-quality basis functions can provide more approximation power across element boundaries.

21.5.1 Further reading

Hughes, Cottrell, and Bazilevs (2005), the original isogeometric-analysis paper
Cottrell, Hughes, and Bazilevs (2009), Isogeometric Analysis
Evans, Bazilevs, Babuška, and Hughes (2009), on the accuracy of smooth splines per degree of freedom
Marussig and Hughes (2018), a review of trimming in isogeometric analysis

title: 22  Class 22: Robin Boundary Conditions
text:
22.1 The Robin boundary condition
To this point, we have used two kinds of boundary conditions. On the Dirichlet boundary \(\Gamma_g\), the value of the solution is prescribed, and on the Neumann boundary \(\Gamma_h\), the flux is prescribed:
\[
u = g \quad \text{on } \Gamma_g,
\qquad\qquad
\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} = \kappa_{ij}u_{,j}n_i = h \quad \text{on } \Gamma_h .
\]
Many boundaries of practical interest are neither. The outside face of a building wall does not have a known temperature, and the heat flowing through it is not known in advance either, since it depends on the temperature of the face itself. Similarly, the end of a pile resting on soft rock is neither held in place nor free, since the force it carries depends on how far the end moves. In both cases, the flux through the boundary depends on the value of the solution at the boundary, and a relationship of this kind is described by a Robin boundary condition. In this class, we will add Robin boundary conditions to the strong, weak, and Galerkin forms of the problem, and determine how they change the stiffness matrix and the force vector. The back face of the brick in Project 2 has a Robin boundary condition, and Homework 16 implements the terms derived here.
A Robin boundary condition prescribes a combination of the value of the solution and its flux on a portion of the boundary, \(\Gamma_r\):
\[
\hat{a}\,u + \left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} = \hat{c}
\qquad \text{on } \Gamma_r ,
\]
or, in index notation,
\[
\hat{a}\,u + \kappa_{ij}u_{,j}n_i = \hat{c}
\qquad \text{on } \Gamma_r .
\]
Here \(\hat{a}:\Gamma_r\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(\hat{c}:\Gamma_r\to\mathbb{R}\) are given functions, in the same way that \(g\) and \(h\) are given functions on \(\Gamma_g\) and \(\Gamma_h\). The hats distinguish them from other uses of the letters \(a\) and \(c\) in this course, such as the bilinear form \(a(\cdot,\cdot)\) and the coefficients \(c_A\) of a test function \(w^h\). When the conductivity is isotropic, \(\kappa_{ij}=\kappa\,\delta_{ij}\), the condition is often written using the normal derivative \(\partial u/\partial n = \nabla u\cdot\underline{n}\), as \(\hat{a}\,u + \kappa\,\partial u/\partial n = \hat{c}\).

title: 22  Class 22: Robin Boundary Conditions
text:
22.1.1 Where Robin conditions come from
A Robin condition arises whenever the boundary is connected to something outside of the domain that responds in proportion to the value of the solution at the boundary. Rearranging the condition as
\[
-\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} = \hat{a}\left(u - \frac{\hat{c}}{\hat{a}}\right)
\]
shows that the flux leaving the domain is proportional to the difference between \(u\) and a reference value \(\hat{c}/\hat{a}\), where \(\hat{a}\) measures how strongly the boundary is connected to its surroundings. What provides this connection depends on the physical problem, and Table 22.1 lists several common cases. A surrounding fluid is the most common case in heat transfer, but it is only one of them, and a pile resting on a spring, for example, involves no fluid at all. Figure 22.1 shows two of these settings, drawn in the same way as the examples of the appendices.






Figure 22.1: Two settings that lead to a Robin condition, drawn as in the appendices. (a) The concrete wall of the 1D heat appendix, with its exterior face now exchanging heat with the outside air by convection, in addition to absorbing sunlight. The heat leaving the face depends on the temperature of the face, so neither the temperature nor the flux there is known in advance. This is the problem solved later in this class. (b) The pile of the rod appendix, with its toe now resting on soft rock that is modeled as a spring. The rock pushes back on the toe in proportion to how far the toe moves, so neither the displacement nor the force at the toe is known in advance.






Table 22.1: Physical settings that lead to a Robin condition \(\hat{a}\,u + \left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} = \hat{c}\). In each case, the flux leaving the domain is proportional to the difference between the solution and a reference value. For the rod, \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\) is replaced by the axial stiffness \(EA\), and the flux is the axial force that the end of the rod transmits to the spring.

The most common case in heat transfer is convection, in which a surface exchanges heat with a surrounding fluid such as air or water. Newton’s law of cooling states that the heat flux leaving the surface is proportional to the difference between the temperature of the surface and the temperature of the fluid away from the surface, \(u_\infty\):
\[
\underline{q}\cdot\underline{n} = h_c\left(u - u_\infty\right),
\]
where \(h_c\) is the convection coefficient, with units of W/(m²·K). Recall from the appendices that the heat flux is given by Fourier’s law, \(\underline{q} = -\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\). Substituting this and rearranging gives
\[
-\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} = h_c\left(u - u_\infty\right)
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
h_c\,u + \left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} = h_c\,u_\infty ,
\]
which is a Robin condition with \(\hat{a} = h_c\) and \(\hat{c} = h_c\,u_\infty\). If the surface also absorbs a known heat flux \(q_s\), such as from sunlight, it is added to the right side, so that \(\hat{c} = h_c\,u_\infty + q_s\).
Typical convection coefficients are 2 to 25 W/(m²·K) for air moving by natural convection (driven only by buoyancy), 25 to 250 W/(m²·K) for air moved by a fan or by wind, and roughly 50 to 20,000 W/(m²·K) for liquids, depending on how they flow. The back face of the brick in Project 2 uses \(h_c = 9.06\) W/(m²·K), which is typical of still air.
The other cases in Table 22.1 have the same form, but do not involve a surrounding fluid. In the rod appendix, the end of a pile resting on rock that is modeled as a spring of stiffness \(k_s\) has the condition \(h = -k_s\,u\), since the spring pushes back on the pile in proportion to how far its end moves. This is a Robin condition with \(\hat{a} = k_s\) and \(\hat{c} = 0\), and the connection to the surroundings is elastic rather than thermal. A thin layer of a different solid material, such as the thermal interface material under the battery cell in the 2D heat appendix, gives a Robin condition by conduction alone, since the heat crossing the layer is proportional to the temperature drop across it. In contaminant transport, the rate at which a substance crosses a surface is often modeled as proportional to the difference in concentration across that surface, which again has the same form.


22.1.2 Robin conditions interpolate Dirichlet and Neumann
The Robin condition can be viewed as lying between the Neumann and Dirichlet conditions. If \(\hat{a} = 0\), it is a Neumann condition with \(h = \hat{c}\). If we instead divide the condition by \(\hat{a}\),
\[
u + \frac{1}{\hat{a}}\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} = \frac{\hat{c}}{\hat{a}} ,
\]
and let \(\hat{a}\) become very large while \(\hat{c}/\hat{a}\) is held fixed, the flux term vanishes, and the condition becomes a Dirichlet condition with \(g = \hat{c}/\hat{a}\). For convection, \(\hat{c}/\hat{a} = u_\infty\), so a very large convection coefficient holds the surface at the temperature of the fluid. Similarly, a very stiff spring holds the end of a rod at the position of the spring’s other end, in the same way as a fixed support.
Whether a particular value of \(\hat{a}\) should be considered large or small depends on the body to which it is applied, since the strength of the connection to the surroundings must be compared with the ability of the body itself to conduct. For convection from a body of thickness \(L\), this comparison is the Biot number
\[
\mathrm{Bi} = \frac{h_c\,L}{\kappa}
\]
which compares the resistance to conduction through the body, \(L/\kappa\), with the resistance to heat transfer across its surface, \(1/h_c\). For a rod of length \(L\) and axial stiffness \(EA\) resting on a spring, the corresponding ratio is \(k_s L/(EA)\), which compares the stiffness of the spring with the axial stiffness of the rod. In either case, when the ratio is much greater than 1, the solution is close to that of a Dirichlet condition, and when it is much less than 1, the solution is close to that of a Neumann condition. The example later in this class shows this directly for convection.

title: 22  Class 22: Robin Boundary Conditions
text:
22.2 The strong form
As before, consider a domain \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_{sd}}\), now with its boundary divided into three parts, \(\Gamma_g\), \(\Gamma_h\), and \(\Gamma_r\). These parts do not overlap, and together they make up the entire boundary \(\Gamma\), so that every point of the boundary has exactly one boundary condition. Given \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\), \(g:\Gamma_g\to\mathbb{R}\), \(h:\Gamma_h\to\mathbb{R}\), \(\hat{a}:\Gamma_r\to\mathbb{R}\), \(\hat{c}:\Gamma_r\to\mathbb{R}\), and a symmetric positive definite \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{n_{sd}\times n_{sd}}\), find \(u:\bar{\Omega}\to\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
(\mathrm{S})\qquad
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
-\nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right) &= f && \text{in } \Omega\\
u &= g && \text{on } \Gamma_g\\
\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} &= h && \text{on } \Gamma_h\\
\hat{a}\,u + \left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} &= \hat{c} && \text{on } \Gamma_r
\end{aligned}
\right.
\]






Figure 22.2: A domain whose boundary is divided into a Dirichlet part \(\Gamma_g\), a Neumann part \(\Gamma_h\), and a Robin part \(\Gamma_r\). Every point of the boundary belongs to exactly one of the three parts. On \(\Gamma_r\), the boundary is connected to its surroundings, drawn here generically as springs to a support, so that the flux through the boundary depends on the value of \(u\) there, and neither is known in advance. Depending on the problem, the connection may be a surrounding fluid, a spring support, a thin layer of another material, or another mechanism of this kind (Table 22.1).

title: 22  Class 22: Robin Boundary Conditions
text:
22.3 The weak form
The weak form is derived in the same way as in Class 4. Multiplying the differential equation by a test function \(w\in\mathcal{V}\) and integrating over \(\Omega\) gives
\[
-\int_\Omega w\,\nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)d\Omega = \int_\Omega w\,f\,d\Omega .
\]
Applying the product rule and the divergence theorem, exactly as in Class 4, moves one derivative onto \(w\) and produces an integral over the boundary:
\[
\int_\Omega \nabla w\cdot\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\;d\Omega
- \int_\Gamma w\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n}\;d\Gamma
= \int_\Omega w\,f\,d\Omega .
\]
The boundary now has three parts, so the boundary integral splits into three integrals, and each is simplified using the boundary condition on its part:
\[
\int_\Gamma w\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n}\;d\Gamma
=
\underbrace{\int_{\Gamma_g} w\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n}\;d\Gamma}_{0, \text{ since } w = 0 \text{ on } \Gamma_g}
+
\underbrace{\int_{\Gamma_h} w\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n}\;d\Gamma}_{\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} = h}
+
\underbrace{\int_{\Gamma_r} w\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n}\;d\Gamma}_{\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} = \hat{c} - \hat{a}\,u}
=
\int_{\Gamma_h} w\,h\;d\Gamma + \int_{\Gamma_r} w\left(\hat{c} - \hat{a}\,u\right)d\Gamma .
\]
On \(\Gamma_r\), the Robin condition was solved for the flux, \(\left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} = \hat{c} - \hat{a}\,u\). Substituting this into the previous equation and moving the term that contains \(u\) to the left side gives
\[
\boxed{\;
\int_\Omega \nabla w\cdot\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\;d\Omega
+ \int_{\Gamma_r} w\,\hat{a}\,u\;d\Gamma
= \int_\Omega w\,f\,d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} w\,h\;d\Gamma + \int_{\Gamma_r} w\,\hat{c}\;d\Gamma
\;}
\]
or, in index notation,
\[
\int_\Omega w_{,i}\,\kappa_{ij}\,u_{,j}\;d\Omega
+ \int_{\Gamma_r} w\,\hat{a}\,u\;d\Gamma
= \int_\Omega w\,f\,d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} w\,h\;d\Gamma + \int_{\Gamma_r} w\,\hat{c}\;d\Gamma .
\]
The weak form is therefore: given the same data as the strong form, find \(u\in\mathcal{S}\) such that the boxed equation holds for every \(w\in\mathcal{V}\). The spaces \(\mathcal{S}\) and \(\mathcal{V}\) are the same as in Class 4, since only the Dirichlet boundary constrains them. Using the shorthand of earlier classes, \(a(w,u) = \int_\Omega \nabla w\cdot\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\,d\Omega\) and \((w,v)_{\Gamma_r} = \int_{\Gamma_r} w\,v\,d\Gamma\), the weak form is written as
\[
(\mathrm{W})\qquad
a(w,u) + (w,\hat{a}\,u)_{\Gamma_r} = (w,f) + (w,h)_{\Gamma_h} + (w,\hat{c})_{\Gamma_r}
\qquad \text{for all } w\in\mathcal{V} .
\]
Three observations about this result are worth noting.

A Robin condition, like a Neumann condition, is a natural boundary condition. It appears in the integrals of the weak form, and not in the definitions of \(\mathcal{S}\) and \(\mathcal{V}\). Consequently, the value of \(u\) on \(\Gamma_r\) is unknown, and the basis functions whose nodes lie on \(\Gamma_r\) carry unknown coefficients, just as those on \(\Gamma_h\) and in the interior do. Only the nodes on \(\Gamma_g\) are prescribed.
Unlike a Neumann condition, a Robin condition contributes a term to the left side of the weak form, since the flux on \(\Gamma_r\) depends on the unknown \(u\). This term will add to the stiffness matrix.
The weak form also implies the strong form. Following the argument of Class 5, choosing test functions that are nonzero only near \(\Gamma_r\) recovers the Robin condition, in the same way that the Neumann condition was recovered on \(\Gamma_h\).

title: 22  Class 22: Robin Boundary Conditions
section: 22.4 The Galerkin form and the matrix equations
text:
22.4 The Galerkin form and the matrix equations
As in Class 7, the trial solution is split into an unknown part and a known part, \(u^h = v^h + g^h\), where
\[
w^h = \sum_{A \notin \Gamma_g} c_A\,N_A ,
\qquad
v^h = \sum_{B \notin \Gamma_g} d_B\,N_B ,
\qquad
g^h = \sum_{\hat{B} \in \Gamma_g} g_{\hat{B}}\,N_{\hat{B}} .
\]
Here \(\hat{B}\) indexes the basis functions whose nodes lie on \(\Gamma_g\). Substituting \(u^h = v^h + g^h\) into the weak form, and moving the known terms that contain \(g^h\) to the right side, gives the Galerkin form: find \(v^h\in\mathcal{V}^h\) such that, for all \(w^h\in\mathcal{V}^h\),
\[
a(w^h,v^h) + (w^h,\hat{a}\,v^h)_{\Gamma_r}
= (w^h,f) + (w^h,h)_{\Gamma_h} + (w^h,\hat{c})_{\Gamma_r}
- a(w^h,g^h) - (w^h,\hat{a}\,g^h)_{\Gamma_r} .
\]
The final term is new. Since the Robin term on the left side contains \(u^h\), the known part \(g^h\) contributes to it as well, and that contribution is moved to the right side in the same way as \(a(w^h,g^h)\).
Substituting the sums for \(w^h\), \(v^h\), and \(g^h\), and choosing \(w^h = N_A\) one basis function at a time, as in Class 7, gives the matrix equation \(\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{d} = \underline{F}\), with
\[
K_{AB} = a(N_A,N_B) + (N_A,\hat{a}\,N_B)_{\Gamma_r}
= \int_\Omega \nabla N_A\cdot\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla N_B\;d\Omega
+ \int_{\Gamma_r} N_A\,\hat{a}\,N_B\;d\Gamma
\]
and
\[
F_A = (N_A,f) + (N_A,h)_{\Gamma_h} + (N_A,\hat{c})_{\Gamma_r}
- \sum_{\hat{B}\in\Gamma_g} g_{\hat{B}}\left[\,a(N_A,N_{\hat{B}}) + (N_A,\hat{a}\,N_{\hat{B}})_{\Gamma_r}\right] .
\]
A Robin boundary condition therefore changes both the stiffness matrix and the force vector.

The stiffness matrix gains the integral \(\int_{\Gamma_r} N_A\,\hat{a}\,N_B\,d\Gamma\). This is nonzero only when both \(N_A\) and \(N_B\) are nonzero on \(\Gamma_r\), which happens only when both of their nodes lie on a Robin face of the same element.
The force vector gains \(\int_{\Gamma_r} N_A\,\hat{c}\,d\Gamma\), which is computed in exactly the same way as the Neumann term, with \(\hat{c}\) in place of \(h\).
The Dirichlet term in \(F_A\) gains a Robin integral as well. This is nonzero only where a node on \(\Gamma_g\) also lies on a Robin face, which occurs at the points (or edges) where \(\Gamma_g\) and \(\Gamma_r\) meet.

Since \(\hat{a}\ge 0\) in physical problems, such as convection (\(\hat{a} = h_c\)) and spring supports (\(\hat{a} = k_s\)), the Robin term adds nonnegative contributions to the stiffness matrix. Class 23 shows that these contributions can make the stiffness matrix invertible even when there is no Dirichlet boundary at all.

title: 22  Class 22: Robin Boundary Conditions
section: 22.5 Example: a wall exposed to outside air
text:
22.5 Example: a wall exposed to outside air
The 1D heat appendix modeled a concrete wall of thickness \(L\) = 0.30 m and conductivity \(\kappa\) = 1.4 W/(m·K), heated internally by the hydration of the cement at \(f\) = 500 W/m³. Its interior face, at \(x = L\), was held at the room temperature \(g\) = 20 °C, and its outer face, at \(x = 0\), absorbed a solar heat flux of 50 W/m² as a Neumann condition. A more realistic model of the outer face also accounts for the heat that it exchanges with the outside air. Taking the outside air to be at \(u_\infty\) = 5 °C and keeping the solar flux \(q_s\) = 50 W/m², the outer face has the Robin condition
\[
h_c\,u(0) - \kappa\,u_{,x}(0) = h_c\,u_\infty + q_s ,
\]
since the outward normal at \(x = 0\) is \(n = -1\). This is a Robin condition with \(\hat{a} = h_c\) and \(\hat{c} = h_c\,u_\infty + q_s\).
In one dimension, \(\Gamma_r\) is a single point, and the boundary integrals reduce to evaluations at that point:
\[
(N_A,\hat{a}\,N_B)_{\Gamma_r} = h_c\,N_A(0)\,N_B(0),
\qquad
(N_A,\hat{c})_{\Gamma_r} = \hat{c}\,N_A(0) .
\]
With linear elements, the only basis function that is nonzero at \(x = 0\) is the one belonging to the first node, so the Robin condition adds \(h_c\) to the first diagonal entry of \(\underline{\underline{K}}\) and adds \(\hat{c} = h_c\,u_\infty + q_s\) to the first entry of \(\underline{F}\), and changes nothing else. Note that the convection coefficient appears in both places: in \(K_{00}\) by itself, and in \(F_0\) multiplied by the air temperature. If the air were at 0 °C, the convective part of \(F_0\) would vanish, and only \(K_{00}\) would change with \(h_c\).
Solving the strong form of this problem exactly shows that the temperature of the outer face is
\[
u(0) = u_\infty + \frac{u_N(0) - u_\infty}{1 + \mathrm{Bi}} ,
\]
where \(u_N(0)\) = 46.8 °C is the temperature of the outer face in the Neumann problem of the appendix (\(h_c = 0\)). The Biot number alone therefore determines where the temperature of the outer face falls between the Dirichlet value \(u_\infty\) and the Neumann value \(u_N(0)\). For example, with \(h_c\) = 10 W/(m²·K), which is typical of outdoor air, \(\mathrm{Bi}\) = 2.14 and the outer face is at 18.3 °C. The widget below solves this problem with linear finite elements and shows the resulting matrix equations.
