Things to try:

Make \(h_c\) as small as possible. The solution approaches the Neumann solution of the appendix, and the outer face approaches 46.8 °C. The Robin term adds almost nothing to \(K_{00}\).
Set \(h_c\) near 10 W/(m²·K). This is typical of outdoor air. The outer face is now much colder than in the Neumann problem, and most of the heat generated in the wall leaves through the outer face rather than into the room.
Make \(h_c\) as large as possible. The outer face approaches the air temperature, as for a Dirichlet condition with \(g = u_\infty\). Both \(K_{00}\) and \(F_0\) grow in proportion to \(h_c\), and they dominate the first equation, which forces \(d_0\) toward \(F_0/K_{00} \approx h_c u_\infty/h_c = u_\infty\).
Change the outside air temperature. The temperatures in the wall change, but in the matrix equations only \(F_0\) changes, by \(h_c\) times the change in \(u_\infty\), since the air temperature is part of the data \(\hat{c}\) and not of the coefficient \(\hat{a}\). Set the air to 0 °C: the convective part of \(F_0\) is then zero, so \(F_0\) no longer changes as \(h_c\) is varied, while \(K_{00}\) still does.
Change the number of elements. Only the first row of \(\underline{\underline{K}}\) and the first entry of \(\underline{F}\) contain the Robin terms, regardless of how many elements are used.

title: 22  Class 22: Robin Boundary Conditions
section: 22.6 Computing the Robin terms on an element
text:
22.6 Computing the Robin terms on an element
In two dimensions, \(\Gamma_r\) is made up of element faces, and the Robin integrals are computed face by face, using the face quadrature of Class 20. For an element \(e\) with a face on \(\Gamma_r\), for example the face \(\xi = 1\), the Robin contributions to the element stiffness matrix and force vector are
\[
k^{e}_{ab} \mathrel{+}= \int_{\Gamma^e_r} N_a\,\hat{a}\,N_b\;d\Gamma
\approx \sum_{g} w_g\,N_a(1,\eta_g)\,\hat{a}\big(\underline{x}(1,\eta_g)\big)\,N_b(1,\eta_g)\,\big\|\underline{t}(1,\eta_g)\big\| ,
\]
\[
f^{e}_{a} \mathrel{+}= \int_{\Gamma^e_r} N_a\,\hat{c}\;d\Gamma
\approx \sum_{g} w_g\,N_a(1,\eta_g)\,\hat{c}\big(\underline{x}(1,\eta_g)\big)\,\big\|\underline{t}(1,\eta_g)\big\| ,
\]
where \(\underline{t} = \partial\underline{x}/\partial\eta\) is the tangent to the face, and \(\|\underline{t}\|\) is the arc-length Jacobian of Class 20. These are the same face integrals used for the Neumann term, with a second basis function in the stiffness term.






Figure 22.3: (a) A biquadratic element in its parent domain, with local nodes numbered as in Homework 16 and its face \(\xi = 1\) on \(\Gamma_r\). Only the basis functions of nodes 2, 5, and 8 are nonzero on that face. (b) The entries of the element stiffness matrix and element force vector to which the Robin face contributes are shaded. The face integrals change only the \(3\times 3\) block for the nodes on the face, and only the three corresponding entries of the force vector. Every entry, shaded or not, also contains the integral over the element interior.



Several practical points follow from these formulas.

Only the basis functions whose nodes lie on the face are nonzero there, as noted in Class 20. For an element of degree \(p\), the Robin face therefore contributes to a \((p+1)\times(p+1)\) block of the element stiffness matrix, as shown in Figure 22.3.
For a straight face and a constant \(\hat{a}\), the integrand of the stiffness term is a polynomial of degree \(2p\) in the face coordinate, so \(p+1\) Gauss points integrate it exactly.
These contributions are assembled into \(\underline{\underline{K}}\) and \(\underline{F}\) in the same way as the interior contributions, using the IEN and ID arrays. If a node on the Robin face is a Dirichlet node, which can occur at an end of the face where \(\Gamma_r\) meets \(\Gamma_g\), its column is not assembled into \(\underline{\underline{K}}\). Instead, \(k^e_{ab}\,g_b\) is subtracted from \(f^e_a\), exactly as is done for the interior terms. This is the term \(-(N_A,\hat{a}\,N_{\hat{B}})_{\Gamma_r}\,g_{\hat{B}}\) in \(F_A\).
In Homework 16, these integrals are computed by the functions LocalStiffnessBoundaryTerms and LocalForceBoundaryTerms.

title: 22  Class 22: Robin Boundary Conditions
text:
22.7 Summary

A Robin boundary condition, \(\hat{a}\,u + \left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} = \hat{c}\) on \(\Gamma_r\), relates the value of the solution to its flux. It describes a boundary that is connected to its surroundings, such as a surface cooled by a fluid (\(\hat{a} = h_c\), \(\hat{c} = h_c\,u_\infty\)), a thin layer of another material, or the end of a rod resting on a spring (\(\hat{a} = k_s\)).
The Robin condition becomes a Neumann condition when \(\hat{a} = 0\), and approaches a Dirichlet condition with \(g = \hat{c}/\hat{a}\) as \(\hat{a}\) becomes large. The Biot number for convection, or \(k_s L/(EA)\) for a spring support, indicates which of these a particular coefficient is closer to.
A Robin condition is a natural boundary condition: it does not change \(\mathcal{S}\) or \(\mathcal{V}\), and the nodes on \(\Gamma_r\) carry unknowns.
It adds \((N_A,\hat{a}\,N_B)_{\Gamma_r}\) to the stiffness matrix and \((N_A,\hat{c})_{\Gamma_r}\) to the force vector, together with a Dirichlet term where \(\Gamma_r\) meets \(\Gamma_g\).
These integrals are computed with the face quadrature of Class 20, and each Robin face contributes to a \((p+1)\times(p+1)\) block of the element stiffness matrix.
Class 23 shows why the stiffness matrix, including these Robin terms, is invertible, and when it is not.

title: 23  Class 23: Minimization, Symmetry, and Positive Definiteness
text:
23.1 Notation
To this point, we have assumed that the problems we are working on can actually be solved, and that each has exactly one solution. In this class, we will show why this is true, and identify when it is not.
We will approach this question in two ways. First, we will show that the weak form is equivalent to a third statement of the problem, in which the solution is the function that minimizes an energy. This viewpoint explains why the solution is unique, and it is the minimization that Class 18 indicated would return here. Second, we will show that the stiffness matrix is symmetric and positive definite, which guarantees that the matrix equations of the finite element method have exactly one solution.
Throughout this class, we include the Robin terms of Class 22. To keep the expressions compact, the left side of the weak form will be combined into a single bilinear form, and the right side into a single linear form.
\[
B(w,u) := a(w,u) + (w,\hat{a}\,u)_{\Gamma_r}
= \int_\Omega \nabla w\cdot\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_r} w\,\hat{a}\,u\;d\Gamma ,
\]
\[
L(w) := (w,f) + (w,h)_{\Gamma_h} + (w,\hat{c})_{\Gamma_r}
= \int_\Omega w\,f\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} w\,h\;d\Gamma + \int_{\Gamma_r} w\,\hat{c}\;d\Gamma .
\]
When there is no Robin boundary, \(B(w,u) = a(w,u)\), which is the form used in Class 18. The weak form of Class 22 is then
\[
(\mathrm{W})\qquad
\text{find } u\in\mathcal{S} \text{ such that } B(w,u) = L(w) \text{ for all } w\in\mathcal{V} .
\]
Three properties of \(B\) will be used repeatedly.
\[
B(w,w) = \int_\Omega \nabla w\cdot\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla w\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_r} \hat{a}\,w^2\;d\Gamma ,
\]
and both integrands are nonnegative.
Each of these assumptions has a physical meaning. The conductivity is symmetric and positive definite, so that heat never flows toward higher temperatures (see the 2D heat appendix). The Robin coefficient is also nonnegative in physical problems. For convection, \(\hat{a} = h_c\ge 0\), so that heat flows from a warmer surface into a cooler fluid and not the reverse, and for a spring support, \(\hat{a} = k_s\ge 0\), so that the spring resists the motion of the end rather than assisting it.
crumbs: 23  Class 23: Minimization, Symmetry, and Positive Definiteness

title: 23  Class 23: Minimization, Symmetry, and Positive Definiteness
text:
\(B\) is bilinear, meaning that it is linear in each of its two arguments, so that, for example, \(B(w, u_1 + \alpha\,u_2) = B(w,u_1) + \alpha\,B(w,u_2)\) for any number \(\alpha\). Similarly, \(L\) is linear.
\(B\) is symmetric, \(B(w,u) = B(u,w)\), whenever the conductivity is symmetric. In index notation, \(w_{,i}\,\kappa_{ij}\,u_{,j} = u_{,j}\,\kappa_{ij}\,w_{,i} = u_{,j}\,\kappa_{ji}\,w_{,i}\), where the last step uses \(\kappa_{ij} = \kappa_{ji}\), and the Robin term is unchanged when \(w\) and \(u\) are exchanged.
\(B(w,w)\ge 0\) whenever the conductivity is positive definite and \(\hat{a}\ge 0\), since
crumbs: 23  Class 23: Minimization, Symmetry, and Positive Definiteness

title: 23  Class 23: Minimization, Symmetry, and Positive Definiteness
text:
23.2 The minimization form
Define the total potential energy of a candidate function \(v\) as
\[
\Pi(v) := \tfrac{1}{2}\,B(v,v) - L(v)
= \frac{1}{2}\int_\Omega \nabla v\cdot\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla v\;d\Omega
+ \frac{1}{2}\int_{\Gamma_r} \hat{a}\,v^2\;d\Gamma
- \int_\Omega v\,f\;d\Omega - \int_{\Gamma_h} v\,h\;d\Gamma - \int_{\Gamma_r} v\,\hat{c}\;d\Gamma .
\]
\(\Pi\) is a functional: it takes an entire function \(v\) as its input, and returns a single number. The minimization form of the problem is
\[
(\mathrm{M})\qquad
\text{find } u\in\mathcal{S} \text{ such that } \Pi(u)\le\Pi(v) \text{ for every } v\in\mathcal{S} .
\]
The name comes from mechanics. For the pile of the rod appendix, which has no Robin boundary,
\[
\Pi(v) = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^L EA\,\left(v_{,x}\right)^2 dx - \int_0^L v\,f\;dx - v(0)\,h .
\]
The first term is the strain energy stored in the pile when it is displaced by \(v\), and the remaining terms are the work done by the distributed load and by the load at the head of the pile. The principle of minimum potential energy states that, of all of the displacements that satisfy the support conditions, the one that actually occurs minimizes this total. For heat conduction, \(\Pi\) is not a physical energy, but it has the same mathematical structure, and it is still common to refer to it as an energy. Its first term is the square of the energy norm of Class 18, \(\|v\|_E^2 = B(v,v)\), and it measures how much \(v\) varies across the domain, weighted by the conductivity.
crumbs: 23  Class 23: Minimization, Symmetry, and Positive Definiteness

title: 23  Class 23: Minimization, Symmetry, and Positive Definiteness
section: 23.3 The weak form and the minimization form are equivalent
text:
23.3 The weak form and the minimization form are equivalent
We now show that, under the assumptions above, a function solves (W) if and only if it solves (M).

23.3.1 From the weak form to the minimization form
Suppose that \(u\) solves (W), and let \(v\in\mathcal{S}\) be any other candidate. Write the difference between them as \(w = v - u\). Since \(u\) and \(v\) both equal \(g\) on \(\Gamma_g\), their difference is zero on \(\Gamma_g\), and therefore \(w\in\mathcal{V}\). Expanding the energy of \(v = u + w\) using the bilinearity of \(B\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pi(u + w)
&= \tfrac{1}{2}B(u,u) + \tfrac{1}{2}B(u,w) + \tfrac{1}{2}B(w,u) + \tfrac{1}{2}B(w,w) - L(u) - L(w) \\[2pt]
&= \underbrace{\left[\tfrac{1}{2}B(u,u) - L(u)\right]}_{\Pi(u)}
+ \underbrace{\left[B(w,u) - L(w)\right]}_{0 \text{ by (W), since } w\in\mathcal{V}}
+ \tfrac{1}{2}B(w,w) ,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the second line uses the symmetry of \(B\) to combine \(\tfrac{1}{2}B(u,w) + \tfrac{1}{2}B(w,u) = B(w,u)\). Therefore, for every \(v\in\mathcal{S}\),
\[
\boxed{\;\Pi(v) = \Pi(u) + \tfrac{1}{2}\,B(v - u,\, v - u)\;}
\]
Since \(B(w,w)\ge 0\), it follows that \(\Pi(v)\ge\Pi(u)\), and \(u\) minimizes the energy.


23.3.2 From the minimization form to the weak form
Suppose instead that \(u\) minimizes \(\Pi\) over \(\mathcal{S}\). Choose any \(w\in\mathcal{V}\) and any number \(\varepsilon\). Then \(u + \varepsilon w\in\mathcal{S}\), since adding a function that is zero on \(\Gamma_g\) does not change the values on \(\Gamma_g\). Define the ordinary function of one variable
\[
\varphi(\varepsilon) := \Pi(u + \varepsilon w)
= \Pi(u) + \varepsilon\left[B(w,u) - L(w)\right] + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\varepsilon^2\,B(w,w) ,
\]
which follows from the same expansion as above, with \(\varepsilon w\) in place of \(w\). Since \(u\) minimizes \(\Pi\), the function \(\varphi\) has its minimum at \(\varepsilon = 0\), and therefore \(\varphi'(0) = 0\) (where the derivative is taken with respect to \(\varepsilon\)).
\[
\varphi'(0) = B(w,u) - L(w) = 0 .
\]
Since \(w\in\mathcal{V}\) was arbitrary, this is the weak form (W).
The weak form therefore states that the derivative of the energy at the solution is zero in every admissible direction \(w\). The test functions are the directions in which the solution can be changed without violating the Dirichlet condition. This is the reason that the weak form is also called the variational form: the calculation above is the basic step of the calculus of variations, and \(B(w,u) - L(w)\) is called the first variation of \(\Pi\) in the direction \(w\). In mechanics, \(w\) is a virtual displacement, and the weak form is the principle of virtual work, which will return in the classes on elasticity.
Figure 23.1 shows this for the wall of Class 22, with its outer face exchanging heat with air at \(h_c\) = 10 W/(m²·K). Three directions \(w_1\), \(w_2\), and \(w_3\) are chosen, each of which is zero at the interior face, where the temperature is prescribed. Moving away from the solution in any of these directions increases the energy, and each curve has zero slope at \(\varepsilon = 0\).






Figure 23.1: (a) The solution \(u\) of the wall problem of Class 22 with \(h_c\) = 10 W/(m²·K), together with six other functions in \(\mathcal{S}\), obtained by adding \(\pm 8\) °C times each of three functions \(w_i\in\mathcal{V}\). Each of these candidates satisfies the Dirichlet condition at \(x = L\). (b) The change in energy along each direction, computed directly from the definition of \(\Pi\). Each curve is a parabola with its minimum at \(\varepsilon = 0\); the slope of each curve at \(\varepsilon = 0\), computed numerically, is zero to within the accuracy of the numerical integration (less than 10-4 in magnitude), which is the weak form for these three choices of \(w\). The curvatures, \(B(w_i,w_i)\) = 14.7, 23.0, and 92.1, increase as the direction varies more rapidly across the wall.





23.3.3 Uniqueness
The energy viewpoint also shows that the solution is unique. Suppose that \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) both solve (W), and let \(e = u_2 - u_1\in\mathcal{V}\). Applying the boxed identity twice, once with \(u = u_1\) and \(v = u_2\), and once with the roles exchanged, gives
\[
\Pi(u_2) = \Pi(u_1) + \tfrac{1}{2}B(e,e)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\Pi(u_1) = \Pi(u_2) + \tfrac{1}{2}B(e,e) .
\]
Adding these two equations gives \(B(e,e) = 0\), that is,
\[
\int_\Omega \nabla e\cdot\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla e\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_r} \hat{a}\,e^2\;d\Gamma = 0 .
\]
Both integrals are nonnegative, so both must be zero.

Since \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\) is positive definite, \(\nabla e\cdot\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla e > 0\) wherever \(\nabla e\neq\underline{0}\). The first integral can only be zero if \(\nabla e = \underline{0}\) throughout \(\Omega\), which means that \(e\) is a constant (assuming that \(\Omega\) is a single connected piece).
If \(\Gamma_g\) is not empty, then \(e = 0\) on \(\Gamma_g\), since \(e\in\mathcal{V}\), and the constant must be zero.
If \(\Gamma_g\) is empty, but \(\hat{a} > 0\) on some part of \(\Gamma_r\), then the second integral can only be zero if \(e = 0\) on that part, and again the constant must be zero.

In either case, \(e = 0\), and \(u_1 = u_2\). The solution of the weak form, and therefore of the strong form, is unique provided that

the conductivity \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\) is symmetric and positive definite throughout \(\Omega\),
\(\hat{a}\ge 0\) on \(\Gamma_r\), and
either \(\Gamma_g\) is not empty, or \(\hat{a} > 0\) on some part of \(\Gamma_r\).

Geometrically, \(\Pi\) can be pictured as a bowl over the space of candidate functions. The weak form states that the bowl is flat at \(u\) in every admissible direction, and the three conditions ensure that the bowl curves upward in every direction, so that it has only one bottom.
The arguments above show that if a solution exists, it is unique, and it minimizes the energy. Showing that a minimizer exists at all in the infinite-dimensional space \(\mathcal{S}\) requires more advanced analysis, in particular the Lax–Milgram theorem, which relies on the same three conditions together with properties of the space \(H^1\). We will take this result as given. For the finite element problem, which has finitely many unknowns, existence follows directly from the properties of the stiffness matrix, as shown below.

title: 23  Class 23: Minimization, Symmetry, and Positive Definiteness
section: 23.4 The finite element problem is also a minimization
text:
23.4 The finite element problem is also a minimization
The Galerkin method looks for \(u^h\) in the smaller space \(\mathcal{S}^h\subset\mathcal{S}\). Writing a candidate as \(v^h + g^h\), with \(v^h = \sum_B d_B N_B\) as in Class 22, and substituting into \(\Pi\) gives
\[
\Pi(v^h + g^h) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\underline{d}^T\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{d} - \underline{d}^T\underline{F} + \text{(terms that do not depend on } \underline{d}\text{)} ,
\]
where \(\underline{\underline{K}}\) and \(\underline{F}\) are the stiffness matrix and force vector of Class 22. In index notation, the first two terms are \(\tfrac{1}{2}d_A K_{AB} d_B - d_A F_A\). The energy is now an ordinary function of the vector of unknowns \(\underline{d}\), and its minimum is found by setting its gradient to zero. Using the symmetry of \(\underline{\underline{K}}\),
\[
\frac{\partial\Pi}{\partial d_A} = K_{AB}\,d_B - F_A = 0
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{d} = \underline{F} ,
\]
which are the Galerkin equations. The matrix of second derivatives of \(\Pi\) is \(\partial^2\Pi/\partial d_A\partial d_B = K_{AB}\), so the shape of the energy as a function of \(\underline{d}\) is determined entirely by \(\underline{\underline{K}}\). For problems with a symmetric bilinear form, such as this one, the Galerkin method is therefore the same as minimizing the energy over \(\mathcal{S}^h\), which is known as the Rayleigh–Ritz method.
This also connects the two minimization statements of Class 18. Since \(\mathcal{S}^h\subset\mathcal{S}\), the boxed identity holds for every \(v\in\mathcal{S}^h\), and states that
\[
\Pi(v) = \Pi(u) + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\left\|v - u\right\|_E^2 .
\]
Since \(\Pi(u)\) is a fixed number, the function in \(\mathcal{S}^h\) with the smallest energy is also the function in \(\mathcal{S}^h\) that is closest to \(u\) in the energy norm. The physical statement (the solution minimizes the energy) and the approximation statement (the finite element solution is the best approximation in the energy norm, which is Céa’s lemma) are therefore two views of the same result.
crumbs: 23  Class 23: Minimization, Symmetry, and Positive Definiteness

title: 23  Class 23: Minimization, Symmetry, and Positive Definiteness
section: 23.5 The stiffness matrix is symmetric and positive definite
text:
23.5 The stiffness matrix is symmetric and positive definite
With the Robin terms included, the entries of the stiffness matrix are \(K_{AB} = B(N_A,N_B)\), for \(A\) and \(B\) not on \(\Gamma_g\). We now show that \(\underline{\underline{K}}\) is symmetric and positive definite.

23.5.1 Symmetry
In index notation,
\[
K_{AB} = \int_\Omega N_{A,i}\,\kappa_{ij}\,N_{B,j}\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_r} N_A\,\hat{a}\,N_B\;d\Gamma ,
\qquad
K_{BA} = \int_\Omega N_{B,i}\,\kappa_{ij}\,N_{A,j}\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_r} N_B\,\hat{a}\,N_A\;d\Gamma .
\]
The two Robin integrals are equal. Renaming the dummy indices \(i\leftrightarrow j\) in the first integral of \(K_{BA}\) gives \(\int_\Omega N_{B,j}\,\kappa_{ji}\,N_{A,i}\,d\Omega = \int_\Omega N_{A,i}\,\kappa_{ji}\,N_{B,j}\,d\Omega\), which equals the first integral of \(K_{AB}\) when \(\kappa_{ji} = \kappa_{ij}\). The same steps in matrix notation are
\[
\left(\nabla N_A\right)^T\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\,\nabla N_B
= \left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}^T\nabla N_A\right)^T\nabla N_B
= \left(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\,\nabla N_A\right)^T\nabla N_B
= \left(\nabla N_B\right)^T\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\,\nabla N_A ,
\]
where the second step uses \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}^T = \underline{\underline{\kappa}}\), and the last step uses the fact that the dot product of two vectors does not depend on their order. Therefore, \(\underline{\underline{K}}\) is symmetric whenever \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\) is symmetric.


23.5.2 Positive definiteness
A symmetric matrix \(\underline{\underline{K}}\) is positive definite if

\(\underline{c}^T\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{c}\ge 0\) for every vector \(\underline{c}\), which alone is called positive semidefinite, and
\(\underline{c}^T\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{c} = 0\) only when \(\underline{c} = \underline{0}\).

Equivalently, every eigenvalue of \(\underline{\underline{K}}\) is positive. To check these properties, take any vector \(\underline{c}\) and build the function \(w^h = \sum_A c_A N_A\in\mathcal{V}^h\) from it. Using summation notation and the bilinearity of \(B\),
\[
\underline{c}^T\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{c}
= c_A\,K_{AB}\,c_B
= c_A\,B(N_A,N_B)\,c_B
= B\!\left(c_A N_A,\; c_B N_B\right)
= B(w^h,w^h)
= \int_\Omega \nabla w^h\cdot\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla w^h\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_r} \hat{a}\,\left(w^h\right)^2 d\Gamma .
\]
The question about the matrix has become the same question that was answered for uniqueness.

Both integrals are nonnegative when \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\) is positive definite and \(\hat{a}\ge 0\), so \(\underline{c}^T\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{c}\ge 0\).
If \(\underline{c}^T\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{c} = 0\), then, by the same argument as before, \(\nabla w^h = \underline{0}\), so \(w^h\) is a constant. This constant is zero if \(\Gamma_g\) is not empty, since every basis function in \(\mathcal{V}^h\) is zero on \(\Gamma_g\), or if \(\hat{a} > 0\) on some part of \(\Gamma_r\). Finally, \(w^h = 0\) implies \(\underline{c} = \underline{0}\), since evaluating \(w^h\) at the node of \(N_A\) gives \(c_A\), because each Lagrange basis function equals one at its own node and zero at all other nodes.

The stiffness matrix is therefore symmetric and positive definite under the same three conditions found for uniqueness. Consequently, \(\underline{\underline{K}}\) is invertible, and \(\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{d} = \underline{F}\) has exactly one solution for any force vector. In terms of the energy, \(\Pi(\underline{d})\) is a bowl with a single lowest point.
crumbs: 23  Class 23: Minimization, Symmetry, and Positive Definiteness

title: 23  Class 23: Minimization, Symmetry, and Positive Definiteness
text:
23.6 When the conditions fail

23.6.1 Only Neumann boundaries
If the entire boundary is a Neumann boundary, the third condition fails. The basis functions sum to one everywhere, \(\sum_A N_A = 1\), so choosing \(\underline{c} = \underline{1} = (1, 1, \ldots, 1)\) gives \(w^h = 1\), whose gradient is zero. Then \(\underline{1}^T\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{1} = 0\), and in fact \(\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{1} = \underline{0}\), so \(\underline{\underline{K}}\) is singular. Physically, when only fluxes are prescribed, adding the same constant to the temperature everywhere changes nothing, since the problem contains no reference temperature. This is the same situation as the floating pile in the rod appendix, which can translate as a rigid body.
A singular system may have no solution or infinitely many solutions. Multiplying \(\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{d} = \underline{F}\) by \(\underline{1}^T\) shows that a solution can exist only if \(\underline{1}^T\underline{F} = 0\), and since the basis functions sum to one, this condition is
\[
\sum_A F_A = \int_\Omega f\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma} h\;d\Gamma = 0 .
\]
This is a statement of steady state: the total heat generated in the body and entering through its boundary must be zero. If this holds, there are infinitely many solutions, which differ from each other by a constant, and an additional condition, such as fixing the temperature at one point, is needed to select one of them. If it does not hold, there is no steady-state solution at all, since the body continues to heat up or cool down. In terms of the energy, \(\Pi(\underline{d} + t\,\underline{1}) = \Pi(\underline{d}) - t\,\underline{1}^T\underline{F}\), so the energy decreases without bound along the direction \(\underline{1}\).


23.6.2 Robin coefficients that are small
If there is no Dirichlet boundary and \(\hat{a} > 0\) on \(\Gamma_r\), the stiffness matrix is positive definite, but its smallest eigenvalue decreases as \(\hat{a}\) decreases. Table 23.1 shows this for a one-dimensional bar with \(\kappa = 1\), length 1, and eight linear elements.

As \(\hat{a}\) decreases, the smallest eigenvalue approaches zero, and the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue, which is called the condition number, grows. A large condition number means that small changes in \(\underline{F}\), including roundoff errors, can produce large changes in \(\underline{d}\). Physically, a boundary that is only weakly connected to its surroundings requires a large difference from the reference value to pass a given flux, such as a large temperature difference for a surface cooled by convection, or a large displacement for the end of a rod resting on a soft spring.


23.6.3 Other ways the conditions can fail

If \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\) is not positive definite somewhere, for example in a region assigned zero conductivity or given incorrect material data, the stiffness matrix can be singular.
If \(\Omega\) consists of separate pieces, such as two parts of an assembly that the mesh does not connect, each piece needs its own Dirichlet boundary or Robin boundary with \(\hat{a} > 0\).
If \(\hat{a} < 0\), which does not occur for convection or for spring supports, positive definiteness can be lost.
Some problems are not symmetric at all. For example, the transport of a contaminant by a moving fluid adds a term of the form \(\int_\Omega w\,\left(\underline{v}\cdot\nabla u\right)d\Omega\) to the weak form, where \(\underline{v}\) is the fluid velocity, and this term changes when \(w\) and \(u\) are exchanged. The stiffness matrix is then not symmetric, and there is no energy whose minimum is the solution. The Galerkin method still applies, and existence and uniqueness can often still be shown using the Lax–Milgram theorem, which does not require symmetry, but the minimization viewpoint of this class is lost.

Things to try:

Dirichlet + Neumann. Without the Dirichlet condition, the energy has no lowest point. The Dirichlet condition restricts the candidates to a line, and along that line there is only one minimum. This is why removing the Dirichlet rows and columns turns a singular matrix into an invertible one.

title: 23  Class 23: Minimization, Symmetry, and Positive Definiteness
text:
23.8 Why this matters in practice

Solvers. Symmetric positive definite systems can be solved with methods that do not work for general matrices. The Cholesky factorization requires about half of the work of a general LU factorization, and the conjugate gradient method, which is widely used for large finite element problems, requires a symmetric positive definite matrix.
Debugging. An error such as LinAlgError: Singular matrix almost always indicates a missing or misapplied boundary condition, for example a model with no Dirichlet boundary, Robin coefficients that were not assembled, or a region of the mesh that is not connected to the rest.
Verification. Three inexpensive checks follow from this class. The assembled stiffness matrix should be symmetric, which can be checked with np.allclose(K, K.T). On a small mesh, its smallest eigenvalue should be positive. For a problem with only Neumann boundaries, \(\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{1}\) should be zero to roundoff, which checks the assembly of the interior terms without requiring an exact solution.
crumbs: 23  Class 23: Minimization, Symmetry, and Positive Definiteness

title: 23  Class 23: Minimization, Symmetry, and Positive Definiteness
text:
23.9 Summary

The weak form is equivalent to the minimization form: the solution minimizes the energy \(\Pi(v) = \tfrac{1}{2}B(v,v) - L(v)\) over all functions that satisfy the Dirichlet condition. The weak form states that the derivative of \(\Pi\) at the solution is zero in every admissible direction, which is why it is also called the variational form.
For every \(v\in\mathcal{S}\), \(\Pi(v) = \Pi(u) + \tfrac{1}{2}\|v - u\|_E^2\). This identity shows that the solution is unique, and that the finite element solution, which minimizes \(\Pi\) over \(\mathcal{S}^h\), is the best approximation in the energy norm.
The stiffness matrix is symmetric when the conductivity is symmetric, and positive definite when the conductivity is positive definite, \(\hat{a}\ge 0\), and either \(\Gamma_g\) is not empty or \(\hat{a} > 0\) on part of \(\Gamma_r\). Under these conditions, \(\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{d} = \underline{F}\) has one solution.
With only Neumann boundaries, \(\underline{\underline{K}}\) is singular, and a solution exists only if the total heat supplied is zero, in which case it is determined only up to a constant.
Small Robin coefficients without a Dirichlet boundary give a matrix that is positive definite but poorly conditioned.
Problems that are not symmetric, such as transport by a moving fluid, have no minimization form, although the Galerkin method still applies.

title: Appendix A — Support: Norms and Function Spaces
text:
Supporting material for Class 3, from a conversation at the board about where the integrals in \(L^2\) and \(H^1\) come from.

B From a discrete norm to an integral
For a finite list of numbers, the norm is the familiar one:

\[
\|\underline{u}\| = \sqrt{u_1^2 + u_2^2 + \cdots + u_n^2}
\qquad\qquad
\|\underline{u}\|^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} u_i^2
\]

Now let those numbers be samples of a function, \(u_i = u(x_i)\). Adding more samples must not make the norm grow without bound, so each term carries a weight \(w_i\) — the piece of the domain it stands for:

\[
\|\underline{u}\|^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} u_i^2 \, w_i
\qquad \xrightarrow[\;n \to \infty\;]{} \qquad
\int_0^L u^2 \, dx
\]







Figure B.1: The integral is the infinite-dimensional version of the vector norm: weight each sample by the piece of domain it represents, then refine.





C The \(L^2\) (Lebesgue) norm

\[
u \in L^2(\Omega)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\int_\Omega u^2 \, d\Omega < \infty
\qquad\qquad
\|u\|_{L^2} = \left(\int_\Omega u^2 \, d\Omega\right)^{1/2}
\]

Membership depends on the domain as much as on the formula. Since the test is on \(u^2\), compare two functions whose squares are the two classic borderline integrands:

\[
u(x) = \frac{1}{x} \;\Rightarrow\; u^2 = \frac{1}{x^2}
\qquad\qquad
v(x) = \frac{1}{x^{1/4}} \;\Rightarrow\; v^2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}
\]


(\(v\) is the fourth root of \(1/x\); squaring it gives \(1/\sqrt{x}\).)







Figure C.1: Both left-hand integrands blow up at the origin, yet only one encloses a finite area — you cannot tell by looking, you have to do the integral. In the tail the verdicts reverse.












\(\Omega = (0,1)\)
\(\Omega = (1,\infty)\)




\(u = \dfrac{1}{x}\)
\(\displaystyle\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{x^2} = \infty\)
\(\displaystyle\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x^2} = 1\)


\(v = \dfrac{1}{x^{1/4}}\)
\(\displaystyle\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}} = 2\)
\(\displaystyle\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}} = \infty\)



Reading those off as membership in \(H^0 = L^2\):


\(\dfrac{1}{x} \notin H^0\big((0,1)\big)\)   but   \(\dfrac{1}{x} \in H^0\big((1,\infty)\big)\)
\(\dfrac{1}{x^{1/4}} \in H^0\big((0,1)\big)\)   but   \(\dfrac{1}{x^{1/4}} \notin H^0\big((1,\infty)\big)\)


The two ends make opposite demands: near a singularity the function must not blow up too fast, while over an infinite tail it must decay fast enough. For a pure power \(u = x^{-p}\), so \(u^2 = x^{-2p}\),

\[
\int_0^1 x^{-2p}\,dx < \infty \iff p < \tfrac{1}{2}
\qquad\qquad
\int_1^\infty x^{-2p}\,dx < \infty \iff p > \tfrac{1}{2}
\]


No single \(p\) satisfies both — so no pure power lies in \(L^2\big((0,\infty)\big)\), \(1/x\) included.



D Sobolev norms: \(H^0\) and \(H^1\)

\[
\underbrace{\|u\|_{H^0} = \left(\int_\Omega u^2\, d\Omega\right)^{1/2}}_{H^0 \;=\; L^2}
\qquad\qquad
\|u\|_{H^1} = \left(\int_\Omega u^2 + \left(u_{,x}\right)^2 d\Omega\right)^{1/2}
\]

The extra derivative term is what makes \(H^1\) a measure of a function’s energy: two functions can be the same “size” in \(L^2\) while costing very different amounts to bend.






Figure D.1: All three have the same \(L^2\) norm; the derivative term grows in proportion to \(k\). That term is the energy \(H^1\) sees and \(L^2\) does not.




This is why the weak form of Class 3 is posed in \(H^1\): the integral \(\int_0^1 w_{,x}u_{,x}\,dx\) only makes sense for functions whose derivatives are square integrable.

text:
B.1 The physical problem
This page and its companion, 1D Poisson III: An Axially Loaded Rod, read the same model problem — the one-dimensional Poisson equation of Hughes, The Finite Element Method, Chapter 1 — in two different physical settings. The mathematics is identical on both pages. The physics is not, and it is the physics that tells you what \(f\), \(g\), and \(h\) are, what units they carry, and which way they point.
Hughes states the model problem with every constant set to one:
Choosing a length of one and a material constant of one hides two things that the pictures below need, so we put them back: the domain becomes \(\Omega = \,]0, L[\), and a material constant \(K\) appears inside the derivative, as in Class 4:
On this page \(u\) is a temperature and \(K = \kappa\) is the thermal conductivity. Everything below is in SI units.
The wall is long and tall compared with its thickness. Far from its edges, nothing changes as you move along the wall or up it — temperature varies only through the thickness, in \(x\). So cut out a strip with a \(1\,\text{m} \times 1\,\text{m}\) face and follow the temperature along it. Every quantity on this page is per square meter of wall face, which is why fluxes are in W/m² and not W.
Three things act on the strip, and each becomes one piece of the strong form:

title: Appendix B — 1D Poisson I: Heat Conduction Through a Wall
text:
B.2 The one-dimensional domain






Figure B.2: The domain \(\Omega\) is the open interval through the thickness; its boundary \(\Gamma\) is just the two faces, each with an outward unit normal.





\(\Omega = \,]0, L[\) is the open interval — the inside of the wall, faces excluded. Hughes writes open intervals with outward-facing brackets.
\(\bar\Omega = [0, L]\) is its closure — the wall including its two faces. The solution \(u\) is defined on \(\bar\Omega\), since we need its value at the faces.
\(\Gamma = \{0, L\}\) is the boundary: in one dimension, just two points.
The outward unit normal \(n\) points out of \(\Omega\): \(n = -1\) at \(x = 0\) and \(n = +1\) at \(x = L\). It is only a sign in 1D, but that sign is what decides whether a Neumann condition reads \(-\kappa u_{,x}(0) = h\) or \(+\kappa u_{,x}(L) = h\).
Each point of \(\Gamma\) gets exactly one boundary condition: \(\Gamma = \Gamma_g \cup \Gamma_h\) and \(\Gamma_g \cap \Gamma_h = \emptyset\).

title: Appendix B — 1D Poisson I: Heat Conduction Through a Wall
section: B.4 Where the differential equation comes from
text:
B.4 Where the differential equation comes from

B.4.1 Conservation of energy on a thin slice






Figure B.3: A slice of the strip of thickness \(\Delta x\). At steady state, heat in plus heat made equals heat out.



Let \(q(x)\) be the heat flux — watts crossing each square meter of a plane at \(x\), counted positive when heat moves toward \(+x\). At steady state the slice’s temperature is not changing, so every watt that enters or is made inside it must leave:

\[
\underbrace{q(x)\cdot 1}_{\text{in}}
+ \underbrace{f\,\Delta x \cdot 1}_{\text{generated}}
- \underbrace{q(x+\Delta x)\cdot 1}_{\text{out}} = 0
\qquad\xrightarrow[\;\text{divide by } \Delta x,\; \Delta x \to 0\;]{}\qquad
-q_{,x} + f = 0
\]


Each term is in watts: W/m² × 1 m² for the fluxes, and W/m³ × (Δx · 1 m²) for the generation. Read the result as “the flux grows exactly as fast as heat is being made”: \(q_{,x} = f\).



B.4.2 Fourier’s law: heat flows downhill
The balance has one equation and two unknowns, \(q\) and \(u\). The material supplies the second relation. Fourier’s law says heat flows from hot to cold, at a rate proportional to how steeply the temperature falls:

\[
q = -\kappa\, u_{,x}
\]







Figure B.4: Fourier’s law. The coloured band is the wall, red where it is hot. Heat flows downhill on the temperature curve: the minus sign in \(q = -\kappa u_{,x}\) makes the flux point opposite to the slope.



Substituting Fourier’s law into the balance gives the differential equation of the strong form, in all three of the notations you will meet:

\[
-\left(\kappa\,u_{,x}\right)_{,x} = f
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\left(\kappa\,u_{,x}\right)_{,x} + f = 0
\quad\xrightarrow{\;\kappa \text{ constant}\;}\quad
\kappa\, u_{,xx} + f = 0
\quad\xrightarrow{\;\kappa = 1\;}\quad
u_{,xx} + f = 0 \;\;\text{(Hughes)}
\]



B.4.3 What the equation says about the shape of \(u\)
With \(\kappa\) constant, \(u_{,xx} = -f/\kappa\): the forcing sets the curvature of the temperature profile, point by point.






Figure B.5: Three walls with the same face temperatures and different forcing. With no source the profile is straight; a source bows it up; a sink bows it down. (\(\kappa\) = 1.4 W/(m·K), \(L\) = 0.30 m.)





\(f = 0\): \(u_{,xx} = 0\), so the profile is a straight line and the flux \(q = -\kappa u_{,x}\) is the same everywhere — what goes in one face comes out the other.
\(f > 0\): \(u_{,xx} < 0\), a hump. The wall is hotter inside than a straight line would predict, because the heat made inside has to flow out through the faces.
\(f < 0\): \(u_{,xx} > 0\), a dip — heat is being removed inside the wall.
crumbs: Appendices
B  1D Poisson I: Heat Conduction Through a Wall

title: Appendix B — 1D Poisson I: Heat Conduction Through a Wall
text:
B.5 The forcing function \(f\)
\(f(x)\) is heat generated per unit volume, in W/m³. It is the only term in the strong form that acts in the interior of \(\Omega\); \(g\) and \(h\) act only at the faces. Integrated through the thickness, it gives the heat made behind each square meter of wall, in W/m²:

\[
\int_0^L f\,dx \quad \left[\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^3}\cdot\text{m}
= \tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}\right]
\qquad\text{e.g.}\qquad 500 \times 0.30 = 150\ \text{W/m}^2
\]







Figure B.6: Three forcing functions. Top: the wall with a \(+\) mark for heat made and a \(-\) mark for heat removed, at a density proportional to \(|f|\). Bottom: the same \(f(x)\) as a graph.





Heat of hydration — cement releases heat as it cures, nearly uniformly through a freshly cast wall. This is the \(f\) used in the example on this page.
Absorbed radiation — sunlight that penetrates a (semi-)transparent layer is absorbed over a short depth \(\delta\), so \(f = f_0 e^{-x/\delta}\) is concentrated near the sunlit face.
Embedded heating or cooling — electric heating cables in the slab give \(f > 0\) where they run; a chilled-water pipe removes heat, \(f < 0\).
\(f = 0\) is the everyday case of an ordinary, inert wall.
crumbs: Appendices
B  1D Poisson I: Heat Conduction Through a Wall

title: Appendix B — 1D Poisson I: Heat Conduction Through a Wall
text:
B.6 Boundary conditions
Each face gets exactly one condition: either its temperature is known, or the heat flux through it is known. Never both — and, as we will see, never neither.

B.6.1 Dirichlet: \(u = g\) on \(\Gamma_g\) — the temperature is known






Figure B.7: A Dirichlet condition pins the value of \(u\) at a face. Every one of these curves satisfies \(u(L) = 20\) °C; the condition says nothing about the slope, which is left for the rest of the problem to decide.





\(g\) is a temperature, in °C.
Physically: the face touches something so large, or so well mixed, that the wall cannot change its temperature — and for the moment can be thought of as room air under a thermostat, an ice bath at 0 °C, flowing water, deep ground.
It is called an essential boundary condition: it is imposed directly on the unknown \(u\). Later, in the weak form, it is built into the trial space \(\mathcal{S}\) rather than appearing in any integral.




B.6.2 Neumann: \((\kappa u_{,x})\,n = h\) on \(\Gamma_h\) — the heat flux is known
Here is the one relation that looks mysterious until you draw it. Start from Fourier’s law: \(q\) is the flux toward \(+x\), so \(q\,n\) is the flux leaving through a face (outward normal), and \(-q\,n\) is the flux entering through it. The Neumann condition fixes the flux entering:

\[
h = -q\,n = -\left(-\kappa u_{,x}\right) n = \left(\kappa\,u_{,x}\right) n
\]

So \((\kappa u_{,x})\,n = h\) is not a new law; it is Fourier’s law evaluated at a face, with \(h\) read as heat flux into the wall, in W/m². Now substitute the two possible normals:

\[
\text{at } x = 0 \;(n = -1): \quad -\kappa\,u_{,x}(0) = h
\qquad\qquad
\text{at } x = L \;(n = +1): \quad +\kappa\,u_{,x}(L) = h
\]







Figure B.8: The Neumann condition at either face, for heating, insulation, and cooling. The black curve is the temperature near the face and the dashed red line is its tangent there. Whichever face it acts on, heat entering (\(h > 0\)) makes the face the hot spot, so the temperature always falls away from the face into the wall — which is a negative slope on the left and a positive slope on the right. That sign flip is exactly the \(n\).





\(h\) is a heat flux, in W/m², positive when heat goes in, on either face.
\(h = 0\) is a perfectly insulated (adiabatic) face: the profile arrives with zero slope. By symmetry, this is also what the mid-plane of a wall heated equally from both sides looks like.
The magnitude of the slope is \(|u_{,x}| = |h|/\kappa\). With \(h\) = 50 W/m² and \(\kappa\) = 1.4 W/(m·K), the temperature changes by 35.7 °C per meter — 0.36 °C over the first centimeter of the wall. A poorer conductor (smaller \(\kappa\)) needs a steeper gradient to carry the same flux.
It is called a natural boundary condition: in the weak form it will appear on its own as the boundary term \(w(0)\,h\), rather than being imposed on \(u\).
A real face exchanging heat with air obeys \(h = h_c\,(u_\infty - u)\), which mixes the value and the slope. That is a Robin condition, and it is not part of Hughes’ model problem.




B.6.3 Which face gets which condition
The model problem does not care which face is Dirichlet and which is Neumann — but the formulas do, through \(n\). There are four ways to assign the two faces:






Figure B.9: The four ways to assign the two faces, each with the same wall and the same \(f\) = 500 W/m³. On the right, blue dots are Dirichlet values the curve must pass through; dashed amber lines are the slopes that Neumann data force on it.





(a) Hughes’ arrangement. Flux given at \(x = 0\), temperature at \(x = L\): \(\;u(L) = g,\;\; -\kappa u_{,x}(0) = h\).
(b) Swapped. Temperature given at \(x = 0\), flux at \(x = L\): \(\;u(0) = g,\;\; +\kappa u_{,x}(L) = h\). Only the sign in front of \(\kappa u_{,x}\) changes. Note that (b) is the mirror image of (a), sun on the right instead of the left — and \(h\) = +50 W/m² in both, because in both the sun pushes heat in. The sign of the heat-flux \(h\) follows the wall, not the \(x\)-axis.
(c) Two Dirichlet faces is a well-posed problem, with two values \(g_0 = u(0)\) and \(g_L = u(L)\). Hughes’ notation then carries a \(g\) for each point of \(\Gamma_g\).
(d) Two Neumann faces is not a well-posed problem, for two reasons:

Uniqueness fails. Flux data only ever see \(u_{,x}\), so adding any constant to a solution gives another one. The temperature level is never pinned down.
Existence needs luck. At steady state, every watt in must come out: \(h_0 + h_L + \int_0^L f\,dx = 0\). The panel uses \(h_L\) = −200 W/m² for exactly this reason (50 in, 150 made, 200 out). Any other \(h_L\) has no steady solution at all — the wall just keeps heating up or cooling down.

So \(\Gamma_g\) must not be empty: at least one face needs a known temperature.

title: Appendix B — 1D Poisson I: Heat Conduction Through a Wall
text:
B.7 The strong form, complete
Collecting the pieces, for Hughes’ arrangement (a):

\[
(\mathrm{S}) \qquad
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Given } f : \bar\Omega \to \RR \;[\text{W/m}^3],\;
  \kappa > 0 \;[\text{W/(m·K)}],\;
  g \;[{}^\circ\text{C}], \text{ and } h \;[\text{W/m}^2],
  \text{ find } u : \bar\Omega \to \RR \;[{}^\circ\text{C}] \text{ such that} \\[3pt]
&\qquad \left(\kappa\,u_{,x}\right)_{,x} + f = 0
   && \text{on } \Omega = \,]0, L[ && \text{(energy balance + Fourier)} \\
&\qquad u(L) = g && && \text{(Dirichlet: known temperature)} \\
&\qquad -\kappa\,u_{,x}(0) = h && && \text{(Neumann: known inflow)}
\end{aligned}
\]

and, for the swapped arrangement (b), replace the last two lines by \(u(0) = g\) and \(+\kappa\,u_{,x}(L) = h\).


It is called the strong form because the differential equation must hold at every point of \(\Omega\). That demands \(u_{,xx}\) exist everywhere — a smooth solution. A wall made of two materials, with \(\kappa\) jumping at an interface, already strains this requirement; the weak form relaxes it.
With constant \(\kappa\) and \(f\), integrating twice gives the exact solution of (a):



\[
u(x) = g + \frac{h}{\kappa}\,(L - x) + \frac{f}{2\kappa}\,\left(L^2 - x^2\right)
\]


which, with \(L = \kappa = 1\), is the \(u(x) = g + (1-x)h + \int_x^1\!\int_0^y f\,dz\,dy\) of Class 4.
crumbs: Appendices
B  1D Poisson I: Heat Conduction Through a Wall

title: Appendix B — 1D Poisson I: Heat Conduction Through a Wall
text:
B.8 Worked example
The concrete wall of Figure B.1: \(L\) = 0.30 m, \(\kappa\) = 1.4 W/(m·K), curing at \(f\) = 500 W/m³, with \(h\) = 50 W/m² of sunlight absorbed at the outside face \(x = 0\) and the inside face \(x = L\) held at \(g\) = 20 °C. This is arrangement (a).

\[
\begin{aligned}
u(x) &= 20 + \frac{50}{1.4}\,(0.30 - x) + \frac{500}{2(1.4)}\,(0.09 - x^2)
  \quad [{}^\circ\text{C}] \\[4pt]
u(0) &= 20 + 10.71 + 16.07 = 46.8\ {}^\circ\text{C}
  \qquad\qquad u_{,x}(0) = -\frac{h}{\kappa} = -35.7\ {}^\circ\text{C/m} \\[4pt]
q(x) &= -\kappa\,u_{,x} = 50 + 500\,x \quad [\text{W/m}^2]
  \qquad\qquad q(L) = 200\ \text{W/m}^2
\end{aligned}
\]







Figure B.10: The solution of the worked example. Top: temperature, pinned at the inside face and leaving the outside face with the slope the sunlight dictates. Bottom: the heat flux \(q = -\kappa u_{,x}\), which grows by exactly the heat made inside the wall.



Every line of the strong form can be checked on the picture:


The differential equation. \(\kappa u_{,xx} = -f\): the temperature curve bends down everywhere, at the same rate, because \(f\) is uniform. Equivalently, \(q_{,x} = f\) = 500 W/m³: the flux line in the lower panel is straight with slope 500.
The Dirichlet condition. The curve passes through 20 °C at \(x = L\).
The Neumann condition. At \(x = 0\) the tangent drops 1.79 °C over the first 5 cm, a slope of −35.7 °C/m, and \(-\kappa u_{,x}(0) = -1.4 \times (-35.7) = 50\) W/m² \(= h\).
The energy balance. 50 W/m² in through the sunlit face plus 150 W/m² made inside equals the 200 W/m² delivered to the room at \(x = L\).


The same wall with the sun on the other side is arrangement (b): \(u(0) = 20\) °C, \(+\kappa u_{,x}(L) = 50\) W/m², and \(u(x) = g + \frac{h + fL}{\kappa}\,x -
\frac{f}{2\kappa}\,x^2\) — the mirror image of the curve above, with the same \(h\). Compare this with the rod, where mirroring the problem flips the sign of \(h\).

title: Appendix C — 1D Poisson II: The Wall, by Galerkin’s Method
text:
C.1 The weak form
The strong-form page set up heat conduction through a concrete wall as Hughes’ model problem. This page solves it approximately, following Hughes, Chapter 1, step by step:
The running example throughout is the one from before, in Hughes’ arrangement (a):
At the bottom of the page there is an explorer where you choose the element degree, the number and spacing of the elements, and the data, and see the matrices, the approximation, and its error update together.
crumbs: Appendices
C  1D Poisson II: The Wall, by Galerkin's Method

title: Appendix C — 1D Poisson II: The Wall, by Galerkin’s Method
text:
C.1.1 Two collections of functions
The weak form looks for \(u\) among trial functions and tests it against weighting (test) functions. The two collections differ only at the Dirichlet end:

\[
\mathcal{S} = \left\{\, u \;\middle|\; u \in H^1(\Omega),\; u(L) = g \,\right\}
\qquad\qquad
\mathcal{V} = \left\{\, w \;\middle|\; w \in H^1(\Omega),\; w(L) = 0 \,\right\}
\]







Figure C.1: Left: a few members of \(\mathcal{S}\). The solution is one of them, but so is every other reasonable temperature profile that is 20 °C at the room. Right: members of \(\mathcal{V}\), the same kind of function with the Dirichlet value replaced by zero.





\(H^1(\Omega)\) asks only that \(u\) and \(u_{,x}\) be square-integrable. In one dimension that means continuous, with a slope that may jump — exactly what a chain of polynomial pieces looks like. The strong form needed \(u_{,xx}\) everywhere; the weak form will need only \(u_{,x}\).
The Dirichlet condition is built into \(\mathcal{S}\): every trial function already satisfies it. That is what “essential” meant on the strong-form page.




C.1.2 Multiply, integrate, and integrate by parts
Take the differential equation, multiply it by any \(w \in \mathcal{V}\), and integrate through the wall:

\[
0 = \int_0^L w\left[\left(\kappa\,u_{,x}\right)_{,x} + f\right] dx
\qquad \text{for every } w \in \mathcal{V}
\]

The product rule, \(\left(w\,\kappa u_{,x}\right)_{,x} = w_{,x}\,\kappa u_{,x} +
w\left(\kappa u_{,x}\right)_{,x}\), moves one derivative off \(u\) and onto \(w\):

\[
\int_0^L w_{,x}\,\kappa\,u_{,x}\,dx
= \int_0^L w f\,dx
+ \Big[\, w\,\kappa\,u_{,x} \,\Big]_{x=0}^{x=L}
= \int_0^L w f\,dx
+ w(L)\,\kappa u_{,x}(L) - w(0)\,\kappa u_{,x}(0)
\]







Figure C.2: The boundary term, one end at a time. At the Neumann end the flux is data, so the term becomes \(w(0)\,h\). At the Dirichlet end the flux is not known — it is the heat delivered to the room, part of the answer — and choosing \(w(L) = 0\) is precisely what removes it. This is why \(\mathcal{V}\) vanishes on \(\Gamma_g\).



With \(-\kappa u_{,x}(0) = h\) and \(w(L) = 0\), what remains is the weak form.

\[
(\mathrm{W}) \qquad
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Given } f,\ g,\ h,\ \kappa, \text{ find } u \in \mathcal{S} \text{ such that for all } w \in \mathcal{V}: \\[3pt]
&\qquad \underbrace{\int_0^L w_{,x}\,\kappa\,u_{,x}\,dx}_{a(w,\,u)}
= \underbrace{\int_0^L w\,f\,dx}_{(w,\,f)} + w(0)\,h
\end{aligned}
\]

Hughes names the two integrals: the bilinear form \(a(w, u)\) and the \(L^2\) inner product \((w, f)\), so that \((\mathrm{W})\) reads compactly as

\[
a(w, u) = (w, f) + w(0)\,h \qquad \forall\, w \in \mathcal{V}
\]

The Neumann term follows the Neumann end. For each arrangement on the strong-form page:









Arrangement
\(\mathcal{S}\)
\(\mathcal{V}\)
Right-hand side




(a) Hughes: \(h\) at \(x=0\), \(g\) at \(x=L\)
\(u(L) = g\)
\(w(L) = 0\)
\((w, f) + w(0)\,h\)


(b) \(g\) at \(x=0\), \(h\) at \(x=L\)
\(u(0) = g\)
\(w(0) = 0\)
\((w, f) + w(L)\,h\)


(c) \(g\) at both ends
\(u(0) = g_0\), \(u(L) = g\)
\(w(0) = w(L) = 0\)
\((w, f)\)





Units. Every term of \((\mathrm{W})\) is W/m² times the units of \(w\). With a dimensionless \(w\), it is a weighted heat balance per square metre of wall.
Meaning. \((\mathrm{W})\) is the energy balance averaged with weight \(w\). One weight checks the balance “on average”; every weight in \(\mathcal{V}\) pins it down at every point. That is the equivalence \((\mathrm{S}) \Leftrightarrow (\mathrm{W})\) proved in Classes 4 and 5.
Only one derivative. \(u_{,x}\) and \(w_{,x}\) appear; \(u_{,xx}\) does not. A temperature profile with a kink — two concrete mixes with different \(\kappa\) — is now admissible.
crumbs: Appendices
C  1D Poisson II: The Wall, by Galerkin's Method

title: Appendix C — 1D Poisson II: The Wall, by Galerkin’s Method
text:
C.2 The Galerkin form
\((\mathrm{W})\) still asks for a whole function. Galerkin’s method replaces \(\mathcal{S}\) and \(\mathcal{V}\) by finite-dimensional collections \(\mathcal{S}^h \subset
\mathcal{S}\) and \(\mathcal{V}^h \subset \mathcal{V}\), built from a small number of basis functions, so that finding \(u^h\) means finding a list of numbers.

C.2.1 Elements, nodes, and Lagrange basis functions
Cut \([0, L]\) into \(n_{el}\) elements \(\Omega^e = [x^e_1, x^e_{n_{en}}]\) of length \(h^e\). On each element, use Lagrange polynomials of degree \(p\), which need \(n_{en} = p + 1\) element nodes, equally spaced. Neighbouring elements share their end nodes, so the mesh has

\[
n_{np} = p\,n_{el} + 1 \quad \text{nodes}, \qquad
x_1 = 0 < x_2 < \cdots < x_{n_{np}} = L
\]

Each element is a copy of one parent element, \(\xi \in [-1, 1]\), with nodes \(\xi_a = -1 + 2(a-1)/p\). The Lagrange function for node \(a\) is one there and zero at the other nodes:

\[
N_a(\xi) = \prod_{b \ne a} \frac{\xi - \xi_b}{\xi_a - \xi_b}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad N_a(\xi_b) = \delta_{ab}
\] \[
p = 1:\;\; N_1 = \tfrac12(1 - \xi),\;\; N_2 = \tfrac12(1 + \xi)
\qquad\quad
p = 2:\;\; N_1 = \tfrac12\xi(\xi - 1),\;\; N_2 = 1 - \xi^2,\;\; N_3 = \tfrac12\xi(\xi + 1)
\] \[
p = 3:\;\; N_{1,4} = \tfrac{1}{16}(1 \mp \xi)(9\xi^2 - 1),\qquad
N_{2,3} = \tfrac{9}{16}(1 - \xi^2)(1 \mp 3\xi)
\]







Figure C.3: Top: the Lagrange functions on the parent element for \(p\) = 1, 2, 3. Bottom: the global basis functions \(N_A\) they make on a mesh of three elements through the wall. Each is one at its own node and zero at every other node. Functions at element-end nodes span two elements; interior nodes (\(p \ge 2\)) stay inside one. The dashed function sits on the Dirichlet node \(x = L\) (filled dot): it will carry the known \(g\), not an unknown.





C.2.2 The Galerkin form, \((\mathrm{G})\)
With Hughes’ numbering, node \(n_{np}\) is on \(\Gamma_g\) and the other \(n = n_{np} - 1\) nodes carry unknowns. Build the approximations from the basis:

\[
w^h = \sum_{A=1}^{n} c_A\,N_A \;\in \mathcal{V}^h
\qquad\qquad
u^h = v^h + g^h,\qquad
v^h = \sum_{B=1}^{n} d_B\,N_B \;\in \mathcal{V}^h,\qquad
g^h = g\,N_{n+1}
\]


\(g^h\) takes care of the Dirichlet value (\(g^h(L) = g\), because \(N_{n+1}(L) = 1\)), and \(v^h\) vanishes at \(L\) like every member of \(\mathcal{V}^h\). So \(u^h \in \mathcal{S}^h\) automatically. Substituting \(u^h\) and \(w^h\) into \((\mathrm{W})\), and moving the known part \(g^h\) to the right, gives


\[
(\mathrm{G}) \qquad
a(w^h, v^h) = (w^h, f) + w^h(0)\,h - a(w^h, g^h)
\qquad \forall\, w^h \in \mathcal{V}^h
\]







Figure C.4: What \(u^h\) is made of, for the wall on three elements. Each thin line is one basis function scaled by its coefficient \(d_A\) — its nodal temperature — and the dashed one is \(g\,N_{n+1}\). Their sum is \(u^h\) (black). With \(p = 1\) the sum is a broken line; with \(p = 2\) it is piecewise quadratic, which here reproduces the exact quadratic profile (grey) perfectly.

title: Appendix C — 1D Poisson II: The Wall, by Galerkin’s Method
text:
C.3 From \((\mathrm{G})\) to \(\mathbf{K}\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{F}\)
Put the expansions into \((\mathrm{G})\). Because \(a(\cdot,\cdot)\) and \((\cdot,\cdot)\) are linear in each slot, the sums and constants come straight out:

\[
\sum_{A=1}^{n} c_A \left[\, \sum_{B=1}^{n} a(N_A, N_B)\,d_B
- (N_A, f) - N_A(0)\,h + a(N_A, N_{n+1})\,g \right] = 0
\]


This must hold for every \(w^h\), that is, for every choice of the \(c_A\). Choose \(c_A = 1\) for one \(A\) and zero for the rest: the bracket for that \(A\) must vanish. So there is one equation per unknown:


\[
\sum_{B=1}^{n} \underbrace{a(N_A, N_B)}_{K_{AB}}\;d_B
= \underbrace{(N_A, f) + N_A(0)\,h - a(N_A, N_{n+1})\,g}_{F_A},
\qquad A = 1, \dots, n
\] \[
\boxed{\;\mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{F}\;}
\qquad
K_{AB} = \int_0^L N_{A,x}\,\kappa\,N_{B,x}\,dx
\qquad
F_A = \int_0^L N_A\,f\,dx + \delta_{A1}\,h - \int_0^L N_{A,x}\,\kappa\,N_{n+1,x}\,dx\;g
\]



\(\mathbf{K}\) is the conductivity (stiffness) matrix, W/(m²·K); \(\mathbf{d}\) holds the unknown nodal temperatures, °C; \(\mathbf{F}\) is the heat-flux vector, W/m².
\(N_A(0) = \delta_{A1}\): only node 1 sits at \(x = 0\), so \(h\) enters only \(F_1\).
Symmetric, since \(a(N_A, N_B) = a(N_B, N_A)\).
Banded. \(K_{AB} = 0\) unless \(N_A\) and \(N_B\) are both non-zero on some element (Figure C.6).
Positive definite, because \(\kappa > 0\) and \(\Gamma_g\) is not empty. With two Neumann ends, arrangement (d), the constant function makes \(\mathbf{K}\mathbf{d} = 0\), so \(\mathbf{K}\) is singular: the non-uniqueness of the strong form, in matrix form.

title: Appendix C — 1D Poisson II: The Wall, by Galerkin’s Method
section: C.4 The element point of view
text:
C.4 The element point of view
Every integral over \([0, L]\) is a sum of integrals over elements, and on element \(e\) only its own \(n_{en}\) functions are non-zero. So all the work reduces to small element arrays, in local numbering \(a, b = 1, \dots, n_{en}\):

\[
k^e_{ab} = \int_{\Omega^e} N_{a,x}\,\kappa\,N_{b,x}\,dx
\qquad\qquad
f^e_a = \underbrace{\int_{\Omega^e} N_a\,f\,dx}_{\text{body}}
+ \underbrace{\delta_{e1}\,\delta_{a1}\,h}_{\text{Neumann end}}
- \underbrace{\sum_{b} k^e_{ab}\,g^e_b}_{\text{Dirichlet end}}
\]

where \(g^e_b\) is \(g\) if local node \(b\) is the Dirichlet node and zero otherwise.

C.4.1 The parent element, the Jacobian, and quadrature






Figure C.5: The isoparametric map for a quadratic element. The same \(N_a(\xi)\) that interpolate temperature also place the element in space. The crosses are the Gauss points, which follow the map.




\[
x(\xi) = \sum_{a=1}^{n_{en}} N_a(\xi)\,x^e_a,
\qquad
x_{,\xi} = \frac{h^e}{2},
\qquad
N_{a,x} = N_{a,\xi}\,\xi_{,x} = N_{a,\xi}\,\frac{2}{h^e}
\] \[
k^e_{ab} = \int_{-1}^{1} N_{a,\xi}\,\kappa\,N_{b,\xi}\,\left(x_{,\xi}\right)^{-1} d\xi
\approx \sum_{l=1}^{n_{int}} N_{a,\xi}(\tilde\xi_l)\,\kappa\,N_{b,\xi}(\tilde\xi_l)\,
\frac{2}{h^e}\,W_l
\qquad
f^e_a \approx \sum_{l=1}^{n_{int}} N_a(\tilde\xi_l)\,f\big(x(\tilde\xi_l)\big)\,\frac{h^e}{2}\,W_l
\]


An \(n_{int}\)-point Gauss rule is exact for polynomials up to degree \(2n_{int} - 1\). The stiffness integrand has degree \(2p - 2\), so \(n_{int} = p\) points already integrate it exactly. The code here uses \(p + 3\), so that non-polynomial \(f\) is integrated accurately as well.

For constant \(\kappa\) and \(f\), the integrals come out in closed form:

\[
p = 1:\quad
\mathbf{k}^e = \frac{\kappa}{h^e}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{f}^e_{\text{body}} = \frac{f\,h^e}{2}\begin{Bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{Bmatrix}
\] \[
p = 2:\quad
\mathbf{k}^e = \frac{\kappa}{3h^e}\begin{bmatrix} 7 & -8 & 1 \\ -8 & 16 & -8 \\ 1 & -8 & 7 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{f}^e_{\text{body}} = \frac{f\,h^e}{6}\begin{Bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{Bmatrix}
\] \[
p = 3:\quad
\mathbf{k}^e = \frac{\kappa}{40h^e}\begin{bmatrix}
148 & -189 & 54 & -13 \\ -189 & 432 & -297 & 54 \\ 54 & -297 & 432 & -189 \\ -13 & 54 & -189 & 148
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{f}^e_{\text{body}} = \frac{f\,h^e}{8}\begin{Bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{Bmatrix}
\]



Every row of \(\mathbf{k}^e\) sums to zero: a uniform temperature carries no heat.
The entries of \(\mathbf{f}^e_{\text{body}}\) add up to \(f\,h^e\), the heat made in the element. It is split among the nodes by how much of the element each basis function “covers” (Simpson’s weights 1, 4, 1 for \(p = 2\)).




C.4.2 Assembly: the ID, IEN, and LM arrays
Hughes keeps the bookkeeping in three integer arrays:








Array
Maps
Meaning




\(\mathrm{ID}(A)\)
global node \(\to\) equation
\(P\) if node \(A\) is unknown number \(P\); \(0\) if \(A\) is on \(\Gamma_g\)


\(\mathrm{IEN}(a, e)\)
local node, element \(\to\) global node
local node \(a\) of element \(e\) is global node \(A\)


\(\mathrm{LM}(a, e)\)
local node, element \(\to\) equation
\(\mathrm{LM}(a,e) = \mathrm{ID}\big(\mathrm{IEN}(a,e)\big)\)



Assembly adds \(k^e_{ab}\) into \(K_{PQ}\) with \(P = \mathrm{LM}(a,e)\) and \(Q = \mathrm{LM}(b,e)\), and \(f^e_a\) into \(F_P\), skipping any zero (Dirichlet) index. Hughes writes the whole loop as

\[
\mathbf{K} = \mathop{\Large\mathsf{A}}_{e=1}^{n_{el}}\left(\mathbf{k}^e\right),
\qquad
\mathbf{F} = \mathop{\Large\mathsf{A}}_{e=1}^{n_{el}}\left(\mathbf{f}^e\right)
\]







Figure C.6: Where each element matrix lands in the global matrix, for four elements of each degree (rows and columns are global node numbers \(A\)). The overlaps are the shared end nodes, and everything outside the coloured squares is zero, so \(\mathbf{K}\) is banded. The hatched row and column belong to the Dirichlet node \(x = L\). That row is not an equation, and the column’s entries, multiplied by \(g\), move to the right-hand side as \(-k^e_{ab}\,g\).

C.5 Worked example: three linear elements
Take \(n_{el} = 3\) equal elements, \(h^e\) = 0.10 m, and \(p = 1\). Then there are four nodes, at \(x\) = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 m, and node 4 is on \(\Gamma_g\):




\(A = 1\)
\(A = 2\)
\(A = 3\)
\(A = 4\)




\(x_A\) (m)
0
0.1
0.2
0.3


\(\mathrm{ID}(A)\)
1
2
3
0







\(e = 1\)
\(e = 2\)
\(e = 3\)




\(\mathrm{IEN}(1, e)\), \(\mathrm{IEN}(2, e)\)
1, 2
2, 3
3, 4


\(\mathrm{LM}(1, e)\), \(\mathrm{LM}(2, e)\)
1, 2
2, 3
3, 0



Every element has \(\kappa/h^e = 1.4/0.1 = 14\) W/(m²·K) and \(f h^e/2 = 25\) W/m²:

\[
\mathbf{k}^1 = \mathbf{k}^2 = \mathbf{k}^3 = \begin{bmatrix}14 & -14 \\ -14 & 14\end{bmatrix}
\] \[
\mathbf{f}^1 = \begin{Bmatrix}25 \\ 25\end{Bmatrix} + \underbrace{\begin{Bmatrix}50 \\ 0\end{Bmatrix}}_{h\ \text{at node 1}} = \begin{Bmatrix}75 \\ 25\end{Bmatrix}
\qquad
\mathbf{f}^2 = \begin{Bmatrix}25 \\ 25\end{Bmatrix}
\qquad
\mathbf{f}^3 = \begin{Bmatrix}25 \\ 25\end{Bmatrix} - \underbrace{\mathbf{k}^3 \begin{Bmatrix}0 \\ 20\end{Bmatrix}}_{g\ \text{at node 4}} = \begin{Bmatrix}305 \\ -255\end{Bmatrix}
\]

Assemble with the LM array. The second entry of \(\mathbf{f}^3\) has \(\mathrm{LM}(2,3) = 0\), so it is dropped:

\[
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}14 & -14 & 0 \\ -14 & 28 & -14 \\ 0 & -14 & 28\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{K}\ [\text{W/(m}^2\text{K)}]}
\begin{Bmatrix} d_1 \\ d_2 \\ d_3 \end{Bmatrix}
= \underbrace{\begin{Bmatrix}75 \\ 50 \\ 330\end{Bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{F}\ [\text{W/m}^2]}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{d} = \begin{Bmatrix}46.79 \\ 41.43 \\ 32.5\end{Bmatrix}\ {}^\circ\text{C}
\]







Figure C.7: The strong-form pictures, redrawn for \(u^h\). Top: the three-element temperature (red) over the exact profile (grey). Bottom: the heat flux \(q^h = -\kappa u^h_{,x}\), constant on each element and jumping at the nodes.





The nodal temperatures are exact. The exact solution at \(x\) = 0, 0.1, 0.2 m is 46.79, 41.43, 32.50 °C, identical to \(\mathbf{d}\). This is special to one dimension with constant \(\kappa\): linear elements are nodally exact (Hughes, Section 1.10). Between the nodes, \(u^h\) is only a chord of the curve.
The Neumann condition holds only weakly. On element 1, \(q^h\) = 75 W/m², not the prescribed \(h\) = 50 W/m²: it is the element’s average flux. \((\mathrm{G})\) builds \(h\) into \(\mathbf{F}\) but never forces \(u^h_{,x}(0)\) to equal \(-h/\kappa\). As the mesh is refined, \(q^h(0) \to h\).
The Dirichlet condition holds exactly, because it was built into \(\mathcal{S}^h\).
The discarded equation is the heat to the room. Row 4 of the full system, \(\sum_b k^3_{2b} U^3_b - f^3_{\text{body},2}\), is the boundary term \(\kappa u_{,x}(L)\) that \(w(L) = 0\) removed. Evaluated, it gives −200.0 W/m², so \(q(L) = 200.0\) W/m², the exact value. Differentiating \(u^h\) on element 3 gives only 175.0 W/m².
With \(p = 2\), even a single element reproduces the exact quadratic profile (Figure C.4), because the exact solution already lies in \(\mathcal{S}^h\).

title: Appendix C — 1D Poisson II: The Wall, by Galerkin’s Method
text:
C.6 How the error shrinks
The uniform \(f\) above makes the exact solution a quadratic, which is too easy: \(p \ge 2\) gets it exactly. Use instead the absorbed-radiation forcing from the strong-form page, \(f = f_0 e^{-x/\delta}\) with \(f_0\) = 2000 W/m³ and \(\delta\) = 4 cm, whose exact solution is not a polynomial:






Figure C.8: Error against element size on uniform meshes, on log-log axes. Left: the error in temperature. Right: the error in its slope, and so in the heat flux. Halving the elements divides the temperature error by \(2^{p+1}\) and the flux error by \(2^{p}\).




\[
\|u - u^h\|_{L^2} = \left(\int_0^L (u - u^h)^2\,dx\right)^{1/2} \le C\,h^{p+1}
\qquad\qquad
|u - u^h|_{H^1} = \left(\int_0^L (u_{,x} - u^h_{,x})^2\,dx\right)^{1/2} \le C\,h^{p}
\]


One more degree buys one more power of \(h\). The flux, which is what a designer usually wants, always converges one order slower than the temperature.

title: Appendix D — 1D Poisson III: An Axially Loaded Rod
text:
D.1 The physical problem
This page is the companion to 1D Poisson I: Heat Conduction Through a Wall. Both read Hughes’ one-dimensional model problem,
or, with the length and the material constant put back, as in Class 4,
On this page \(u\) is an axial displacement and \(K = EA\) is the axial stiffness. The equations are letter-for-letter those of the wall. The difference is in what \(h\) means, and it changes the sign of \(h\) in a way that trips people up; see the boundary conditions below.
The pile is long and slender, and the loads act along its axis, so the only motion that matters is along the axis. Every cross-section at depth \(x\) moves the same distance \(u(x)\) down the pile: one number per cross-section, a function of one variable.
Nothing about the equation cares that the pile is vertical. \(x\) can point any way, as long as every sign is read relative to it. Here \(+x\) is down.

D.2 The one-dimensional domain






Figure D.2: The same domain as for the wall: the open interval \(\Omega\), its two end points \(\Gamma\), and the outward unit normal at each.





\(\Omega = \,]0, L[\) is the inside of the rod; \(\bar\Omega = [0, L]\) adds its two ends.
\(\Gamma = \{0, L\}\), with outward normals \(n = -1\) at \(x = 0\) and \(n = +1\) at \(x = L\).
Each end gets exactly one condition: its displacement is known, or the force on it is known. \(\Gamma = \Gamma_g \cup \Gamma_h\), \(\Gamma_g \cap \Gamma_h = \emptyset\).

title: Appendix D — 1D Poisson III: An Axially Loaded Rod
section: D.4 Where the differential equation comes from
text:
D.4 Where the differential equation comes from

D.4.1 Kinematics: displacement and strain






Figure D.3: Top: a rod before and after loading (displacements greatly exaggerated). Each material point \(x_i\) moves to \(x_i + u(x_i)\). Bottom: the same displacements as a function. Where the curve is steep, neighbouring points separate fast — the rod is stretched there.



The displacement \(u(x)\) is how far the material point that started at \(x\) has moved along the axis. Two neighbouring points \(\Delta x\) apart end up \(\Delta x + \Delta u\) apart, so the strain — change in length per unit length — is the slope of the displacement:

\[
\varepsilon = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \frac{\left(\Delta x + \Delta u\right) - \Delta x}{\Delta x}
= u_{,x}
\qquad\qquad
u_{,x} > 0 \;\text{stretched (tension)}, \qquad u_{,x} < 0 \;\text{shortened (compression)}
\]


A uniform shift of the whole rod, $u = $ constant, has \(u_{,x} = 0\): it moves the rod without straining it. Hold on to this; it is why a rod with no support is not a solvable problem.



D.4.2 Material: Hooke’s law, from stress to force






Figure D.4: Left: a linear elastic material, \(\sigma = E\varepsilon\). Right: the stress on a cut, added up over the cross-section, is the internal axial force \(N\) — drawn here in tension, pulling outward on the cut face.




\[
N = \sigma A = E A\,\varepsilon = EA\,u_{,x}
\qquad\qquad [\text{Pa}\cdot\text{m}^2 = \text{N}]
\]

This is the rod’s version of Fourier’s law, with one sign difference: here there is no minus sign. Heat flows down the temperature gradient, but a rod pulls back along its stretch.


D.4.3 Equilibrium of a thin slice






Figure D.5: Free body of a slice of length \(\Delta x\). The rest of the rod pulls on each face with the internal force \(N\); the distributed load contributes \(f\,\Delta x\).



Sum the forces in \(+x\). The rod to the left pulls the slice toward \(-x\) with \(N(x)\); the rod to the right pulls it toward \(+x\) with \(N(x+\Delta x)\):

\[
-N(x) + N(x + \Delta x) + f\,\Delta x = 0
\qquad\xrightarrow[\;\text{divide by } \Delta x,\; \Delta x \to 0\;]{}\qquad
N_{,x} + f = 0
\]


Read it as “the internal force drops by exactly the load applied along the way”: \(N_{,x} = -f\). In the pile, friction pushes up (\(f < 0\)), so \(N\) grows toward \(+x\). The compression is largest at the head and the soil takes some of it off as you go down.

Substituting \(N = EA\,u_{,x}\) gives the differential equation of the strong form:

\[
-\left(EA\,u_{,x}\right)_{,x} = f
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\left(EA\,u_{,x}\right)_{,x} + f = 0
\quad\xrightarrow{\;EA \text{ constant}\;}\quad
EA\,u_{,xx} + f = 0
\quad\xrightarrow{\;EA = 1\;}\quad
u_{,xx} + f = 0 \;\;\text{(Hughes)}
\]



D.4.4 What the equation says about the shape of \(u\)






Figure D.6: Three rods with the same end displacements and different distributed loads (\(EA = 2.7\times10^9\) N, \(L\) = 10 m). With no load the displacement is linear and the strain is the same everywhere; a load bows it.





\(u_{,xx} = -f/EA\): the load sets the curvature of the displacement, just as heat generation set the curvature of the temperature.
\(f = 0\): \(u\) is linear, \(\varepsilon\) and \(N\) are constant — the familiar \(\delta = PL/EA\) bar.
\(f \ne 0\): the strain, and therefore \(N\), changes along the rod at the rate \(-f\).
crumbs: Appendices
D  1D Poisson III: An Axially Loaded Rod

title: Appendix D — 1D Poisson III: An Axially Loaded Rod
text:
D.5 The forcing function \(f\)
\(f(x)\) is an axial load per unit length of rod, in N/m, positive when it points toward \(+x\). It is the only data that acts in the interior of \(\Omega\). Integrated over the length, it is the total distributed force, in N:

\[
\int_0^L f\,dx \quad \left[\tfrac{\text{N}}{\text{m}}\cdot\text{m} = \text{N}\right]
\qquad\text{e.g.}\qquad (-40\ \text{kN/m})(10\ \text{m}) = -400\ \text{kN}
\quad\text{(400 kN carried by friction, upward)}
\]







Figure D.7: Three distributed axial loads. Arrow length is proportional to \(|f|\), and the sign of \(f\) is read against the \(x\) arrow drawn in each panel.





Self-weight of a vertical member: \(f = \rho g A\). It is often negligible — 38.5 N/m for a 500 mm² steel rod — but not for long hoist cables or tall columns.
Skin friction along a pile or ground anchor: the soil resists the motion, so \(f\) points opposite to the motion.
Inertial (centrifugal) load on a spinning member: \(f = \rho A\omega^2 x\), which grows with distance from the hub.
Loads that act at a point (a bracket bolted halfway along) are not an \(f\) in the strong form: \(f\) would have to be a delta function, and \(u_{,xx}\) would not exist there. The weak form handles them naturally; the strong form does not.
crumbs: Appendices
D  1D Poisson III: An Axially Loaded Rod

title: Appendix D — 1D Poisson III: An Axially Loaded Rod
text:
D.6 Boundary conditions
Each end gets exactly one condition: either its displacement is known, or the force applied to it is known. Never both, and never neither.

D.6.1 Dirichlet: \(u = g\) on \(\Gamma_g\) — the displacement is known






Figure D.8: Two Dirichlet conditions. Left: a support that does not move. Right: an end driven a known distance, drawn exaggerated; the dashed outline is where the rod was.





\(g\) is a displacement, in m. \(g = 0\) is the ordinary fixed support.
A Dirichlet condition pins the value of \(u\) and says nothing about the slope, and so nothing about the force there. The force the support supplies — the reaction — is an output, found after solving: \(N\) at that end.
It is an essential boundary condition. In the weak form, it is built into the trial space \(\mathcal{S}\).




D.6.2 Neumann: \((EA\,u_{,x})\,n = h\) on \(\Gamma_h\) — the end force is known
At an end with no support, the only thing holding the rod in equilibrium is the applied force. Take a sliver of rod right at the end. The applied force \(h\) acts on its outer face, and the rest of the rod pulls on its inner face with \(N\), toward the inside:

\[
\text{at } x = L:\quad h - N(L) = 0
\qquad\qquad
\text{at } x = 0:\quad h + N(0) = 0
\]

Both are one statement, \(N\,n = h\). With \(N = EA\,u_{,x}\), that is exactly the Neumann condition of the strong form:

\[
h = \sigma A\, n = \left(EA\,u_{,x}\right) n
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\text{at } x = 0:\; -EA\,u_{,x}(0) = h
\qquad\qquad
\text{at } x = L:\; +EA\,u_{,x}(L) = h
\]







Important\(h\) means something different here than for the wall



For the rod, \(h = \sigma A\,n\) is the \(x\)-component of the applied force vector: \(h > 0\) means the force points toward \(+x\), whichever end it acts on. So \(h > 0\) pushes on the left end (compression) but pulls on the right end (tension).
For the wall, \(h = -q\,n\) is the heat flux into the body: \(h > 0\) means heat enters, whichever face it acts on.
The equations \(\mp K u_{,x} = h\) are identical, so the slopes in the two problems behave identically. What changes is which way the arrow in the picture points.








Figure D.9: The Neumann condition at either end of a rod. The black curve is the displacement near the end and the dashed red line its tangent — the strain there. Compare row by row with the same figure for the wall: the slopes are identical, but for the rod a positive \(h\) always points toward \(+x\), so on the right end it pulls, where for the wall it pushed heat in.





\(h\) is a force, in N, positive toward \(+x\) (or, per unit area, a traction in Pa).
\(h = 0\) is a free end: no force, so zero strain — the displacement curve arrives flat.
The magnitude of the slope is \(|h|/EA\). For the pile, \(900\ \text{kN} / 2.7\times10^9\
\text{N} = 3.33\times10^{-4}\): the head is shortened by 0.33 mm per meter.
It is a natural boundary condition. In the weak form it appears as the boundary term \(w(0)\,h\).
A spring support, \(h = -k_s\,u\), mixes value and slope. That is a Robin condition and is not part of the model problem.




D.6.3 Which end gets which condition






Figure D.10: The four ways to assign the two ends, for the pile of Figure D.1. Blue dots are Dirichlet values; dashed red lines are the slopes (strains) that Neumann data force on the curve.





(a) Hughes’ arrangement. Force given at \(x = 0\), displacement at \(x = L\): \(\;u(L) = g,\;\; -EA\,u_{,x}(0) = h\). This is the pile: 900 kN pushing down (toward \(+x\)) on the head, the toe fixed on rock.
(b) Swapped. Displacement given at \(x = 0\), force at \(x = L\): \(\;u(0) = g,\;\; +EA\,u_{,x}(L) = h\). Drawn here as the mirror image of (a) — the same pile, stood on its head. Because \(x\) now runs from the toe to the head, the column load points toward \(-x\) and \(h\) = −900 kN; the friction flips too, \(f\) = +40 kN/m. Compare the wall, where the mirror image kept \(h\) = +50 W/m². A force has a direction in space; a heat inflow does not.
(c) Two Dirichlet ends is well-posed: here the head is jacked down 2 mm and the toe is fixed. The curve is a straight line plus the small bow from the friction.
(d) Two Neumann ends is not well-posed:

Uniqueness fails. Force data see only \(u_{,x}\), so any rigid-body shift \(u + C\) is also a solution. Nothing stops the pile from floating.
Existence needs equilibrium. The applied forces must balance: \(h_0 + h_L + \int_0^L f\,dx = 0\). The panel uses \(h_L\) = −500 kN — the rock’s reaction, handed in as data — so that \(900 - 500 - 400 = 0\). Any other \(h_L\) and the rod accelerates, and there is no static solution.

So \(\Gamma_g\) must not be empty: at least one end must be held.

D  1D Poisson III: An Axially Loaded Rod

title: Appendix D — 1D Poisson III: An Axially Loaded Rod
text:
D.7 The strong form, complete
For Hughes’ arrangement (a):

\[
(\mathrm{S}) \qquad
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Given } f : \bar\Omega \to \RR \;[\text{N/m}],\;
  EA > 0 \;[\text{N}],\;
  g \;[\text{m}], \text{ and } h \;[\text{N}],
  \text{ find } u : \bar\Omega \to \RR \;[\text{m}] \text{ such that} \\[3pt]
&\qquad \left(EA\,u_{,x}\right)_{,x} + f = 0
   && \text{on } \Omega = \,]0, L[ && \text{(equilibrium + Hooke)} \\
&\qquad u(L) = g && && \text{(Dirichlet: known displacement)} \\
&\qquad -EA\,u_{,x}(0) = h && && \text{(Neumann: known end force)}
\end{aligned}
\]

and, for the swapped arrangement (b), \(u(0) = g\) and \(+EA\,u_{,x}(L) = h\).


Strong because the equation must hold at every point, which demands \(u_{,xx}\) everywhere. A rod whose area steps from one size to another, or a point load partway along, already breaks this; the weak form will not mind.
With constant \(EA\) and \(f\), the exact solution of (a) is



\[
u(x) = g + \frac{h}{EA}\,(L - x) + \frac{f}{2EA}\,\left(L^2 - x^2\right)
\qquad\qquad
N(x) = EA\,u_{,x} = -h - f\,x
\]
crumbs: Appendices
D  1D Poisson III: An Axially Loaded Rod

title: Appendix D — 1D Poisson III: An Axially Loaded Rod
text:
D.8 Worked example: the pile
The pile of Figure D.1: \(L\) = 10 m, \(E\) = 30 GPa, \(A\) = 0.09 m², so \(EA = 2.7\times10^{9}\) N. A column pushes down on the head with 900 kN (\(h\) = +900 kN, toward \(+x\)); skin friction of 40 kN/m acts upward (\(f\) = −40 kN/m); the toe sits on rock (\(g\) = 0).

\[
\begin{aligned}
u(x) &= \frac{900\times10^{3}}{2.7\times10^{9}}\,(10 - x)
  + \frac{-40\times10^{3}}{2(2.7\times10^{9})}\,(100 - x^2) \quad [\text{m}] \\[4pt]
u(0) &= 3.333 - 0.741 = 2.59\ \text{mm (the head settles)}
  \qquad\qquad u_{,x}(0) = -\frac{h}{EA} = -3.333\times10^{-4} \\[4pt]
N(x) &= EA\,u_{,x} = -900 + 40\,x \quad [\text{kN}]
  \qquad\qquad N(0) = -900\ \text{kN}, \quad N(L) = -500\ \text{kN}
\end{aligned}
\]







Figure D.11: The pile’s solution. Top: displacement, zero at the rock and leaving the head with the slope the column load dictates. Bottom: the internal axial force \(N = EA\,u_{,x}\), all compression, decreasing in magnitude as friction takes load into the soil.



Every line of the strong form, checked on the picture:


The differential equation. \(EA\,u_{,xx} = -f > 0\): the displacement curve bends upward uniformly. Equivalently \(N_{,x} = -f\) = +40 kN/m: the force line in the lower panel is straight.
The Dirichlet condition. \(u = 0\) at the rock.
The Neumann condition. At the head the tangent drops 0.67 mm over 2 m, a slope of \(-3.33\times10^{-4}\), and \(-EA\,u_{,x}(0) = -2.7\times10^{9}\times(-3.33\times10^{-4})
= 900\) kN \(= h\).
Equilibrium of the whole pile. 900 kN down at the head = 400 kN of friction + 500 kN at the toe. The Dirichlet end’s reaction, 500 kN, came out of the solution.
