title: Appendix E — 1D Poisson IV: The Rod, by Galerkin’s Method
text:
E.1 The weak form: virtual work
The strong-form page set up an end-bearing pile as Hughes’ model problem. This page solves it approximately, step by step, exactly as the wall was solved. The mathematics is the same, so this page concentrates on what each step means mechanically. There, the weak form is the principle of virtual work.
The running example is the pile, in Hughes’ arrangement (a), with \(x\) pointing down:
crumbs: Appendices
E  1D Poisson IV: The Rod, by Galerkin's Method

title: Appendix E — 1D Poisson IV: The Rod, by Galerkin’s Method
text:
E.1.1 Displacements and virtual displacements

\[
\mathcal{S} = \left\{\, u \;\middle|\; u \in H^1(\Omega),\; u(L) = g \,\right\}
\qquad\qquad
\mathcal{V} = \left\{\, w \;\middle|\; w \in H^1(\Omega),\; w(L) = 0 \,\right\}
\]







Figure E.1: Left: members of \(\mathcal{S}\), displacement fields that respect the support. The real one is among them. Right: members of \(\mathcal{V}\), virtual displacements: imagined motions that the supports would allow, and so are zero at the rock.




In structural mechanics \(w\) has a name and a meaning. It is a virtual displacement, a small motion you imagine imposing, consistent with the supports. Since the rock does not move, neither may \(w\) at \(x = L\).



E.1.2 Multiply, integrate, and integrate by parts
Multiply the equilibrium equation by \(w\) and integrate down the pile:

\[
0 = \int_0^L w\left[\left(EA\,u_{,x}\right)_{,x} + f\right] dx
\;\;\xrightarrow{\;\text{by parts}\;}\;\;
\int_0^L w_{,x}\,EA\,u_{,x}\,dx
= \int_0^L w f\,dx + w(L)\,EA\,u_{,x}(L) - w(0)\,EA\,u_{,x}(0)
\]







Figure E.2: The boundary term, one end at a time. At the head, the force is data, so its term becomes \(w(0)\,h\): the virtual work of the column load. At the toe, the force is the unknown rock reaction, and a support reaction does no work through a virtual displacement the support forbids.




\[
(\mathrm{W}) \qquad
\underbrace{\int_0^L w_{,x}\,EA\,u_{,x}\,dx}_{a(w,\,u)\;=\;\text{internal virtual work}}
\;=\;
\underbrace{\int_0^L w\,f\,dx + w(0)\,h}_{(w,\,f)\,+\,w(0)h\;=\;\text{external virtual work}}
\qquad \forall\, w \in \mathcal{V}
\]



Internal virtual work. \(w_{,x}\) is the virtual strain and \(EA\,u_{,x} = N\) is the real axial force, so \(a(w,u) = \int N\,\delta\varepsilon\,dx\).
External virtual work. The distributed load moves through \(w\) along the pile; the column load moves through \(w(0)\) at the head.
\((\mathrm{W})\) is the principle of virtual work: a displacement field that respects the supports is the equilibrium one exactly when internal and external virtual work agree for every admissible virtual displacement.
Units: N·m (joules) times the units of \(w\) per meter of \(u\), on both sides.











Arrangement
\(\mathcal{S}\)
\(\mathcal{V}\)
External virtual work




(a) Hughes: \(h\) at \(x=0\), \(g\) at \(x=L\)
\(u(L) = g\)
\(w(L) = 0\)
\((w, f) + w(0)\,h\)


(b) \(g\) at \(x=0\), \(h\) at \(x=L\)
\(u(0) = g\)
\(w(0) = 0\)
\((w, f) + w(L)\,h\)


(c) \(g\) at both ends
\(u(0) = g_0\), \(u(L) = g\)
\(w(0) = w(L) = 0\)

title: Appendix E — 1D Poisson IV: The Rod, by Galerkin’s Method
text:
E.2 The Galerkin form

E.2.1 Elements, nodes, and Lagrange basis functions
The pile is cut into \(n_{el}\) elements with Lagrange polynomials of degree \(p\) on each, exactly as for the wall. There are \(n_{en} = p + 1\) nodes per element and \(n_{np} = p\,n_{el} + 1\) nodes in all, with node \(n_{np}\) at the rock.






Figure E.3: Top: Lagrange functions on the parent element, \(p\) = 1, 2, 3. Bottom: the global basis functions they make on three elements down the pile. The dashed function belongs to the node at the rock (filled dot), which carries the known \(g = 0\) rather than an unknown.





E.2.2 The Galerkin form, \((\mathrm{G})\)

\[
w^h = \sum_{A=1}^{n} c_A\,N_A,
\qquad
u^h = v^h + g^h = \sum_{B=1}^{n} d_B\,N_B + g\,N_{n+1}
\] \[
(\mathrm{G}) \qquad
a(w^h, v^h) = (w^h, f) + w^h(0)\,h - a(w^h, g^h)
\qquad \forall\, w^h \in \mathcal{V}^h
\]


Here each \(d_B\) is the displacement of node \(B\), and each \(N_A\) is a virtual displacement pattern: move node \(A\) by one unit and leave every other node where it is. Galerkin’s method asks for virtual work to balance for each of these patterns, not for every conceivable one.







Figure E.4: What \(u^h\) is made of for the pile on three elements: each basis function scaled by its nodal displacement \(d_A\), summed. With \(p = 1\) the pile’s displacement is a broken line through the exact nodal values; with \(p = 2\) it is exact, because the true displacement is quadratic for uniform friction.
crumbs: Appendices
E  1D Poisson IV: The Rod, by Galerkin's Method

title: Appendix E — 1D Poisson IV: The Rod, by Galerkin’s Method
text:
E.3 From \((\mathrm{G})\) to \(\mathbf{K}\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{F}\)
Substituting the expansions and using the linearity of \(a\) and \((\cdot,\cdot)\) in each slot:

\[
\sum_{A=1}^{n} c_A \left[\, \sum_{B=1}^{n} a(N_A, N_B)\,d_B
- (N_A, f) - N_A(0)\,h + a(N_A, N_{n+1})\,g \right] = 0
\qquad \text{for all } c_A
\] \[
\boxed{\;\mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{F}\;}
\qquad
K_{AB} = \int_0^L N_{A,x}\,EA\,N_{B,x}\,dx
\qquad
F_A = \int_0^L N_A\,f\,dx + \delta_{A1}\,h - \int_0^L N_{A,x}\,EA\,N_{n+1,x}\,dx\;g
\]



\(\mathbf{K}\) is the stiffness matrix, N/m: \(K_{AB}\) is the force at node \(A\) needed to hold the pile in the shape “node \(B\) moved by one meter, every other node fixed”.
\(\mathbf{F}\) is the vector of equivalent nodal forces, N. \((N_A, f)\) is the share of the skin friction that node \(A\) carries, and the column load goes to node 1 only.
Symmetric (Maxwell–Betti reciprocity), banded, and positive definite because the rock holds the pile. With both ends free, arrangement (d), a rigid-body translation \(\mathbf{d} = \{1, 1, \dots, 1\}\) gives \(\mathbf{K}\mathbf{d} = 0\), so \(\mathbf{K}\) is singular: the floating pile, in matrix form.

E  1D Poisson IV: The Rod, by Galerkin's Method

title: Appendix E — 1D Poisson IV: The Rod, by Galerkin’s Method
section: E.4 The element point of view
text:
E.4 The element point of view

\[
k^e_{ab} = \int_{\Omega^e} N_{a,x}\,EA\,N_{b,x}\,dx
= \int_{-1}^{1} N_{a,\xi}\,EA\,N_{b,\xi}\,\frac{2}{h^e}\,d\xi
\qquad\qquad
f^e_a = \int_{\Omega^e} N_a\,f\,dx + \delta_{e1}\,\delta_{a1}\,h - \sum_b k^e_{ab}\,g^e_b
\]







Figure E.5: The isoparametric map for one quadratic element of the pile, from 3 m to 6 m depth, with its Gauss points.



For constant \(EA\) and \(f\), these are the familiar bar elements:

\[
p = 1:\;\;
\mathbf{k}^e = \frac{EA}{h^e}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix},\;\;
\mathbf{f}^e_{\text{body}} = \frac{f\,h^e}{2}\begin{Bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{Bmatrix}
\qquad\quad
p = 2:\;\;
\mathbf{k}^e = \frac{EA}{3h^e}\begin{bmatrix} 7 & -8 & 1 \\ -8 & 16 & -8 \\ 1 & -8 & 7 \end{bmatrix},\;\;
\mathbf{f}^e_{\text{body}} = \frac{f\,h^e}{6}\begin{Bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{Bmatrix}
\] \[
p = 3:\;\;
\mathbf{k}^e = \frac{EA}{40h^e}\begin{bmatrix}
148 & -189 & 54 & -13 \\ -189 & 432 & -297 & 54 \\ 54 & -297 & 432 & -189 \\ -13 & 54 & -189 & 148
\end{bmatrix},\;\;
\mathbf{f}^e_{\text{body}} = \frac{f\,h^e}{8}\begin{Bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{Bmatrix}
\]



\(p = 1\) is the spring \(k = EA/h^e\) from mechanics of materials: the linear element is an axial spring.
Each row of \(\mathbf{k}^e\) sums to zero, because a rigid translation of the element needs no force.
The body terms add up to \(f\,h^e\), the element’s total friction, shared among its nodes.



E.4.1 Assembly with ID, IEN, and LM
The arrays and the assembly operator are identical to the wall’s (see the wall page for the table). \(k^e_{ab}\) is added into \(K_{PQ}\) with \(P = \mathrm{LM}(a,e)\) and \(Q = \mathrm{LM}(b,e)\), and anything with a zero index is skipped:

\[
\mathbf{K} = \mathop{\Large\mathsf{A}}_{e=1}^{n_{el}}\left(\mathbf{k}^e\right),
\qquad
\mathbf{F} = \mathop{\Large\mathsf{A}}_{e=1}^{n_{el}}\left(\mathbf{f}^e\right),
\qquad
\mathrm{LM}(a,e) = \mathrm{ID}\big(\mathrm{IEN}(a,e)\big)
\]







Figure E.6: Element stiffness matrices tiling the global stiffness for four elements of each degree. Where two squares overlap, two elements share a node, like two springs joined end to end. The hatched row and column belong to the node at the rock: its displacement is known, and its row would be the reaction equation.

text:
E.6 How the error shrinks
Uniform friction makes the answer a quadratic, which \(p \ge 2\) reproduces exactly. So give the soil a stiff layer instead: a band of extra friction around 6 m depth, \(f = -40 - 150\,e^{-((x - 6)/0.6)^2}\) kN/m. Its exact solution is not a polynomial:






Figure E.8: Displacement error (left) and strain error (right) against element size, on log-log axes. Each halving of the elements divides the displacement error by \(2^{p+1}\) and the strain, or force, error by \(2^{p}\), once the elements are small enough to resolve the stiff layer.




\[
\|u - u^h\|_{L^2} \le C\,h^{p+1}
\qquad\qquad
|u - u^h|_{H^1} = \left(\int_0^L \left(\varepsilon - \varepsilon^h\right)^2 dx\right)^{1/2} \le C\,h^{p}
\]

title: Appendix F — 2D Poisson I: Heat Flow in a Battery Cell
text:
F.1 The physical problem
This page is the two-dimensional sequel to 1D Poisson I: Heat Conduction Through a Wall. The wall was a problem in one coordinate: temperature changed only through its thickness. Here heat flows through the cross-section of a lithium-ion battery cell, and temperature changes in two directions at once. The physics is the same two ideas — energy is conserved, and heat flows from hot to cold. What changes is the calculus. Each derivative in the 1D strong form becomes a gradient, a divergence, or a Laplacian, and the wall’s two boundary points become a boundary curve. The goal of this page is to make each of those objects something you can see.
Hughes states the model problem for any number of space dimensions \(n_{sd}\) (Chapter 2), in index notation:
Substituting the last relation into the others gives the form used in Class 4, shown here in both notations:
For most of this page the material conducts equally well in every direction — it is isotropic — so \(\kappa_{ij} = \kappa\,\delta_{ij}\) and the differential equation becomes
In one dimension the index has a single value, \(i = 1\), and every sum above has one term: \(q_{i,i}\) is \(q_{,x}\), and \(\kappa_{ij}u_{,j}n_i\) is \(\kappa u_{,x}\,n\). That is the wall. On this page \(i\) runs over 1 and 2, \(u\) is a temperature, \(q_i\) is the heat flux vector, and everything is in SI units.
A battery module in an electric vehicle packs prismatic lithium-ion cells side by side, large face to large face. Here each cell is 100 mm wide, 200 mm tall, and 27 mm thick. A liquid-cooled aluminum plate is bonded along one narrow side of the whole row, copper busbars are welded across the terminal tabs on top, and foam fills the rest of the enclosure. During a fast charge, the current flowing through the electrodes and electrolyte generates heat throughout every cell, and the resistance of the tab welds adds heat that flows down into the cells through their tabs.
Why two dimensions. Every cell in the row is identical and heated identically, so by symmetry no heat crosses the large face between one cell and the next. Nothing then varies through the thickness, and the temperature depends only on the position \((x_1, x_2)\) in the plane of the large face. This is the argument that made the wall one-dimensional, applied to one direction instead of two. There, nothing varied along the wall or up it. Here, nothing varies along the row. So take a slice parallel to the large face and follow the temperature across it. Every quantity on this page is per meter of depth in the stacking direction, which is why the total heat made comes out in W/m. To get watts for one 27 mm cell, multiply by \(T = 0.027\) m.
Two things are new compared with the wall. Each “face” is now an edge with a length, and the data can change from point to point along it: \(h\) is 5000 W/m² on the tabs and zero on the rest of the top edge. And the insulated edges, which the wall example did not have, still carry a boundary condition. “Insulated” means \(h = 0\). It does not mean “no condition”.

title: Appendix F — 2D Poisson I: Heat Flow in a Battery Cell
text:
F.2 The two-dimensional domain






Figure F.2: Left: the cell’s cross-section. \(\Gamma_g\) (blue) is the cooled edge; \(\Gamma_h\) (amber) is everything else, including the two tabs (violet). Each arrow is the outward unit normal on its edge. Right: on a general domain the normal turns as the boundary curves, and a hole adds a second piece of boundary.





\(\Omega = \,]0, W[\, \times \,]0, H[\) is the open rectangle: the cross-section without its edges. A point in it is \(\underline{x} = (x_1, x_2)\), or \(x_i\) in index notation. Many books write \(x\) and \(y\) instead of \(x_1\) and \(x_2\).
\(\bar\Omega = [0, W] \times [0, H]\) is its closure, edges included. The solution \(u\) is defined on \(\bar\Omega\) because we need its values on the edges.
\(\Gamma\) is the boundary. In 1D it was two points. Now it is a closed curve — here the four edges, \(2(W + H) = 0.6\) m long in total. Integrals over \(\Omega\) are area integrals, \(d\Omega = dx_1\,dx_2\) (m²). Integrals over \(\Gamma\) are line integrals, with \(d\Gamma\) (m) measured along the curve.
The outward unit normal \(\underline{n} = (n_1, n_2)\) has length one, \(n_i n_i = 1\), and points out of \(\Omega\). In 1D it was a sign, \(\pm 1\). Now it is a vector: constant along each straight edge, but turning from point to point along a curved boundary. At a corner it is not defined. Corners have zero length, so the boundary integrals never notice them.
A boundary can come in several pieces. The wall of a channel through the body is part of \(\Gamma\), and its outward normal points into the channel — out of \(\Omega\).
\(\Gamma_g\) (blue) and \(\Gamma_h\) (amber) split \(\Gamma\) so that every point gets exactly one boundary condition. See the partition below.

title: Appendix F — 2D Poisson I: Heat Flow in a Battery Cell

section: F.4 Index notation in two dimensions
text:
F.4 Index notation in two dimensions
The strong form will be written two ways from here on: in vector notation (\(\nabla u\), \(\nabla\cdot\underline{q}\), \(\underline{q}\cdot\underline{n}\)) and in index notation (\(u_{,i}\), \(q_{i,i}\), \(q_i n_i\)), as introduced in Class 3. The rules you need:


An index runs over the space dimensions: \(i = 1, 2\) here (\(i = 1, 2, 3\) in 3D, and only \(i = 1\) in 1D).
A comma means a partial derivative with respect to the coordinate named by the index after it: \(u_{,i} = \partial u / \partial x_i\), so \(u_{,1} = \partial u/\partial x_1\) and \(u_{,12} = \partial^2 u / \partial x_1 \partial x_2\). Indices before the comma label components: \(q_{2,1} = \partial q_2 / \partial x_1\).
A free index appears once in a term, and the expression stands for one equation for each of its values: \(q_i = -\kappa u_{,i}\) is two equations, \(q_1 = -\kappa u_{,1}\) and \(q_2 = -\kappa u_{,2}\).
A repeated (dummy) index is summed over all its values: \(q_{i,i} = q_{1,1} + q_{2,2}\). Its letter does not matter: \(q_{i,i} = q_{k,k}\).
No index may appear more than twice in one term, and every term of an equation must carry the same free indices. \(q_i = f\) is meaningless (a vector cannot equal a scalar), and so is \(u_{,i} n_i n_i\).
Count the free indices to know what you are holding: none is a scalar (\(u\), \(f\), \(q_{i,i}\), \(u_{,i}n_i\)), one is a vector (\(x_i\), \(u_{,i}\), \(q_i\), \(n_i\)), two is a matrix (\(\kappa_{ij}\), \(u_{,ij}\)).
The Kronecker delta \(\delta_{ij}\) is 1 when \(i = j\) and 0 otherwise, the identity matrix. Summing against it renames an index: \(\delta_{ij}\,u_{,j} = u_{,i}\).

\(u_{,12} = u_{,21}\) for a smooth \(u\) (mixed partial derivatives commute), so the matrix \(u_{,ij}\) is symmetric.

title: Appendix F — 2D Poisson I: Heat Flow in a Battery Cell
section: F.5 The temperature gradient: \(\nabla u = u_{,i}\)
text:
F.5 The temperature gradient: \(\nabla u = u_{,i}\)






Figure F.3: The temperature in the cell during the fast charge (the worked example at the end of this page). (a) \(u\) drawn as a height above the cross-section, with its contour lines — the isotherms — projected onto the floor. The red arrow on the floor, below \(P\), is \(\nabla u\): the direction in which the surface above climbs fastest. (b) The same field seen from above, with \(\nabla u\) at a grid of points. (c) The gradient at \(P\) and its components: the slopes you would measure walking parallel to each axis.



In 1D the slope \(u_{,x}\) was a single number. Its sign said which way was uphill (toward \(+x\) or \(-x\)) and its size said how steep. In 2D, uphill can be any direction in the plane, so the slope becomes a vector:

\[
\nabla u \;=\; u_{,i} \;=\;
\begin{bmatrix} u_{,1} \\ u_{,2} \end{bmatrix}
\;=\;
\begin{bmatrix} \partial u / \partial x_1 \\ \partial u / \partial x_2 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad [{}^\circ\text{C/m}]
\]

Its components are the ordinary slopes along the two axes. To get the slope in any other direction, take the component of \(\nabla u\) along it. Moving in the direction of a unit vector \(\underline{e}\), the temperature changes at the rate

\[
\frac{du}{ds} \;=\; \nabla u\cdot\underline{e} \;=\; u_{,i}\,e_i
\;=\; u_{,1}e_1 + u_{,2}e_2 \;=\; |\nabla u|\cos\theta
\]

where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\underline{e}\) and \(\nabla u\). Three facts follow, and all three are visible in Figure F.3:


The rate is largest, \(|\nabla u|\), when \(\underline{e}\) points along \(\nabla u\). The gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent, and its length is that steepest slope.
The rate is zero when \(\underline{e}\) is perpendicular to \(\nabla u\). Moving that way, \(u\) does not change — that is the direction of the isotherm, the curve of constant temperature, through the point. So \(\nabla u\) is perpendicular to the isotherms.
Where the isotherms crowd together, the temperature changes a lot over a short distance: \(|\nabla u|\) is large.



At the point \(P = (0.06,\ 0.15)\) m, \(\nabla u = (64.8,\ 38.6)\) °C/m. Walking in the \(+x_1\) direction, the temperature rises 0.65 °C per centimeter; walking in \(+x_2\), it rises 0.39 °C per centimeter. The steepest rise, 0.75 °C per centimeter, is in the direction 31° above the \(x_1\)-axis, and along the isotherm through \(P\) it does not rise at all.

section: F.6 Fourier’s law: heat flows straight downhill
text:
F.6 Fourier’s law: heat flows straight downhill
The material relation is the same as in 1D, now applied to each component:

\[
\underline{q} = -\kappa\,\nabla u
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
q_i = -\kappa\,u_{,i}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\begin{cases}
q_1 = -\kappa\,u_{,1} \\
q_2 = -\kappa\,u_{,2}
\end{cases}
\]







Figure F.4: Fourier’s law. (a) The heat-flux lines of the worked example, drawn thicker where \(|\underline{q}|\) is larger: heat made everywhere in the cell, and heat entering through the tabs, all runs downhill to the cooling plate, crossing the isotherms at right angles. (b) In an isotropic material, \(\underline{q}\) points straight down the temperature gradient. (c) In a layered material with the same gradient, the flux is steered along the layers.





The minus sign does what it did in 1D, but now it reverses a direction: \(\underline{q}\) points exactly opposite \(\nabla u\) — straight downhill, from hot to cold, crossing the isotherms at right angles.
Its size is \(|\underline{q}| = \kappa\,|\nabla u|\), in W/m². A poorer conductor needs a steeper gradient to carry the same flux.
For a unit vector \(\underline{m}\), the product \(\underline{q}\cdot\underline{m} =
q_i m_i\) is the heat flux across a line whose unit normal is \(\underline{m}\). It is largest across the isotherm and zero across a heat-flux line. Taking \(\underline{m} = \underline{n}\) on the boundary gives the heat leaving \(\Omega\), which is exactly what the Neumann condition will fix.



At \(P\): \(\underline{q} = -25\,(64.8,\ 38.6) = (-1620,\ -966)\) W/m², with \(|\underline{q}| = 1886\) W/m². Heat at \(P\) is moving down and to the left — toward the cooling plate.


F.6.1 When the material has a grain: \(q_i = -\kappa_{ij}\,u_{,j}\)
Isotropy is an assumption about the material, and a battery cell is not isotropic. It is a stack of layers, and it conducts about 25 times better along them than across them. Our slice happens to lie parallel to the layers, so within the slice the cell is isotropic. Had we sliced across the thickness, the layers would show, and Fourier’s law would need a matrix:

\[
\underline{q} = -\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\,\nabla u
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
q_i = -\kappa_{ij}\,u_{,j}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\begin{bmatrix} q_1 \\ q_2 \end{bmatrix}
= -\begin{bmatrix} \kappa_{11} & \kappa_{12} \\ \kappa_{21} & \kappa_{22} \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} u_{,1} \\ u_{,2} \end{bmatrix}
\]



Now \(\underline{q}\) is generally not parallel to \(-\nabla u\). Heat is steered toward the direction that conducts best (Figure F.4 c).
\(\kappa_{ij}\) is symmetric, \(\kappa_{12} = \kappa_{21}\), and positive definite: \(\kappa_{ij}v_iv_j > 0\) for every nonzero vector \(v_i\). The second property guarantees \(\underline{q}\cdot\nabla u = -\kappa_{ij}u_{,i}u_{,j} < 0\). Heat can be steered sideways, but it never flows uphill.
The isotropic case is \(\kappa_{ij} = \kappa\,\delta_{ij}\), and then \(\kappa_{ij}u_{,j} = \kappa\,u_{,i}\). The rest of this page uses it, while Class 4 and Hughes keep the general \(\kappa_{ij}\). Every statement still works for the anisotropic case if \(\kappa\nabla u\) is replaced by \(\underline{\underline{\kappa}}\nabla u\).

section: F.7 Where the differential equation comes from
text:
F.7 Where the differential equation comes from

F.7.1 Conservation of energy on a small rectangle






Figure F.5: A small rectangle of the slice, \(\Delta x_1\) wide and \(\Delta x_2\) tall (and one meter deep). At steady state, heat in through its four sides plus heat made inside equals heat out. Each side passes only the flux component normal to it: \(q_1\) through the left and right sides, \(q_2\) through the bottom and top.



Cut a small rectangle out of the slice (Figure F.5). At steady state its temperature is not changing, so every watt that enters or is made inside must leave. The fluxes are counted positive in the \(+x_1\) and \(+x_2\) directions, exactly as \(q\) was counted positive toward \(+x\) in the wall:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\underbrace{q_1(x_1, x_2)\,\Delta x_2 - q_1(x_1 + \Delta x_1, x_2)\,\Delta x_2}
_{\text{net in, left and right}} \\
&\quad+\;
\underbrace{q_2(x_1, x_2)\,\Delta x_1 - q_2(x_1, x_2 + \Delta x_2)\,\Delta x_1}
_{\text{net in, bottom and top}} \\
&\quad+\;
\underbrace{f\,\Delta x_1\,\Delta x_2}_{\text{made}}
\;=\; 0
\end{aligned}
\]

Divide by \(\Delta x_1\,\Delta x_2\) and let both shrink to zero. Each difference quotient becomes a partial derivative:

\[
-\frac{\partial q_1}{\partial x_1} - \frac{\partial q_2}{\partial x_2} + f = 0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-\nabla\cdot\underline{q} + f = 0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-q_{i,i} + f = 0
\]

The combination \(q_{1,1} + q_{2,2}\) is the divergence of \(\underline{q}\):

\[
\nabla\cdot\underline{q} \;=\; q_{i,i} \;=\;
\frac{\partial q_1}{\partial x_1} + \frac{\partial q_2}{\partial x_2}
\qquad [\text{W/m}^3]
\]


Each term of the balance is in watts per meter of depth: W/m² × m for the fluxes, and W/m³ × m² for the generation. Read the result as “at every point, the net rate at which heat flows away equals the rate at which it is made”: \(\nabla\cdot\underline{q} = f\), Hughes’ \(q_{i,i} = f\). The 1D balance \(q_{,x} = f\) is the same statement with one pair of faces instead of two.



F.7.2 The divergence theorem: the same balance for any region
Add up this balance over all the small rectangles that make up a region \(\omega\). On every internal side, what leaves one rectangle enters its neighbor, so those terms cancel in pairs. Only the flux through the outer boundary \(\partial\omega\) survives:

\[
\int_\omega \nabla\cdot\underline{q}\;d\Omega
= \int_{\partial\omega} \underline{q}\cdot\underline{n}\;d\Gamma
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\int_\omega q_{i,i}\;d\Omega = \int_{\partial\omega} q_i\,n_i\;d\Gamma
\]

This is the divergence theorem. Combined with \(\nabla\cdot\underline{q} = f\), it says that the heat leaving any region through its boundary equals the heat made inside it. The differential equation is the pointwise version of that statement. In 1D the region is an interval \([a, b]\), its boundary is the two end points, and the theorem is the fundamental theorem of calculus, with \(n(a) = -1\) and \(n(b) = +1\) doing the bookkeeping:

\[
\int_a^b q_{,x}\;dx \;=\; q(b) - q(a) \;=\; q(b)\,n(b) + q(a)\,n(a)
\]


The divergence theorem is also what turns the strong form into the weak form: it is how integration by parts works in more than one dimension (Class 4).

section: F.8 The Laplacian: divergence of the gradient
text:
F.8 The Laplacian: divergence of the gradient
Substituting Fourier’s law into the balance gives the differential equation of the strong form:

\[
\begin{aligned}
-\nabla\cdot\left(\kappa\nabla u\right) = f
\quad&\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-\left(\kappa\,u_{,i}\right)_{,i} = f \\
\xrightarrow{\;\kappa\text{ constant}\;}\quad
-\kappa\,\Delta u = f
\quad&\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-\kappa\,u_{,ii} = f \\
&\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-\kappa\left(\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x_1^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x_2^2}\right) = f \\
\xrightarrow{\;\kappa = 1\;}\quad
u_{,ii} + f = 0 \quad&\phantom{\Longleftrightarrow}\quad \text{(Hughes)}
\end{aligned}
\]

The operator \(\Delta u = \nabla\cdot\nabla u = u_{,ii}\) is the Laplacian, also written \(\nabla^2 u\). The notation \(\nabla\cdot\nabla u\) says what it does: take the gradient (a vector), then its divergence (back to a scalar). In 1D it is simply \(u_{,xx}\).

F.8.1 What the Laplacian says about the shape of \(u\)
In 1D, \(u_{,xx} = -f/\kappa\) fixed the curvature of the temperature profile at every point. In 2D the equation fixes only the sum of the two curvatures:

\[
u_{,11} + u_{,22} = -\frac{f}{\kappa}
\]

The temperature may bend down sharply in one direction and up in the other, as long as the sum comes out right. Figure F.6 shows the three basic shapes and, below each, the heat-flux field that goes with it.






Figure F.6: The three shapes a temperature can take near a point, with \(\kappa = 1\). Top: \(u\), with a ring of radius \(r\) around the center and, dashed, the ring’s average height. Bottom: the heat flux \(\underline{q} = -\nabla u\) and the same ring. A peak sheds heat through the ring (a source), a valley gathers it (a sink), and a saddle passes as much in as out, being neither a source nor a sink.





Peak (\(f > 0\)). Both curvatures are negative. Heat flows away from the top in every direction, so more leaves any small circle than enters it: \(\nabla\cdot\underline{q} > 0\), a source.
Valley (\(f < 0\)). Both curvatures are positive. Heat flows in from every direction: \(\nabla\cdot\underline{q} < 0\), a sink.
Saddle (\(f = 0\)). The curvatures cancel. Heat spreads out along \(x_1\) exactly as fast as it converges along \(x_2\), so as much enters any small circle as leaves it: \(\nabla\cdot\underline{q} = 0\). With no source, this is the only kind of point there is. The temperature cannot have a peak or a valley inside \(\Omega\), so its hottest and coldest points lie on the boundary (the maximum principle). With \(f > 0\), as in the cell, valleys are ruled out, so the coldest point is on the boundary — here, on the cooling plate.


The circles in Figure F.6 give a second reading of the Laplacian: it compares a point with its neighbors. Averaging \(u\) around a small circle of radius \(r\) centered at \(\underline{x}\) gives

\[
\bar u_r \;=\; u(\underline{x}) + \frac{r^2}{4}\,\Delta u(\underline{x}) + \cdots
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
u(\underline{x}) - \bar u_r \;\approx\; \frac{r^2}{4\kappa}\,f(\underline{x})
\]


so wherever heat is made, a point is hotter than the average of the ring around it, and where \(f = 0\) it is exactly that average. The same idea on a square grid with spacing \(s\) is the five-point stencil \(\tfrac14\left(u_E + u_W + u_N + u_S\right) - u_C \approx \tfrac{s^2}{4}\,\Delta u\) — the 2D version of \(\tfrac12\left(u(x - s) + u(x + s)\right) - u(x) \approx
\tfrac{s^2}{2}\,u_{,xx}\).

In the cell, \(-f/\kappa = -25{,}000/25 = -1000\) °C/m² everywhere. The two curvatures change from point to point, sometimes wildly, but their sum never does:

title: Appendix F — 2D Poisson I: Heat Flow in a Battery Cell
text:
F.9 The forcing function \(f\)
\(f(\underline{x})\) is the heat generated per unit volume, in W/m³. It is the only piece of data that acts in the interior of \(\Omega\) — \(g\) and \(h\) act only on the boundary — and in 2D it can vary in both directions. Integrated over the slice, it gives the heat made per meter of depth:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\int_\Omega f\;d\Omega \quad \left[\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^3}\cdot\text{m}^2
= \tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}}\right] \\[4pt]
&\text{e.g.}\quad 25{,}000 \times (0.10 \times 0.20) = 500\ \text{W/m} \\
&\text{and for one 27 mm cell,}\quad 500 \times 0.027 = 13.5\ \text{W}
\end{aligned}
\]







Figure F.7: Four forcing functions in the same cell, red where heat is made and blue where it is absorbed. The number above each panel is the heat made per meter of depth. Each panel has its own color scale; in (d) the peak is about a thousand times the background.





Uniform generation — current through the electrodes and electrolyte during a steady fast charge heats the whole cell nearly evenly. This is the \(f\) of the worked example.
Current crowding — all the current funnels through the thin current-collector foils toward the tabs, so resistive heating is concentrated near them.
Gentle charging — the electrochemical reaction itself can absorb heat (the “reversible” or entropic heat). At a low charging current this can outweigh the resistive heating, and \(f < 0\): the cell is a heat sink.
An internal short circuit — a defect lets current flow straight through a spot a few millimeters across. That spot alone makes as much heat as the whole cell normally does, and the temperature there spikes. This is how thermal runaway starts.
\(f = 0\) is a cell at rest.

title: Appendix F — 2D Poisson I: Heat Flow in a Battery Cell
text:
F.10 Boundary conditions
As in 1D, every point of the boundary gets exactly one condition: either its temperature is known, or the heat flux through it is known. Three things are new in 2D. The boundary is a curve, the data can vary along it, and the flux condition speaks to only one direction.

F.10.1 Dirichlet: \(u = g\) on \(\Gamma_g\) — the temperature is known






Figure F.8: The Dirichlet condition pins the value of \(u\) all along \(\Gamma_g\); the strip beside the cooled edge shows \(g\) in the same colors as the map. Black lines are heat-flux lines. (a) With \(g\) constant, the edge is an isotherm, so heat meets the plate at right angles. (b) If the coolant enters at the bottom and warms by 3 °C on its way up, \(g\) varies along the edge, the isotherms end on it, and heat arrives at an angle.





\(g\) is a temperature, in °C — but in 2D it is a function on \(\Gamma_g\), \(g : \Gamma_g \to \RR\), with one value for each point of the cooled edge. In 1D it was a single number at a single point.
The condition fixes the value of \(u\) along the edge: the temperature landscape is nailed to the curve \(g\) there. It says nothing about the heat flowing through the edge. How much heat the plate removes, and where, is an output of the problem — like a reaction force in statics.
When \(g\) is constant, the edge is an isotherm, so \(\nabla u\) is perpendicular to it and heat flows straight into the plate. When \(g\) varies, the isotherms end on the edge.
It is an essential boundary condition, imposed directly on \(u\). In the weak form it is built into the trial space \(\mathcal{S}\) rather than appearing in any integral.
Strictly, a thin layer of thermal interface material sits between cell and plate, and the heat through it is proportional to the temperature drop across it — a Robin condition. Letting that layer’s resistance go to zero gives the Dirichlet condition.




F.10.2 Neumann: \((\kappa\nabla u)\cdot\underline{n} = h\) on \(\Gamma_h\) — the heat flux is known
As in 1D, the Neumann condition is Fourier’s law evaluated on the boundary. The flux leaving through the boundary is \(\underline{q}\cdot\underline{n}\), since \(\underline{n}\) points outward, so the flux entering is \(-\underline{q}\cdot\underline{n}\). The Neumann condition fixes the flux entering:

\[
\begin{aligned}
h \;&=\; -\underline{q}\cdot\underline{n}
\;=\; -\left(-\kappa\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n}
\;=\; \left(\kappa\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} \\
\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
h \;&=\; -q_i\,n_i \;=\; \kappa\,u_{,i}\,n_i
\end{aligned}
\]

With a conductivity tensor it reads \(h = \kappa_{ij}u_{,j}n_i\). The dot product \(\nabla u\cdot\underline{n} = u_{,i}n_i\) is the slope of \(u\) in the outward direction, the normal derivative \(\partial u/\partial n\), so the condition says \(\kappa\,\partial u/\partial n = h\): the temperature’s outward slope is \(h/\kappa\). On each edge of the rectangle the normal picks out one component of the gradient:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{left } (x_1 = 0)\colon && \underline{n} = (-1, 0) && \Longrightarrow\quad -\kappa\,u_{,1} = h \\
&\text{right } (x_1 = W)\colon && \underline{n} = (1, 0) && \Longrightarrow\quad +\kappa\,u_{,1} = h \\
&\text{bottom } (x_2 = 0)\colon && \underline{n} = (0, -1) && \Longrightarrow\quad -\kappa\,u_{,2} = h \\
&\text{top } (x_2 = H)\colon && \underline{n} = (0, 1) && \Longrightarrow\quad +\kappa\,u_{,2} = h
\end{aligned}
\]

The left and right lines are the wall’s two conditions, \(-\kappa u_{,x}(0) = h\) and \(+\kappa u_{,x}(L) = h\), word for word.






Figure F.9: (a) The top 4.5 cm of the cell. At each marked boundary point, the red arrow is \(\nabla u\), split into its normal part (amber) and its tangential part (gray). The Neumann condition fixes only the normal part: 200 °C/m under each tab, zero between them. The tangential part is whatever the rest of the problem makes it. (b)–(d) An edge with the same tangential slope and three values of \(h\). The amber arrows are heat flux, and the gray lines are isotherms.





\(h\) is a heat flux in W/m², positive when heat flows in, on any edge, whichever way the edge faces — just as for the wall.
Only the normal part of \(\nabla u\) is fixed. The tangential part, the slope along the boundary, is left for the rest of the problem to decide. In 1D there is no “along the boundary”, so the Neumann condition fixed the whole derivative. In 2D it fixes one component of two.
\(h = 0\) is an insulated (adiabatic) boundary. \(\nabla u\) lies along the edge, so the isotherms meet it at right angles and heat slides along it without crossing. A plane of symmetry carries the same condition, and that is exactly why the large faces between identical cells could be dropped from the problem.
The size of the normal slope is \(|h|/\kappa\). Under the tabs, \(u_{,2} = 5000/25 = 200\) °C/m, which is 0.2 °C per millimeter, rising toward the tab.
It is a natural boundary condition. In the weak form it appears on its own, as the boundary integral \(\int_{\Gamma_h} w\,h\;d\Gamma\).
A surface cooled by air obeys \(h = h_c\,(u_\infty - u)\), which mixes the value and the slope. That is a Robin condition, and it is not part of Hughes’ model problem.



In numbers: at the middle of the near tab, \(\nabla u = (153,\ 200)\) °C/m; at the middle of the far tab, \((45,\ 200)\) °C/m; halfway between them, \((94,\ 0)\) °C/m. The second component is set by \(h\) in every case. The first is not: it is large near the cooling plate and small far from it, and no boundary condition on the top edge could have predicted it.



F.10.3 \(\Gamma_g\) and \(\Gamma_h\) partition the boundary
The two parts of the boundary must satisfy

\[
\Gamma = \overline{\Gamma_g \cup \Gamma_h}
\qquad\qquad
\Gamma_g \cap \Gamma_h = \emptyset
\]

Together \(\Gamma_g\) and \(\Gamma_h\) cover the whole boundary, and they do not overlap, so each point of \(\Gamma\) belongs to exactly one of them: they partition \(\Gamma\). The bar (the closure) only restores the handful of points where the two parts meet, such as the two corners of the cooled edge, and those have no length. The two requirements guard against two different failures, shown in Figure F.10.






Figure F.10: Four ways to assign conditions to the cell’s boundary: blue is \(\Gamma_g\), amber is \(\Gamma_h\) (violet on the tabs). Only (a) is a partition of \(\Gamma\) into a Dirichlet part and a Neumann part.





Covering, \(\overline{\Gamma_g \cup \Gamma_h} = \Gamma\): no gaps. On a stretch of boundary with no condition, the problem does not say what happens there: it could be insulated, or pressed against a hot plate. Infinitely many temperature fields then satisfy everything else. Remember that “insulated” is a condition, \(h = 0\), and not a missing one.
Disjoint, \(\Gamma_g \cap \Gamma_h = \emptyset\): no overlaps. Prescribing both the temperature and the flux on the same stretch asks too much. For arbitrary data no solution exists, and for the rare data that allow one, the solution is wildly sensitive to them.
\(\Gamma_g\) must not be empty. With only flux data, (i) \(u\) is determined at best up to an added constant, because flux data only ever see \(\nabla u\). And (ii) a steady solution exists only if the heat going in balances, which follows from the divergence theorem applied to all of \(\Omega\):



\[
\int_\Omega f\;d\Omega + \int_\Gamma h\;d\Gamma = 0
\]



For the cell, \(500 + 200 \ne 0\). Without the cooling plate there is no steady state: the cell heats up forever. This is the 2D version of the wall’s two-Neumann-faces case.
In 2D, \(\Gamma_g\) also needs length. Holding a single point at a fixed temperature is not enough, because a point has no length for heat to leave through. A point that absorbed a finite heat flow \(Q\) (W per meter of depth) would sit at the bottom of a logarithmic well, \(u \approx \frac{Q}{2\pi\kappa}\ln r\), which is infinitely deep.
The partition is point by point, not edge by edge. \(\Gamma_g\) could be the middle half of one edge, with \(\Gamma_h\) everywhere else. And different stretches of \(\Gamma_h\) may carry different \(h\): the tabs and the insulated edges are all part of \(\Gamma_h\).




F.10.4 Which edges get which condition
The model problem does not care which part of the boundary is \(\Gamma_g\), but the solution does. Here is the same cell, with the same \(f\) and the same tabs, under four partitions:






Figure F.11: One cell, one \(f\), the same tabs, four partitions of \(\Gamma\). Blue edges are \(\Gamma_g\) (held at 25 °C); everything else is \(\Gamma_h\). The isotherms are 2 °C apart, all four panels share one color scale, and a white dot marks the hottest point. In (d) the whole insulated side is equally hot.





(a) Side-cooled, the worked example: 36.6 °C at the hottest point, on the top edge under the far tab.
(b) Bottom-cooled. Same cell, same heat, but now it has to travel the 200 mm height instead of the 100 mm width, and the tabs are as far from the plate as they can be. The hottest point reaches 62.0 °C. The bulk temperature rise grows with the square of the conduction length, so doubling the length quadruples it. Where the cooling plate goes matters as much as how cold it is.
(c) Cooled on both sides. Each plate takes 350 W/m and the hottest point drops to 29.7 °C.
(d) Side-cooled with the tabs off. Nothing in the data depends on \(x_2\) any more, so neither does the solution. The isotherms are vertical, and the problem is the wall (next section). Hottest point: 30.0 °C, along the whole insulated side.

text:
F.11 How the 1D wall sits inside the 2D cell
Switch the tabs off, so that \(h = 0\) on all of \(\Gamma_h\). Now nothing in the problem — \(f\), \(g\), \(h\), or the shape of \(\Omega\) — changes with \(x_2\), so neither can \(u\): \(u = u(x_1)\) and \(u_{,2} = 0\) everywhere. Each line of the 2D strong form then collapses to a line of the 1D one:








2D, cell
with \(u_{,2} = 0\)
1D, wall




\(-\kappa\left(u_{,11} + u_{,22}\right) = f\) in \(\Omega\)
\(-\kappa\,u_{,11} = f\)
the differential equation


\(u(0, x_2) = g\)
\(u(0) = g\)
Dirichlet face at \(x = 0\)


\(+\kappa\,u_{,1}(W, x_2) = 0\)
\(+\kappa\,u_{,1}(W) = 0\)
Neumann face at \(x = L\), \(n = +1\), \(h = 0\)


\(\mp\kappa\,u_{,2} = 0\) on the bottom and top
\(0 = 0\)
nothing: satisfied automatically



This is arrangement (b) of the wall — temperature given at \(x = 0\), flux at \(x = L\) — with \(L = W\) and \(h = 0\), and its solution is the wall’s:

\[
\begin{aligned}
u(x_1) &= g + \frac{f}{\kappa}\left(W x_1 - \frac{x_1^2}{2}\right) \\
u_{\max} = u(W) &= g + \frac{f\,W^2}{2\kappa} = 25 + \frac{25{,}000 \times 0.01}{2 \times 25}
= 30\ {}^\circ\text{C}
\end{aligned}
\]







Figure F.12: Temperature across the cell at five heights (inset), with the tabs on, compared with the 1D wall solution (dashed). Near the bottom the 2D profile is the wall’s parabola, lifted by the little tab heat that reaches that far. Near the top the tabs take over and the problem is genuinely two-dimensional. The kinks in the top curve sit at the ends of the tabs, where \(h\) jumps.




With the tabs on, the 1D solution is still the right answer far from them. At \(x_2 = 0.02\) m the 2D profile is the 1D parabola lifted by 0.6 °C, the share of the tab heat that reaches that far down. Near the top, the tabs dominate. This is the general pattern: a 1D model is accurate where the data do not vary in the other direction, and fails near the features that make them vary. The wall on the first page was exactly such a model: one strip, far from the wall’s edges.

text:
F.12 The strong form, complete
Collecting the pieces, in both notations:

\[
(\mathrm{S}) \quad
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Given } f : \Omega \to \RR \;[\text{W/m}^3],\;\; \kappa > 0 \;[\text{W/(m·K)}], \\
&g : \Gamma_g \to \RR \;[{}^\circ\text{C}], \text{ and }
  h : \Gamma_h \to \RR \;[\text{W/m}^2], \\
&\text{where } \Gamma = \overline{\Gamma_g \cup \Gamma_h} \text{ and }
  \Gamma_g \cap \Gamma_h = \emptyset, \\
&\text{find } u : \bar\Omega \to \RR \;[{}^\circ\text{C}] \text{ such that} \\[4pt]
&\quad -\nabla\cdot\left(\kappa\nabla u\right) = f
  \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; -\left(\kappa\,u_{,i}\right)_{,i} = f
  && \text{in } \Omega \\
&\quad u = g && \text{on } \Gamma_g \\
&\quad \left(\kappa\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n} = h
  \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; \kappa\,u_{,i}\,n_i = h
  && \text{on } \Gamma_h
\end{aligned}
\]

The three lines are the energy balance with Fourier’s law substituted in, the known temperatures, and the known inflows.
For the cell, with \(\Omega = \,]0, W[\, \times \,]0, H[\), written out piece by piece:








Where
Condition





in \(\Omega\)
\(-\kappa\left(u_{,11} + u_{,22}\right) = f\)
the differential equation


\(x_1 = 0\)
\(u(0, x_2) = g\)
the cooling plate (\(\Gamma_g\))


\(x_1 = W\)
\(+\kappa\,u_{,1}(W, x_2) = 0\)
the insulated side


\(x_2 = 0\)
\(-\kappa\,u_{,2}(x_1, 0) = 0\)
the insulated bottom


\(x_2 = H\)
\(+\kappa\,u_{,2}(x_1, H) = h(x_1)\)
5000 W/m² on the tabs, 0 between and beside them





It is called the strong form because the differential equation must hold at every point of \(\Omega\), which demands that \(u\) have two derivatives everywhere. Our data already strain this. At the four ends of the tabs, \(h\) jumps from 0 to 5000 W/m², and there \(\nabla u\) is unbounded: it grows like \(\ln r\) as you approach the end of a tab. The growth is mild, but it has no limit. (Look for the kinks in the top curve of Figure F.12.) The weak form, which only integrates, does not mind.
Every figure on this page is a picture of one line of the strong form.








NoteThe exact solution, for the curious





Split the solution into a piece that carries \(f\) and a piece that carries the tab flux:
\[
\begin{aligned}
u(x_1, x_2) &= g + \frac{f}{\kappa}\left(W x_1 - \frac{x_1^2}{2}\right) \\
&\quad + \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \frac{h_m}{\kappa}\,
  \frac{\sin(\mu_m x_1)\,\cosh(\mu_m x_2)}{\mu_m \sinh(\mu_m H)}
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\mu_m = \frac{(m - \frac12)\pi}{W},
\qquad h_m = \frac{2}{W}\int_0^W h(x_1)\sin(\mu_m x_1)\,dx_1
\]
The first two terms are the wall’s solution: they satisfy the differential equation, the Dirichlet condition, and \(h = 0\) on the other three edges. Each term of the sum satisfies \(\Delta u = 0\) (the \(\sin\) curves one way and the \(\cosh\) the other, by equal amounts), vanishes on \(x_1 = 0\), has zero slope on \(x_1 = W\) and \(x_2 = 0\), and together they add up to \(\kappa u_{,2} = h(x_1)\) on the top edge. This is separation of variables. Most of the figures and numbers on this page come from this formula, summed to hundreds of terms. The bottom-cooled and two-sided cells of Figure F.11, and the explorer below, are computed numerically instead, because most problems have no such formula. That is the reason for the finite element method.

title: Appendix F — 2D Poisson I: Heat Flow in a Battery Cell
text:
F.13 Worked example
The cell of Figure F.1 during a fast charge: \(W\) = 0.10 m, \(H\) = 0.20 m, \(\kappa\) = 25 W/(m·K), \(f\) = 25,000 W/m³, and \(g\) = 25 °C on the cooled side. On the two tabs, \(x_1 \in [0.015, 0.035]\) m and \([0.065, 0.085]\) m, \(h\) = 5000 W/m², and \(h = 0\) on the rest of \(\Gamma_h\).






Figure F.13: The solution of the worked example. (a) The temperature, with heat-flux lines drawn thicker where more heat flows. All of them end on the cooling plate. (b) The heat crossing the cooled edge, per square meter of plate, at each height. The heat made inside the cell would leave uniformly (red). The tab heat leaves mostly near the top (violet), close to where it came in.



Every line of the strong form can be checked on the solution:


The differential equation. At every point, \(u_{,11} + u_{,22} = -f/\kappa =
-1000\) °C/m² (the table in the Laplacian section), even where the two curvatures individually swing between −6600 and +5600 °C/m². Equivalently, \(\nabla\cdot\underline{q} = f\): each small piece of the slice exports exactly the 25,000 W/m³ it makes.
The Dirichlet condition. \(u(0, x_2)\) lies between 25.00 and 25.00 °C all along the cooled edge — that is, \(u = g\). Since \(f > 0\), the coldest points of the cell must lie on the boundary, and here they are exactly this edge.
The Neumann conditions. At the middle of the far tab, \(\kappa\,u_{,2}(0.075, H) = 5000\) W/m² \(= h\). Halfway between the tabs, \(\kappa\,u_{,2}(0.05, H) = 0\) W/m². On the insulated side and bottom, \(|u_{,1}(W, x_2)|\) and \(|u_{,2}(x_1, 0)|\) never exceed \(10^{-12}\) °C/m, so the isotherms meet those edges at right angles.
The energy balance (per meter of depth). The cell makes 500 W/m and takes in 200 W/m through the tabs, and 700.0 W/m leaves through the cooling plate. For one 27 mm cell that is 18.9 W delivered to the coolant. The plate’s share is not uniform: 2726 W/m² at the bottom of the cooled edge, rising to 6362 W/m² at the top, where the tab heat arrives.
The hot spot. 36.6 °C, on the top edge under the far tab, at \(x_1 \approx 0.079\) m. That is 6.6 °C hotter than the same cell with the tabs off: the tabs, which bring in 29% of the heat, cause more than half of the worst-case temperature rise.

title: Appendix G — 2D Poisson II: The Battery Cell, by Galerkin’s Method
text:
G.1 The weak form
The strong-form page set up heat flow in a battery cell as the two-dimensional model problem. This page solves it approximately, step by step, the same way 1D Poisson II solved the wall:
The steps are the same as in 1D, and so are most of the formulas, with \(\int_0^L\) replaced by \(\int_\Omega\). Two things are genuinely new, and they get the most space here: the basis functions now live on two-dimensional elements, and each element is placed in the plane by an isoparametric map whose Jacobian is a matrix. The bookkeeping (ID, IEN, LM) is unchanged, but its effect on the global matrix looks very different, so this page draws it out in full, including which rows and columns the Dirichlet nodes cut out.
The running example is the side-cooled cell:
\(W\) = 0.10 m and \(H\) = 0.20 m. At the bottom of the page, an explorer lets you choose the elements, the mesh, and the Dirichlet nodes, and see every array update.
crumbs: Appendices
G  2D Poisson II: The Battery Cell, by Galerkin's Method

title: Appendix G — 2D Poisson II: The Battery Cell, by Galerkin’s Method
text:
G.1.1 Two collections of functions
As in 1D, the weak form looks for \(u\) among trial functions and tests it against weighting functions, which differ only on \(\Gamma_g\):

\[
\mathcal{S} = \left\{\, u \in H^1(\Omega) \;\middle|\; u = g \text{ on } \Gamma_g \,\right\}
\qquad\qquad
\mathcal{V} = \left\{\, w \in H^1(\Omega) \;\middle|\; w = 0 \text{ on } \Gamma_g \,\right\}
\]







Figure G.1: Left: a member of \(\mathcal{S}\). Any reasonable temperature field over the cell will do, as long as it equals 25 °C along the cooled edge (blue). The solution is one of them. Right: a member of \(\mathcal{V}\), the same kind of function, but zero along the cooled edge.





\(H^1(\Omega)\) asks that \(u\) and its gradient be square-integrable: \(\int_\Omega \left(u^2 + u_{,i}u_{,i}\right) d\Omega < \infty\). For the piecewise polynomials used below, that comes down to one requirement: they must be continuous across element edges. A crease along an edge is allowed, but a discontinuity is not.
As in 1D, the Dirichlet condition is built into \(\mathcal{S}\), and \(\mathcal{V}\) vanishes where \(\mathcal{S}\) is pinned.




G.1.2 Multiply, integrate, and integrate by parts
Multiply the differential equation by any \(w \in \mathcal{V}\) and integrate over the cross-section:

\[
\begin{aligned}
0 &= \int_\Omega w\left[\nabla\cdot\left(\kappa\nabla u\right) + f\right] d\Omega \\
\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0 &= \int_\Omega w\left[\left(\kappa\,u_{,i}\right)_{,i} + f\right] d\Omega
\qquad \text{for every } w \in \mathcal{V}
\end{aligned}
\]

In 1D, integration by parts moved a derivative from \(u\) to \(w\). In 2D the same move takes two steps: the product rule, then the divergence theorem from the strong-form page.

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{product rule:} &
\nabla\cdot\left(w\,\kappa\nabla u\right) &= \nabla w\cdot\kappa\nabla u
  + w\,\nabla\cdot\left(\kappa\nabla u\right) \\
& & \Longleftrightarrow\quad
\left(w\,\kappa\,u_{,i}\right)_{,i} &= w_{,i}\,\kappa\,u_{,i} + w\left(\kappa\,u_{,i}\right)_{,i} \\[6pt]
&\text{divergence theorem:} &
\int_\Omega \nabla\cdot\left(w\,\kappa\nabla u\right) d\Omega
  &= \int_\Gamma w\,\kappa\nabla u\cdot\underline{n}\;d\Gamma \\
& & \Longleftrightarrow\quad
\int_\Omega \left(w\,\kappa\,u_{,i}\right)_{,i} d\Omega &= \int_\Gamma w\,\kappa\,u_{,i}\,n_i\;d\Gamma
\end{aligned}
\]

Together they give

\[
\int_\Omega \nabla w\cdot\kappa\nabla u\;d\Omega
= \int_\Omega w\,f\;d\Omega
+ \int_{\Gamma_g} w\,\underbrace{\kappa\nabla u\cdot\underline{n}}_{\text{unknown}}\;d\Gamma
+ \int_{\Gamma_h} w\,\underbrace{\kappa\nabla u\cdot\underline{n}}_{=\;h}\;d\Gamma
\]







Figure G.2: The boundary term, one piece of \(\Gamma\) at a time. On \(\Gamma_h\) the flux is data: \(h\) on the tabs and zero on the insulated edges, which therefore drop out entirely. On \(\Gamma_g\) the flux is the heat delivered to the cooling plate, which is part of the answer; choosing \(w = 0\) on \(\Gamma_g\) is what removes it.



What remains is the weak form:

\[
(\mathrm{W}) \qquad
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Given } f,\ g,\ h,\ \kappa, \text{ find } u \in \mathcal{S}
  \text{ such that for all } w \in \mathcal{V}: \\[3pt]
&\qquad \underbrace{\int_\Omega \nabla w\cdot\kappa\nabla u\;d\Omega}_{a(w,\,u)}
= \underbrace{\int_\Omega w\,f\;d\Omega}_{(w,\,f)}
+ \underbrace{\int_{\Gamma_h} w\,h\;d\Gamma}_{(w,\,h)_\Gamma}
\end{aligned}
\]

or, in index notation and in Hughes’ compact form,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_\Omega w_{,i}\,\kappa\,u_{,i}\;d\Omega
&= \int_\Omega w\,f\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} w\,h\;d\Gamma \\
a(w, u) &= (w, f) + (w, h)_\Gamma \qquad \forall\, w \in \mathcal{V}
\end{aligned}
\]



The 1D weak form is the special case. With one coordinate, \(\int_\Omega\) becomes \(\int_0^L\), \(w_{,i}u_{,i}\) becomes \(w_{,x}u_{,x}\), and \(\int_{\Gamma_h} w\,h\,d\Gamma\) becomes the single term \(w(0)\,h\), because the boundary is a point.
Units. Each term is W per meter of depth, times the units of \(w\): a weighted heat balance for the slice.
The insulated edges are free. They carry a boundary condition, \(h = 0\), but it costs nothing: the natural condition is satisfied, in the weak sense, simply by not adding a term. For the cell, \((w, h)_\Gamma\) is an integral over the two tabs only.
Only first derivatives. The strong form needed \(u_{,11} + u_{,22}\) at every point, which failed at the tab ends. The weak form needs only \(\nabla u\) to be square-integrable, and the log-singular gradient there is.
crumbs: Appendices
G  2D Poisson II: The Battery Cell, by Galerkin's Method

title: Appendix G — 2D Poisson II: The Battery Cell, by Galerkin’s Method
text:
G.2 The Galerkin form
\((\mathrm{W})\) asks for a whole function. Galerkin’s method replaces \(\mathcal{S}\) and \(\mathcal{V}\) by finite-dimensional collections, \(\mathcal{S}^h\) and \(\mathcal{V}^h\), each spanned by a finite number of basis functions, so that finding \(u^h\) means finding a list of numbers.

G.2.1 Nodes, elements, and a mesh of the cell
Cut the cell into \(n_{el}\) quadrilateral elements, \(n_1\) across and \(n_2\) up. On each element, place a grid of \((p + 1) \times (p + 1)\) nodes: its four corners when \(p = 1\), and also its mid-sides and centre when \(p = 2\). Neighbouring elements share the nodes on their common edge, so the mesh has

\[
n_{np} = \left(p\,n_1 + 1\right)\left(p\,n_2 + 1\right) \quad \text{nodes},
\qquad
n_{en} = (p + 1)^2 \quad \text{nodes per element}
\]







Figure G.3: Meshes of the cell. Node numbers \(A\) run along \(x_1\) first, row by row, and element numbers \(e\) the same way. Filled nodes lie on \(\Gamma_g\), the cooled edge, where the temperature is known; the open nodes carry the unknowns. (c) Moving the interior nodes changes the shape of every element, and with nine nodes per element even the edges curve, but the connectivity, and so every array on this page, stays the same.





G.2.2 The Galerkin form, \((\mathrm{G})\)
Each node \(A\) gets a global basis function \(N_A\), built in the next section. Let \(\eta_g\) be the set of nodes on \(\Gamma_g\) and \(\eta - \eta_g\) the rest. Build the approximations from the basis:

\[
\begin{aligned}
w^h &= \sum_{A \in \eta - \eta_g} c_A\,N_A \;\in \mathcal{V}^h \\
u^h &= v^h + g^h,\qquad
v^h = \sum_{B \in \eta - \eta_g} d_B\,N_B \;\in \mathcal{V}^h,\qquad
g^h = \sum_{B \in \eta_g} g_B\,N_B
\end{aligned}
\]


\(g^h\) carries the Dirichlet data: \(g_B = g(\underline{x}_B)\) at each node on \(\Gamma_g\). Every \(N_A\) with \(A \notin \eta_g\) vanishes on \(\Gamma_g\), so \(w^h\) and \(v^h\) do too. Substituting into \((\mathrm{W})\) and moving the known \(g^h\) to the right gives


\[
(\mathrm{G}) \qquad
a(w^h, v^h) = (w^h, f) + (w^h, h)_\Gamma - a(w^h, g^h)
\qquad \forall\, w^h \in \mathcal{V}^h
\]



G.2.3 What the Galerkin step gives up, and what it keeps
\((\mathrm{S}) \Leftrightarrow (\mathrm{W})\) is exact: no information is lost. The approximation happens here, and only here, when \(\mathcal{S}\) and \(\mathcal{V}\) are replaced by \(\mathcal{S}^h\) and \(\mathcal{V}^h\). (Two smaller approximations come later: \(g^h\) matches \(g\) only at the nodes when \(g\) varies along the edge, and the element integrals are done by quadrature.)
What the Galerkin step keeps is a precise sense in which \(u^h\) is the best choice. \((\mathrm{W})\) holds for every \(w \in \mathcal{V}\), so in particular for every \(w^h \in \mathcal{V}^h\). Subtracting \((\mathrm{G})\) from it leaves

\[
a\left(w^h,\; u - u^h\right) = \int_\Omega \nabla w^h\cdot\kappa\nabla\left(u - u^h\right) d\Omega = 0
\qquad \forall\, w^h \in \mathcal{V}^h
\]


The error is orthogonal to every function the mesh can represent, measured with \(a(\cdot,\cdot)\) as the inner product. It follows (Figure G.4) that, among all the trial functions the mesh can build, \(u^h\) is the one closest to \(u\) in the energy norm:


\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left\| u - u^h \right\|_E \;\le\; \left\| u - v \right\|_E
\quad \text{for every } v \in \mathcal{S}^h, \\
&\text{where}\quad
\left\|v\right\|_E^2 = a(v, v) = \int_\Omega \kappa\,\nabla v\cdot\nabla v\;d\Omega
\end{aligned}
\]







Figure G.4: The Galerkin approximation as a projection. The exact \(u\) generally does not lie in \(\mathcal{S}^h\); \(u^h\) is its foot in \(\mathcal{S}^h\), with the error perpendicular to \(\mathcal{S}^h\) when angles are measured by \(a(\cdot,\cdot)\). A finer mesh or higher-degree elements enlarge \(\mathcal{S}^h\) and bring its closest point nearer to \(u\).





\(\|v\|_E^2 = \int_\Omega \kappa\,|\nabla v|^2\,d\Omega\) weighs the gradient, and for heat conduction it is the rate at which a temperature field \(v\) dissipates heat. So Galerkin’s \(u^h\) is the member of \(\mathcal{S}^h\) whose heat flow is closest to the true one, in that energy-weighted sense.
The quality of \(u^h\) is therefore settled entirely by how well \(\mathcal{S}^h\) can approximate \(u\). The rest of the method only has to find that best member. Choosing \(\mathcal{S}^h\) means choosing the basis functions, which is the next section.

text:
G.3 Basis functions in two dimensions

G.3.1 What the basis has to do
Galerkin’s method works with any basis, but four properties make the finite element basis the standard choice:


Conforming. \(\mathcal{S}^h\) must lie inside \(H^1(\Omega)\), so every \(N_A\) must be continuous across element edges.
Local. \(N_A\) is non-zero only on the few elements that touch node \(A\). Then \(a(N_A, N_B) = 0\) unless nodes \(A\) and \(B\) share an element, and \(\mathbf{K}\) is sparse.
Nodal. \(N_A(\underline{x}_B) = \delta_{AB}\), so the coefficient \(d_A\) is the temperature at node \(A\), and a Dirichlet value is imposed simply by fixing a nodal value.
Complete. The basis reproduces every constant and every linear field exactly: \(\sum_A N_A = 1\) and \(\sum_A \underline{x}_A N_A = \underline{x}\). That is what lets \(u^h\) approach any smooth \(u\) as the elements shrink.


All four come from one construction: build a few standard functions on a single parent element, then copy them onto every element of the mesh.


G.3.2 The parent square and the tensor product
The parent element is the square \(\hat\Omega = [-1, 1]^2\), with coordinates \((\xi, \eta)\), also written \(\xi_1 = \xi\) and \(\xi_2 = \eta\). Its shape functions are products of the 1D Lagrange functions from 1D Poisson II, one factor for each direction:

\[
N_a(\xi, \eta) = N_{i(a)}(\xi)\;N_{j(a)}(\eta),
\qquad\qquad
N_a(\xi_b, \eta_b) = \delta_{ab}
\]

For \(p = 1\), the 1D functions are \(\tfrac12(1 - \xi)\) and \(\tfrac12(1 + \xi)\), and the four products are the bilinear functions. Local nodes are numbered counter-clockwise from the lower-left corner, as in Class 10:










\(a\)
1
2
3
4




\((\xi_a, \eta_a)\)
\((-1, -1)\)
\((1, -1)\)
\((1, 1)\)
\((-1, 1)\)


\(N_a(\xi, \eta)\)
\(\tfrac14(1 - \xi)(1 - \eta)\)
\(\tfrac14(1 + \xi)(1 - \eta)\)
\(\tfrac14(1 + \xi)(1 + \eta)\)
\(\tfrac14(1 - \xi)(1 + \eta)\)



or, all at once, \(N_a = \tfrac14\left(1 + \xi_a\xi\right)\left(1 + \eta_a\eta\right)\).






Figure G.5: The four bilinear shape functions on the parent square. Each is one at its own node (black) and zero at the other three. The purple curves on the back walls are its two 1D factors: \(N_{i}(\xi)\) (solid) and \(N_{j}(\eta)\) (dashed). Along any line \(\xi\) = const or \(\eta\) = const the function is a straight line, but the surface itself is twisted, not flat.





Bilinear is not linear. \(N_3 = \tfrac14(1 + \xi + \eta + \xi\eta)\) contains the product \(\xi\eta\). Along any grid line it is linear, but along a diagonal it is quadratic, and the surface is a gently twisted saddle rather than a plane.
Partition of unity. At every point, \(N_1 + N_2 + N_3 + N_4 = 1\). A uniform temperature is represented exactly, which is why every row of \(\mathbf{k}^e\) will sum to zero.
Edges see only their own nodes. On the edge \(\eta = -1\), \(N_3 = N_4 = 0\), and \(N_1\) and \(N_2\) reduce to the 1D functions \(\tfrac12(1 \mp \xi)\). That single fact makes \(u^h\) continuous between elements, as shown below.
The gradient in the parent coordinates is \(\nabla_\xi N_a = \left(N_{a,\xi},\; N_{a,\eta}\right) =
\tfrac14\left(\xi_a(1 + \eta_a\eta),\; \eta_a(1 + \xi_a\xi)\right)\).




G.3.3 Biquadratic elements
For \(p = 2\) the 1D factors are the three quadratics \(\tfrac12\xi(\xi - 1)\), \(1 - \xi^2\), and \(\tfrac12\xi(\xi + 1)\), and their nine products need nine nodes: the corners, the mid-sides, and the centre. Hughes numbers the corners first, as for Q4, then the mid-sides counter-clockwise from the bottom, then the centre:






Figure G.6: The biquadratic element. Left: the nine local nodes, with the 1D indices \((i, j)\) of each product. Right: one function of each kind. A corner function dips below zero between the nodes (red); a mid-side function is a 1D quadratic bump times a 1D edge function; the centre function is the product of two bumps and vanishes on the whole boundary of the element.





The same four properties hold: \(N_a(\xi_b, \eta_b) = \delta_{ab}\), \(\sum_a N_a = 1\), and on each edge only the three nodes of that edge are non-zero, varying as the 1D quadratics.
Q9 reproduces every polynomial of degree 2 in \(\xi\) and \(\eta\) (and a few of degree 3 and 4), so on a mesh of rectangles it represents the tab-free solution of the cell, a quadratic in \(x_1\), exactly.
Dropping the centre node gives the 8-node serendipity element, which is not a tensor product. The tensor-product family used here extends to any degree \(p\) with \((p + 1)^2\) nodes.




G.3.4 From parent functions to global basis functions
Each element is a copy of the parent square (the next section says exactly how). Global node \(A\) is local node \(a\) of every element with \(\mathrm{IEN}(a, e) = A\), and on each of those elements the global function is the parent function carried over:

\[
N_A(\underline{x}) =
\begin{cases}
N_a\big(\xi(\underline{x})\big) & \text{on each element } e \text{ with } \mathrm{IEN}(a, e) = A \\[2pt]
0 & \text{on every other element}
\end{cases}
\]







Figure G.7: Global basis functions on the \(2 \times 4\) meshes of Figure G.3. Each is one at its own node (black dot), zero at every other node, and zero outside the elements that contain its node. The bilinear one is a four-sided “tent”. The biquadratic ones come in three kinds, according to where the node sits in its elements.





Why \(u^h\) is continuous. Two neighbouring elements share an edge and the nodes on it. Along that edge, only the functions of those nodes are non-zero, and from either side each one is the same 1D Lagrange function of position along the edge. So \(u^h\) takes the same values from both sides: it is continuous, with a crease (a jump in slope) allowed across the edge. That is exactly what \(H^1\) needs.
Why \(\mathbf{K}\) is sparse. The tent of node 8 overlaps only the tents of its eight neighbours. So row 8 of \(\mathbf{K}\) has at most nine non-zeros, however large the mesh. A Q9 corner-type node overlaps 25 functions; a centre node overlaps only the nine of its element.


Adding up the scaled tents gives the approximation:

\[
u^h(\underline{x}) = \sum_{A \in \eta - \eta_g} d_A\,N_A(\underline{x})
+ \sum_{A \in \eta_g} g_A\,N_A(\underline{x})
\]







Figure G.8: The Galerkin solution built from the tents, on the two meshes of Figure G.3, next to the exact temperature. The dots are the nodal values: unknowns \(d_A\), and \(g\) = 25 °C along the cooled edge. The bilinear surface is made of twisted flat-ish panels that meet along creases. The biquadratic one bends inside each element and is already hard to tell from the exact solution, except near the tabs.

text:
G.4 The isoparametric map

G.4.1 Placing an element in the plane
To carry the parent functions onto a physical element, the element itself is described with the same functions: its nodes’ coordinates are interpolated exactly the way temperatures are.

\[
\underline{x}(\xi, \eta) = \sum_{a=1}^{n_{en}} N_a(\xi, \eta)\;\underline{x}^e_a
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x_i(\xi, \eta) = \sum_{a=1}^{n_{en}} N_a(\xi, \eta)\;x^e_{ia}
\]

That is what iso-parametric means: geometry and solution use the same parameters. For a rectangle aligned with the axes, this is just a stretch; for any other element, it is a genuine change of coordinates.






Figure G.9: The isoparametric map \(\underline{x}(\xi, \eta) = \sum_a N_a(\xi, \eta)\,\underline{x}^e_a\) takes the parent square’s grid, nodes, and Gauss points onto the physical element. With bilinear functions the grid lines stay straight; with biquadratic ones, the mid-side nodes bend them. At one point, the black arrows are the images of the parent’s unit directions, the two columns of \(DF\), and the small orange square becomes the orange patch.





G.4.2 The Jacobian matrix and its determinant
How lengths and areas change under the map is recorded by its derivative, the Jacobian matrix (the deformation gradient of Class 9):

\[
\begin{aligned}
DF = \frac{\partial \underline{x}}{\partial \underline{\xi}}
&= \begin{bmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial \xi} & \dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial \eta} \\[8pt]
\dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial \xi} & \dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial \eta}
\end{bmatrix}
= \sum_{a=1}^{n_{en}} \underline{x}^e_a \left(\nabla_\xi N_a\right)^T \\[4pt]
\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial \xi_j} &= \sum_{a=1}^{n_{en}} x^e_{ia}\,\frac{\partial N_a}{\partial \xi_j},
\qquad\qquad
J = \det DF
\end{aligned}
\]



The columns of \(DF\) are tangent vectors. Column 1, \(\partial\underline{x}/\partial\xi\), points along the image of a \(\xi\) grid line, and column 2 along the image of an \(\eta\) grid line (1).
\(J\) is the area stretch. The tiny square \(d\xi\,d\eta\) becomes a parallelogram spanned by the two columns, with area \(J\,d\xi\,d\eta\). So \(d\Omega = J\,d\xi\,d\eta\), and every element integral can be done on the parent square: \(\int_{\Omega^e} (\cdot)\,d\Omega = \int_{-1}^{1}\!\int_{-1}^{1} (\cdot)\,J\,d\xi\,d\eta\).
For an axis-aligned \(h_1 \times h_2\) rectangle the map is a pure stretch: \(DF = \mathrm{diag}\!\left(h_1/2,\; h_2/2\right)\) and \(J = h_1 h_2 / 4\), one quarter of the element’s area, because the parent square has area 4. That is the 2D version of \(x_{,\xi} = h^e/2\).
\(J\) must stay positive. \(J > 0\) everywhere means the map is one-to-one and keeps the node ordering counter-clockwise. A badly shaped element folds over itself, and \(J\) changes sign (Figure G.10).








Figure G.10: Three bilinear elements coloured by \(J(\xi, \eta)\), blue where positive and red where negative, with the images of the parent grid lines. The folded element’s map is not one-to-one: part of the parent square lands on top of another part, and an element integral over it would count some area negatively. Meshing codes check for \(J > 0\) at the quadrature points before anything is assembled.





G.4.3 Derivatives: the chain rule
The weak form needs \(\nabla_{\!x} N_a\), derivatives with respect to the physical coordinates, but \(N_a\) is a known function of \((\xi, \eta)\). The chain rule connects the two:

\[
\frac{\partial N_a}{\partial x_i}
= \frac{\partial N_a}{\partial \xi_j}\,\frac{\partial \xi_j}{\partial x_i}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\nabla_{\!x} N_a = DF^{-T}\,\nabla_{\!\xi} N_a
\] \[
DF^{-1} = \frac{1}{J}\begin{bmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial \eta} & -\dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial \eta} \\[8pt]
-\dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial \xi} & \dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial \xi}
\end{bmatrix}
\]


\(\partial\xi_j/\partial x_i\) is the matrix \(DF^{-1}\), by the inverse function theorem, so the inverse map \(\underline{\xi}(\underline{x})\) is never needed. Everything is evaluated forward from \((\xi, \eta)\), at the quadrature points. For an axis-aligned rectangle the rule reduces to \(\nabla_{\!x} N_a = \left(\tfrac{2}{h_1}N_{a,\xi},\; \tfrac{2}{h_2}N_{a,\eta}\right)\), the 2D version of \(N_{a,x} = \tfrac{2}{h^e}N_{a,\xi}\).







Figure G.11: The chain rule, seen. Left: \(N_3\) on the parent square, with its contour lines and its gradient at nine points. Right: the same function carried onto the Q4 element of 1, with \(\nabla_{\!x} N_3\) at the images of the same nine points. The arrows are not just the left-hand arrows rescaled: \(DF^{-T}\) turns them so that they stay perpendicular to the new contour lines, which is what a gradient must do.









NoteOne point, worked by hand





Take the Q4 element of 1, with corners \(\underline{x}^e_1, \dots,
\underline{x}^e_4\) = \((0, 0)\), \((5, 0.8)\), \((5.8, 4.6)\), \((0.6, 3.8)\), and the point \((\xi, \eta) = (0.35,\ -0.25)\).
\[
DF = \sum_a \underline{x}^e_a\left(\nabla_\xi N_a\right)^T = \begin{bmatrix}2.538 & 0.3675 \\ 0.4 & 1.9\end{bmatrix},
\qquad J = \det DF = 4.674
\]
For \(N_3 = \tfrac14(1 + \xi)(1 + \eta)\):
\[
\nabla_\xi N_3 = \tfrac14\begin{bmatrix} 1 + \eta \\ 1 + \xi \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0.1875 \\ 0.3375\end{bmatrix}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\nabla_x N_3 = DF^{-T}\,\nabla_\xi N_3 = \begin{bmatrix}0.0473 \\ 0.1685\end{bmatrix}
\]
Check: \(\nabla_x N_3 \cdot \partial\underline{x}/\partial\xi = 0.1875 = N_{3,\xi}\) and \(\nabla_x N_3 \cdot \partial\underline{x}/\partial\eta = 0.3375 = N_{3,\eta}\). Moving along a mapped grid line, \(N_3\) changes at exactly the rate it changes along the parent grid line.

text:
G.5 From \((\mathrm{G})\) to \(\mathbf{K}\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{F}\)
The algebra is exactly the 1D algebra. Put the expansions into \((\mathrm{G})\) and pull the sums and coefficients out of the (bi)linear forms:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{A \in \eta - \eta_g} c_A \Bigg[\; &\sum_{B \in \eta - \eta_g} a(N_A, N_B)\,d_B \\
&- (N_A, f) - (N_A, h)_\Gamma + \sum_{B \in \eta_g} a(N_A, N_B)\,g_B \Bigg] = 0
\end{aligned}
\]


The \(c_A\) are arbitrary, so each bracket vanishes: one equation for each node not on \(\Gamma_g\). Number those equations with the ID array, \(P = \mathrm{ID}(A)\) and \(Q = \mathrm{ID}(B)\):


\[
\boxed{\;\mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{F}\;}
\qquad
K_{PQ} = \int_\Omega \nabla N_A\cdot\kappa\nabla N_B\;d\Omega = \int_\Omega N_{A,i}\,\kappa\,N_{B,i}\;d\Omega
\] \[
F_P = \int_\Omega N_A\,f\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} N_A\,h\;d\Gamma
- \sum_{B \in \eta_g} \left(\int_\Omega N_{A,i}\,\kappa\,N_{B,i}\;d\Omega\right) g_B
\]



Units, per meter of depth: \(\mathbf{K}\) in W/(m·K), \(\mathbf{d}\) in °C, and \(\mathbf{F}\) in W/m. Each equation is a heat balance for the patch of elements around one node.
Symmetric, because \(a(N_A, N_B) = a(N_B, N_A)\).
Sparse. \(K_{PQ} = 0\) unless nodes \(A\) and \(B\) share an element (Figure G.7). A row has at most 9 non-zeros for Q4, and at most 25 for Q9.
Positive definite, as long as \(\Gamma_g\) has some length: then the only \(\mathbf{d}\) with \(\mathbf{d}^T\mathbf{K}\mathbf{d} = a(v^h, v^h) = 0\) is zero. With every edge Neumann, a uniform temperature would give zero, and \(\mathbf{K}\) would be singular, which is the strong form’s “up to a constant” again.
Banded, but the band is up to you. In 1D, \(\mathbf{K}\) came out tridiagonal (for \(p = 1\)) automatically. In 2D, how far the non-zeros sit from the diagonal depends on how the nodes are numbered (Figure G.15).

section: G.6 The element point of view
text:
G.6 The element point of view

G.6.1 Element arrays
Every integral over \(\Omega\) is a sum over elements, and on element \(e\) only its own \(n_{en}\) functions are non-zero. So the work reduces to the small element arrays, in local numbering \(a, b = 1, \dots, n_{en}\):

\[
k^e_{ab} = \int_{\Omega^e} \nabla N_a\cdot\kappa\nabla N_b\;d\Omega
\] \[
f^e_a = \underbrace{\int_{\Omega^e} N_a\,f\;d\Omega}_{\text{body}}
+ \underbrace{\int_{\Gamma^e_h} N_a\,h\;d\Gamma}_{\text{element sides on } \Gamma_h}
- \underbrace{\sum_{b=1}^{n_{en}} k^e_{ab}\,g^e_b}_{\text{Dirichlet nodes}}
\]

where \(g^e_b\) is the prescribed temperature if local node \(b\) is on \(\Gamma_g\), and zero otherwise.


G.6.2 On the parent square, by quadrature
With \(d\Omega = J\,d\xi\,d\eta\) and the chain rule, both area integrals move to the parent square, where a tensor-product Gauss rule evaluates them. The rule’s points are all pairs \((\tilde\xi_i, \tilde\eta_j)\) of 1D Gauss points, and its weights are the products \(W_l = w_i w_j\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
k^e_{ab} &= \int_{-1}^{1}\!\!\int_{-1}^{1}
\left(DF^{-T}\nabla_{\!\xi}N_a\right)\cdot\kappa\left(DF^{-T}\nabla_{\!\xi}N_b\right) J\;d\xi\,d\eta \\
&\approx \sum_{l=1}^{n_{int}}
\left[\left(DF^{-T}\nabla_{\!\xi}N_a\right)\cdot\kappa\left(DF^{-T}\nabla_{\!\xi}N_b\right) J\right]_{\tilde{\underline{\xi}}_l} W_l
\end{aligned}
\] \[
f^e_{a,\text{body}} \;\approx\; \sum_{l=1}^{n_{int}} N_a(\tilde{\underline{\xi}}_l)\,
f\big(\underline{x}(\tilde{\underline{\xi}}_l)\big)\,J(\tilde{\underline{\xi}}_l)\,W_l
\]



\(n_{int} = 2 \times 2\) points for Q4 and \(3 \times 3\) for Q9, the crosses in

On rectangles with constant \(\kappa\), these rules are exact.

On distorted elements, \(DF^{-1}\) turns the stiffness integrand into a rational function, and quadrature becomes one of the small approximations mentioned earlier. It is a good one: the error it adds shrinks as fast as the discretization error.


The whole computation of \(\mathbf{k}^e\) is one loop, over each of the elements.



G.6.3 The Neumann term: an integral along element sides
\(\int_{\Gamma^e_h} N_a\,h\,d\Gamma\) is needed only for element sides that lie on \(\Gamma_h\), and only where \(h \ne 0\): for the cell, the top sides of the top row of elements. Along such a side, the parent coordinate that runs along it plays the role of \(\xi\) in 1D, and the length stretch is the size of the corresponding column of \(DF\). On the top side, \(\eta = 1\):

\[
\int_{\Gamma^e_h} N_a\,h\;d\Gamma
= \int_{-1}^{1} N_a(\xi, 1)\;h\big(\underline{x}(\xi, 1)\big)\;
\left\|\frac{\partial\underline{x}}{\partial\xi}(\xi, 1)\right\| d\xi
\]


Only the \(p + 1\) nodes on that side get anything, because every other \(N_a\) vanishes on it. For a straight side with evenly spaced nodes, \(\|\partial\underline{x}/\partial\xi\|\) is half the side’s length: the 1D Jacobian \(h^e/2\) again. Because \(h\) jumps at the tab ends, the integral is split there, so that no Gauss rule straddles a jump.







Figure G.12: The Neumann term for the worked example’s top edge. Each tab lies inside one element side, exactly in its middle, so its 5000 W/m² × 0.02 m = 100 W/m is split evenly between the two nodes of that side. Node 14 collects 50 W/m from each tab. The total, 200 W/m, is exactly the heat the tabs bring in.





G.6.4 Closed forms for a rectangle
For an \(h_1 \times h_2\) rectangle with constant \(\kappa\) and \(f\), the Q4 arrays come out in closed form:

\[
\mathbf{k}^e = \frac{\kappa}{6}\left(\frac{h_2}{h_1}\begin{bmatrix}
2 & -2 & -1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 & 2
\end{bmatrix}
+ \frac{h_1}{h_2}\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 & -1 \\ -1 & -2 & 2 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & 1 & 2
\end{bmatrix}\right)
\] \[
\text{a square, } h_1 = h_2: \qquad
\mathbf{k}^e = \frac{\kappa}{6}\begin{bmatrix}
4 & -1 & -2 & -1 \\ -1 & 4 & -1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1 & 4 & -1 \\ -1 & -2 & -1 & 4
\end{bmatrix}
\] \[
\text{Q4:}\quad \mathbf{f}^e_{\text{body}} = \frac{f\,A^e}{4}\begin{Bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \end{Bmatrix}^T
\] \[
\text{Q9:}\quad \mathbf{f}^e_{\text{body}} = \frac{f\,A^e}{36}
\begin{Bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 4 & 4 & 4 & 4 & 16 \end{Bmatrix}^T
\]



No element size appears in the square element’s \(\mathbf{k}^e\), only \(\kappa\). In 1D, \(k^e \propto \kappa/h^e\): the gradient scales like \(1/h\), so the product of two gradients scales like \(1/h^2\), and the element’s length gives back one power of \(h\). In 2D its area gives back \(h^2\), so only the shape, \(h_2/h_1\), matters.
Rows sum to zero, because a uniform temperature carries no heat.
Node 1 is coupled most strongly to the opposite corner, node 3 (\(-2\)), not to its edge neighbours (\(-1\)). Heat between two nodes flows through the element’s interior, and the diagonal pair shares it all.
The body load is not split evenly for Q9. Corners get 1/36 of the element’s heat, mid-sides 4/36, and the centre 16/36: the products of Simpson’s weights 1, 4, 1. (For the 8-node serendipity element the corner shares are even negative, \(-1/12\). A consistent load does not have to look intuitive.)
